## 1. A test is a function that does not panic

A Rust test is an ordinary function marked with the `#[test]` attribute. `cargo test` builds a test program, calls every such function, and reports each one. A test passes if it returns without panicking and fails if it panics. That is the whole model: every check inside a test is "panic if this is wrong".

The standard library gives you three assertion macros:

MacroPanics whenReport on failure

`assert!(cond)``cond` is falsethe expression text

`assert_eq!(left, right)`the two are not equal (`==`)both values, printed with `Debug`

`assert_ne!(left, right)`the two are equalboth values

Any extra arguments become a custom message, written like `format!`: `assert!(err.contains("no comma"), "unexpected error: {err}")`. The values compared with `assert_eq!` must implement `PartialEq` and `Debug`.

Change `Some(2.0)` to `Some(3.0)` in the `mean_of_two` test of the `stats` package and run it:

```
tests::mean_of_two --- FAILED
---- tests::mean_of_two stdout ----
thread 'tests::mean_of_two' panicked at src/lib.rs:54:9:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: Some(2.0)
 right: Some(3.0)
test result: FAILED. 6 passed; 1 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 11 "Writing Automated Tests", and Rust by Example, "Testing" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

## 2. Testing failure paths

Some functions are supposed to panic on bad input. Mark such a test `#[should_panic]`: it then passes only if the function panics.

```
#[test]
#[should_panic(expected = "at most 100")]
fn fraction_rejects_big_scores() {
    to_fraction(101);
}
```

`expected = "..."` makes the test stricter: the panic message must contain that text (a substring match, not the whole message). Without `expected`, any panic counts, including one from a completely different line, such as an index out of bounds further down. A plain `#[should_panic]` test can therefore pass for the wrong reason.

Prefer `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]`. Pick text that only the panic you mean would produce.

A test can also return `Result<(), E>`. Then `?` works inside it, and returning `Err` fails the test. This is handy when the code under test returns `Result` (13):

```
#[test]
fn parse_pair_ok() -> Result<(), String> {
    let (a, b) = parse_pair("3, 4")?;
    assert_eq!(a + b, 7);
    Ok(())
}
```

A test marked `#[ignore]` (optionally `#[ignore = "reason"]`) is compiled but skipped unless you ask for it with `cargo test -- --ignored`. Use it for slow tests.

## 3. Unit tests: `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`

By convention unit tests sit at the bottom of the file they test, in a module:

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*; // bring the parent module's items, private ones too

    #[test]
    fn private_sum_works() {
        assert_eq!(sum(&[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), 6.0);
    }
}
```

Two things make this work:

- `#[cfg(test)]` is conditional compilation: the item exists only when the crate is compiled for `cargo test`. A normal `cargo build` leaves the whole module out, so tests cost nothing in the real program. Any item can carry `#[cfg(test)]`, not just a module.

- `tests` is a child module, and a child module can see its parent's private items (07). So `use super::*;` brings in `sum` even though `sum` is not `pub`.

## 4. Integration tests: the `tests/` directory

Files in a `tests/` directory next to `src/` are integration tests. Cargo compiles each file as a separate crate that depends on your library, exactly as another project would. Consequences:

- They see only the public API, and call it by the crate name: `stats::to_fraction`. Private functions are out of reach.

- The library they link is built the normal way, without `cfg(test)`. Anything marked `#[cfg(test)]` in `src/` does not exist for them, even if it is `pub`.

- No `#[cfg(test)]` is needed inside `tests/` files: cargo only builds them for testing.

Shared helpers for several test files go in `tests/common/mod.rs`, and each test file says `mod common;`. Why not `tests/common.rs`? Every `.rs` file directly in `tests/` becomes its own test crate, so `common.rs` would show up in the output as a test binary with 0 tests. Files in subdirectories are not treated that way.

```
// tests/public_api.rs
mod common;

#[test]
fn fractions_of_shared_scores() {
    let fractions: Vec<f64> = common::scores().into_iter().map(stats::to_fraction).collect();
    assert_eq!(fractions, vec![0.0, 0.5, 1.0]);
}
```

Try calling the private `stats::sum` from this file: the compiler answers `error[E0603]: function `sum` is private`. Calling a `#[cfg(test)] pub` item gives `error[E0425]: cannot find function` with a note that the item "was configured out".

## 5. Doc tests

Code blocks in `///` documentation comments are tests too. `cargo test` asks rustdoc to compile and run each example:

```
/// Returns the mean of `values`, or `None` when the slice is empty.
///
/// ```
/// assert_eq!(stats::mean(&[2.0, 4.0]), Some(3.0));
/// assert_eq!(stats::mean(&[]), None);
/// ```
pub fn mean(values: &[f64]) -> Option<f64> { /* ... */ }
```

Each example is compiled like a small separate program that uses your library from outside. So it calls `stats::mean`, not `mean`, and it sees only public items. The point of doc tests is that documentation stays true: users copy examples, so an example that no longer matches the code is a real bug, and the doc test catches it.

Doc-test results appear in their own section, named after the file and line of the example:

```
   Doc-tests stats
running 1 test
test src/lib.rs - mean (line 16) ... ok
```

## 6. Keep logic in a library

A package with only `src/main.rs` is a binary crate and has no library. Integration tests and doc tests both work by linking to the library, so in such a package they have nothing to call: a file in `tests/` cannot even name the crate (`error[E0433]`). Binaries can still have unit tests inside `main.rs`.

The usual structure, which the Book recommends and 16 builds on: put the logic in `src/lib.rs`, and keep `src/main.rs` a thin shell that reads input, calls the library and prints. Then every part of the logic can be tested from all three kinds of test.

## 7. What `cargo test` runs

The three kinds of test binary: where the tests live, whether `cfg(test)` is on, what they can see, and how to select them.

For a package with a library, `cargo test` builds and runs, in this order:

- the unit-test binary: the library compiled with `cfg(test)`, containing every `#[test]` in `src/`;

- one binary per file in `tests/`;

- the doc tests.

Here is the real output for the `stats` package (the run command uses `-q`, which prints one character per test: `.` passed, `i` ignored, `F` failed):

```
$ cargo test --offline -q
running 8 tests
i.......
test result: ok. 7 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
running 2 tests
..
test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
running 1 test
.
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

Two facts about running that matter in practice:

- Tests inside one binary run in parallel, on several threads (by default one per CPU core). There is no guaranteed order. Tests that share anything outside their own variables (a file with a fixed name, an environment variable, a global) can interfere with each other, and which one fails can change from run to run.

- Output is captured. `println!` output of a passing test is hidden; for a failing test it is shown under "stdout". Use `-- --show-output` to see it for passing tests too.

If one test binary fails, cargo stops and does not run the later binaries (add `--no-fail-fast` to run them all).

## 8. Choosing what runs

Arguments before `--` go to cargo; arguments after `--` go to every test binary.

CommandRunsOn `stats`

`cargo test`unit, every `tests/` file, doc tests7 passed 1 ignored, 2 passed, 1 passed

`cargo test --lib`unit tests only7 passed, 1 ignored

`cargo test --test public_api`that one `tests/` file only2 passed

`cargo test --doc`doc tests only1 passed

`cargo test mean`tests whose full name contains `mean`, in every binaryunit: 2 passed, 1 ignored, 5 filtered out; public_api: 1 passed, 1 filtered out

`cargo test --lib -- --exact tests::mean_of_two`the test whose full name is exactly that1 passed, 7 filtered out

`cargo test --lib -- --ignored`only the ignored tests1 passed, 7 filtered out

`cargo test -- --test-threads=1`everything, one test at a time

`--lib`, `--test name` and `--doc` each skip the other kinds. A local run with `--lib` never builds the doc tests, so a broken example passes locally and fails in a CI job that runs plain `cargo test`.

A filter is a substring match on the test's path (`tests::mean_of_two`), so `cargo test total` also runs `total_empty` and `subtotal`. Add `-- --exact` to match the whole name.

## 9. Tests that catch bugs

A test suite is only as good as the bugs it would catch. A single happy-path test proves that one path works, nothing more. Write tests from the function's promises (its doc comment) and its edges:

EdgeExamples

sizeempty input, one item, two items, odd and even counts

orderunsorted input, already sorted, reversed, equal values

sign and rangezero, negative numbers, `i32::MAX` and `i32::MIN` (overflow)

textempty string, spaces, upper and lower case, punctuation, non-ASCII characters

error pathseach documented error, checked for the right error, not just "some error"

side effectsis the caller's data unchanged when the function promises it is?

A good habit: before trusting a test, imagine a plausible wrong version of the function (off by one, wrong order, overflow, a missing check) and ask "would this test fail?". If not, the test is missing a case.

Remember that debug builds panic on integer overflow (01) and `cargo test` builds in debug mode. A test with `i32::MAX` makes an overflow visible as a panic instead of a silently wrong number.

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why can a unit test call a private function when an integration test cannot?

- What could make a `#[should_panic]` test pass even though the code is wrong?

- Which kinds of test does `cargo test --lib` skip, and why could that matter in CI?

- Why is the shared helper in `tests/common/mod.rs` and not `tests/common.rs`?

- Two tests in the same file both write to the same temporary file. What can go wrong?

Sources: The Rust Programming Language, ch. 11.1-11.3; Rust by Example, "Unit testing", "Documentation testing" and "Integration testing" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

[entity 963 · cargo-test-map.png · diagram]
Diagram: what `cargo test` builds and runs, as three columns.

1. Unit tests: live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in src/lib.rs (and its modules). cfg(test) is ON. They see everything, private items too (`use super::*;`). One binary. Select with `cargo test --lib`.
2. Integration tests: live in tests/*.rs, with helpers in tests/common/mod.rs. cfg(test) is OFF for the library. They see the public API only (`stats::mean`; each file is a separate crate). One binary per file in tests/. Select with `cargo test --test public_api`.
3. Doc tests: code blocks in `///` comments. cfg(test) is OFF for the library. They see the public API only (`stats::mean`, not `mean`). Built by rustdoc. Select with `cargo test --doc`. They need a library: not run for src/main.rs.

Below: `cargo test <filter> -- <flags>`. An arrow from <filter>: cargo keeps tests whose name CONTAINS it. An arrow from <flags>: passed to every test binary: `--exact`, `--ignored`, `--show-output`, `--test-threads=N`.

/// Letter grade for a 0-100 score: 90 and up 'A', 80 and up 'B',
/// 70 and up 'C', anything lower 'F'.
/// Panics with "score must be at most 100, got <n>" above 100.
pub fn grade(score: u32) -> char {
    assert!(score <= 100, "score must be at most 100, got {score}");
    match score {
        90.. => 'A',
        80.. => 'B',
        70.. => 'C',
        _ => 'F',
    }
}

/// Parses "name:score" (spaces around either part are ignored).
/// Errors: "no ':' in <text>", "empty name", "bad score: <parse error>".
pub fn parse_entry(text: &str) -> Result<(String, u32), String> {
    let (name, score) = text.split_once(':').ok_or(format!("no ':' in {text:?}"))?;
    let name = name.trim();
    if name.is_empty() {
        return Err(String::from("empty name"));
    }
    let score = score.trim().parse::<u32>().map_err(|e| format!("bad score: {e}"))?;
    Ok((name.to_string(), score))
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn grades_at_the_boundaries() {
        assert_eq!(grade(100), 'A');
        assert_eq!(grade(90), 'A');
        assert_eq!(grade(89), 'B');
        assert_eq!(grade(80), 'B');
        assert_eq!(grade(70), 'C');
        assert_eq!(grade(69), 'F');
        assert_eq!(grade(0), 'F');
    }

    #[test]
    #[should_panic(expected = "at most 100")]
    fn grade_rejects_scores_above_100() {
        grade(101);
    }

    // Returns Result: an Err fails the test, and ? works inside.
    #[test]
    fn parse_entry_ok() -> Result<(), String> {
        let (name, score) = parse_entry(" ada : 93 ")?;
        assert_eq!(name, "ada");
        assert_eq!(score, 93);
        Ok(())
    }

    #[test]
    fn parse_entry_errors() {
        let err = parse_entry("ada 93").unwrap_err();
        assert!(err.contains("no ':'"), "unexpected error: {err}");
        let err = parse_entry("ada:lots").unwrap_err();
        assert!(err.contains("bad score"), "unexpected error: {err}");
        assert_ne!(parse_entry(":5"), Ok((String::new(), 5)), "an empty name is an error");
    }
}

/// Number of words in `text` after cleaning; words that clean to "" do not count.
pub fn word_count(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.split_whitespace().map(clean).filter(|w| !w.is_empty()).count()
}

/// The longest word in `text`, cleaned (see `word_count`). Ties go to the
/// first one. `None` when there are no words.
///
/// ```
/// assert_eq!(wordlist::longest_word("A big, BIGGER day."), Some(String::from("bigger")));
/// assert_eq!(wordlist::longest_word(""), None);
/// ```
pub fn longest_word(text: &str) -> Option<String> {
    let mut best: Option<String> = None;
    for w in text.split_whitespace().map(clean).filter(|w| !w.is_empty()) {
        if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|b| w.len() > b.len()) {
            best = Some(w);
        }
    }
    best
}

// Private: trims non-alphanumeric characters from both ends and lowercases.
fn clean(word: &str) -> String {
    word.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()).to_lowercase()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    // A unit test can reach the private helper.
    #[test]
    fn clean_strips_punctuation_and_lowers() {
        assert_eq!(clean("Hello,"), "hello");
        assert_eq!(clean("--"), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn longest_word_ties_go_to_the_first() {
        assert_eq!(longest_word("ab cd e"), Some(String::from("ab")));
        assert_eq!(longest_word("  "), None);
    }
}

## 1. Packages and crates

So far every program was one file. Real programs are split into pieces, and Rust has three words for the pieces:

WordWhat it isYou see it as

cratethe unit the compiler builds in one go: a library or a binarya crate root file: `src/lib.rs`, `src/main.rs`, `src/bin/x.rs`

packageone or more crates built together by Cargoa `Cargo.toml`

modulea named scope inside a crate that groups items and controls privacy`mod name;` or `mod name { ... }`

A package holds at most one library crate (`src/lib.rs`) and any number of binary crates (`src/main.rs`, plus one per file in `src/bin/`). Each crate root is compiled separately and has its own `crate::`. That is why, in `wordcount`, `main.rs` writes `wordcount::report` and not `crate::report`: the binary is a separate crate that uses the library, by the package name.

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, chapters 7 and 14, and Rust by Example (modules, Cargo), both MIT/Apache-2.0. Open `inline_mods.rs`, `paths.rs` and the `wordcount` package alongside it.

## 2. The module tree

A crate is a tree of modules. The root is the crate root file, named `crate`. The tree grows only from `mod` declarations:

```
mod shapes {            // a module written inline
    pub struct Rect { pub width: u32, pub height: u32, id: u32 }
    pub mod area {      // a child module of shapes
        pub fn of(r: &super::Rect) -> u32 { r.width * r.height }
    }
}
```

The tree for `wordcount`'s library:

```
crate          (src/lib.rs)
├── count      (src/count.rs)
└── report     (src/report.rs)
    └── format (src/report/format.rs)
```

A file is not compiled until its parent module declares it with `mod name;`. Cargo does not compile every `.rs` file in `src/`, and `use` never loads a file. A file nobody declares is simply ignored, and paths to it fail with `error[E0432]: unresolved import`.

## 3. Privacy

Every item (function, struct, module, const) is private by default: visible in the module that defines it and in that module's descendants. Children can see their ancestors' private items; a parent cannot see a child's private items.

MarkerVisible in

(nothing)this module and its children

`pub(super)`the parent module (and so everything the parent's privacy reaches)

`pub(crate)`the whole crate, but not other crates

`pub`anywhere the path to it is visible, including other crates

To reach an item, every module on the path must be visible too. A `pub fn` inside a private module is still unreachable from outside that module's parent:

```
error[E0603]: module `parse` is private
```

Privacy is decided by the item's author, not the caller. The caller can only use what the author exposed.

## 4. Privacy of fields and variants

A `pub struct` makes the type name public. Each field stays private unless it is marked `pub` itself:

```
mod shapes {
    pub struct Rect {
        pub width: u32,
        pub height: u32,
        id: u32,          // private
    }
    impl Rect {
        pub fn new(width: u32, height: u32) -> Rect {
            Rect { width, height, id: 7 }
        }
    }
}
```

Outside `shapes`, code can read `r.width` but not `r.id` (`error[E0616]: field `id` of struct `Rect` is private`). It also cannot write a struct literal `Rect { .. }`, because a literal must set every field, including `id`. The only way to get a `Rect` is through `new`.

This is how a type keeps a rule. If a constructor checks the rule and the field is private, every value of that type obeys the rule, forever: no other code can build or change one behind your back.

Enums are the opposite: all variants of a `pub enum` are public, along with their data. An enum cannot hide its contents this way.

## 5. Paths

A path names an item in the tree:

Path starts withMeansExample

`crate::`absolute, from this crate's root`crate::shapes::area::of`

`self::`this module (usually optional)`self::sub::only_parent()`

`super::`the parent module`super::Rect`

a name in scoperelative to this module`area::of(&r)`

another crate's namethat crate's root`wordcount::count_words`

A package named with a dash, such as `stats-core`, is written with an underscore in paths: `stats_core::`.

## 6. use

`use` creates a shortcut name for a path. It does not load anything and it does not change privacy.

```
use shapes::Rect;       // structs and enums: bring in the type itself
use shapes::area;       // functions: bring in the parent module, call area::of
use crate::tools::name as tool_name; // `as` renames
```

A `use` applies only in the module (or function body) where it is written. A `use` at the top of `main.rs` does not reach a `mod report { ... }` below it: inside `report`, write a full path or a `use` of its own.

- `pub use` re-exports: the name becomes part of this module's public API. `pub use count::count_words;` in `lib.rs` lets callers write `wordcount::count_words`, and you can reorganise the inner modules later without breaking them.

- A glob `use tools::*;` brings in every visible name from `tools`. If this module defines an item with the same name, the local item wins over the glob name, silently. A named import of a clashing name is an error instead.

## 7. Modules in files

`mod report;` (with a semicolon instead of a body) tells the compiler to load the module from a file, relative to the module that declares it:

DeclarationWritten inLoads

`mod report;``src/lib.rs` (crate root)`src/report.rs` (or the older `src/report/mod.rs`)

`mod format;``src/report.rs``src/report/format.rs`

`mod helpers;``src/config.rs``src/config/helpers.rs`, not `src/helpers.rs`

Declare each module once, in its parent. Everywhere else, refer to it by path. Declaring the same file twice (say, `mod text;` in both `lib.rs` and `main.rs`) compiles it twice into two crates, giving two unrelated types with the same name:

```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
expected `tally::text::Counts`, found `text::Counts`
```

## 8. Cargo and dependencies

`Cargo.toml` describes a package and what it depends on:

```
[package]
name = "cli"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]            # linked into every build: cargo build, run, test
mathlib = { path = "../mathlib" }

[dev-dependencies]        # only for tests, examples and benchmarks (cargo test)
```

LineCargo looks for

`x = { path = "../x" }`local code in that folder

`x = "0.1"`a package called `x` on crates.io, any 0.1.* version (offline: fails)

`Cargo.lock` records the exact versions Cargo resolved, so every later build uses the same ones. Keep it in version control for programs. In this course's sandbox Cargo runs `--offline`: anything not already on the machine (only `tokio` and `tokio-stream`) cannot be fetched.

Useful commands: `cargo build`, `cargo run` (build then run), `cargo test`, `cargo check` (type-check only, fastest).

## 9. Profiles and workspaces

A profile is a set of compiler settings. `cargo build` uses `dev` (`opt-level = 0`, fast to compile, debug checks such as integer overflow panics). `cargo build --release` uses `release` (`opt-level = 3`). Cargo tells you which one it used:

```
Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)
Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s)
```

A workspace is a folder of packages developed together:

```
# Cargo.toml at the workspace root
[workspace]
members = ["app", "mathlib"]
resolver = "3"
```

- Members share one `Cargo.lock` and one `target/`, both at the root.

- Profiles (`[profile.dev]`, `[profile.release]`) are set at the root and apply to every member.

- Members still declare each other as dependencies (`mathlib = { path = "../mathlib" }`). Being in the same workspace does not make one member visible to another.

mod units {
    const MM_PER_CM: u32 = 10; // private to `units`, visible to its children

    /// Centimetres to millimetres. Use MM_PER_CM.
    pub fn cm_to_mm(cm: u32) -> u32 {
        cm * MM_PER_CM
    }

    pub mod area {
        /// Area of a rectangle given in cm, in square millimetres.
        /// Convert each side with the parent's cm_to_mm.
        pub fn rect_mm2(w_cm: u32, h_cm: u32) -> u32 {
            super::cm_to_mm(w_cm) * super::cm_to_mm(h_cm)
        }
    }
}

mod report {
    /// One line like "3x2 cm = 600 mm2", using units::area::rect_mm2.
    pub fn line(w_cm: u32, h_cm: u32) -> String {
        let mm2 = crate::units::area::rect_mm2(w_cm, h_cm);
        format!("{w_cm}x{h_cm} cm = {mm2} mm2")
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn converts_cm() {
        assert_eq!(units::cm_to_mm(3), 30);
        assert_eq!(units::cm_to_mm(0), 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn area_in_mm2() {
        assert_eq!(units::area::rect_mm2(3, 2), 600);
        assert_eq!(units::area::rect_mm2(1, 1), 100);
    }

// Exercise 2: a private field that keeps a rule.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_celsius.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// Celsius can never be below -273. The field is private, so code outside
// `temperature` (including the tests below) can only make a Celsius through
// `new` or `warmer`. Replace the three todo!()s so the rule always holds.

mod temperature {
    /// Whole degrees Celsius, never below -273.
    pub struct Celsius {
        degrees: i32,
    }

    impl Celsius {
        /// None when `degrees` is below -273.
        pub fn new(degrees: i32) -> Option<Celsius> {
            if degrees < -273 { None } else { Some(Celsius { degrees }) }
        }

        pub fn degrees(&self) -> i32 {
            self.degrees
        }

        /// The temperature `by` degrees warmer (by may be negative).
        /// None when the result would break the rule.
        pub fn warmer(&self, by: i32) -> Option<Celsius> {
            Celsius::new(self.degrees + by) // reuse the one place that checks the rule
        }
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::temperature::Celsius;

    fn deg(c: Option<Celsius>) -> Option<i32> {
        match c {
            Some(c) => Some(c.degrees()),
            None => None,
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn accepts_valid_temperatures() {
        assert_eq!(deg(Celsius::new(20)), Some(20));
        assert_eq!(deg(Celsius::new(-273)), Some(-273));
    }

    #[test]
    fn rejects_below_absolute_zero() {
        assert!(Celsius::new(-274).is_none());
    }

    #[test]
    fn warmer_keeps_the_rule() {
        let c = Celsius::new(-270).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(deg(c.warmer(5)), Some(-265));
        assert_eq!(deg(c.warmer(-3)), Some(-273));
        assert!(c.warmer(-4).is_none());
    }
}

### pub items in private modules · 2 Nov

- A `pub fn` inside a private module is not reachable just because the fn is `pub`. Every module on the path must also be visible to the caller.
- A private module is visible in the module that declares it, plus all of that module's descendants. So the caller's position decides, not the fn's own module.
- Example: `mod store { pub fn load() {} }` written at the crate root. `store` is private, but it is declared in the crate root, so the whole crate can see the name and `main` may call `store::load()`.
- A private module nested deeper is only visible inside its declaring module and that module's descendants, so a `pub fn` inside it stops there (`error[E0603]: module ... is private`).

fn load(attempt: u32) -> Result<i32, Box<dyn Error>> {

## 1. Why generics

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 10.1-10.2, and Rust by Example (Generics, Bounds, Traits, impl Trait), MIT/Apache-2.0.

Suppose you wrote a function that finds the largest `i32` in a slice, then needed the same for `char`. The two bodies would be identical; only the type differs. A type parameter lets you write the body once:

```
fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T {
    let mut largest = &list[0];
    for item in list {
        if item > largest {
            largest = item;
        }
    }
    largest
}
```

Read `<T: PartialOrd>` as "for any type `T` that can be compared with `<` and `>`". The caller picks `T` at each call (`largest(&[34, 50])` uses `i32`, `largest(&['y', 'm'])` uses `char`). The body must compile for every `T` the bounds allow, not just the ones you happen to call it with. `largest.rs` runs this on numbers, chars and Strings.

## 2. Bounds unlock operations

Inside a generic body, the compiler knows nothing about `T` except what the bounds promise. Remove `: PartialOrd` from `largest` and the comparison is refused, even though every type you call it with could be compared:

```
error[E0369]: binary operation `>` cannot be applied to type `&T`
 --> largest.rs:4:17
  |
4 |         if item > largest {
  |            ---- ^ ------- &T
  |            |
  |            &T
help: consider restricting type parameter `T` with trait `PartialOrd`
```

Each operation you want needs its trait:

You want to writeBoundNotes

`a > b`, `a <= b``T: PartialOrd`

`a == b``T: PartialEq`

`a - b` giving a `T``T: Sub<Output = T>`from `std::ops`; same idea for `Add`, `Mul`

`println!("{x}")``T: Display``{x:?}` needs `Debug`

`let x = slice[0];` (an owned copy)`T: Copy`or `T: Clone` and write `slice[0].clone()`

`T::default()``T: Default`0 for numbers, empty for String and Vec

Two of these need a closer look.

The `Output` of an operator trait. `Sub` is declared as `trait Sub<Rhs = Self> { type Output; fn sub(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self::Output; }`. The result type is a separate choice of each implementor, so `T: Sub` alone says "`a - b` is allowed and produces something". If you need the result to be a `T` again (to store it back in a `T` variable or return it), say so: `T: Sub<Output = T>`.

Copying out of a borrowed slice. A `&[T]` lets you look at elements, not take them. `let x = list[0];` would move the element out of a slice you only borrowed, so it is allowed only when `T: Copy` (then it is a copy, not a move). With `T: Clone` you can write `list[0].clone()`; returning `&T` (as `largest` does) needs neither.

```
use std::ops::Mul;

// x * x for any type that can be multiplied by itself, giving the same type back.
fn square<T>(x: T) -> T
where
    T: Mul<Output = T> + Copy,   // Copy: x is used twice, so it must not move
{
    x * x
}

## 3. Generic types and conditional methods

Structs and enums take type parameters too. You already use two: `Option<T>` and `Vec<T>`.

```
struct Point<T> {
    x: T,
    y: T,          // both fields are the same T
}

impl<T> Point<T> {              // for every Point<T>
    fn x(&self) -> &T { &self.x }
}

impl Point<f64> {               // only for Point<f64>
    fn distance_from_origin(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.x.powi(2) + self.y.powi(2)).sqrt()
    }
}
```

The header of each `impl` block decides which types get its methods.

HeaderMethods exist for

`impl<T> Point<T>`every `Point`

`impl Point<f64>`only `Point<f64>`

`impl<T: Display + PartialOrd> Duo<T>`only when `T` meets the bound

Calling a method on a type its impl does not cover is a compile error (E0599), and when the method exists but a bound is unmet, the message says "its trait bounds were not satisfied". A type cannot get the same method name from two impl blocks that overlap (E0592). A method can also have its own type parameters, separate from the struct's: `fn with_y<U>(&self, y: U) -> (T, U)` in `point.rs`.

## 4. What generics cost: monomorphization

The compiler turns generic code into ordinary code by making one concrete copy for each type it is used with. This is called monomorphization.

monomorphization.png: one generic function, one generated copy per type.

- At run time there is no lookup and no boxing: `largest::<i32>` runs exactly like a hand-written `largest_i32`.

- The price is paid at compile time: more code to compile, and a larger binary.

- The body is type-checked once, against the bounds. That is why a missing bound is an error even if every call would work.

Sub-module 12 shows the other approach, trait objects (`dyn Trait`), which keeps one copy and decides at run time.

## 5. Traits, default methods and overrides

A trait is a named set of methods a type can promise to have. A method without a body is required; a method with a body is a default that implementors get for free and may override.

```
trait Summary {
    fn author(&self) -> String;                      // required
    fn summarize(&self) -> String {                  // default
        format!("(Read more from {}...)", self.author())
    }
}

struct Post { author: String }
impl Summary for Post {
    fn author(&self) -> String { format!("@{}", self.author) }
    // summarize: uses the default
}
```

A default method may call any other method of the trait. When it calls `self.author()`, the implementing type's own `author` runs. The same is true for other default methods: if a type overrides one default, every other default that calls it uses the override. In `traits.rs`, `Reply` overrides `summarize`, so `notify(&reply)` prints the reply's version.

A default method can only use what the trait promises about `Self`. It cannot read the implementor's fields (it does not know them), and it cannot use `{self}` unless `Self: Display` is promised. You can require more for one method only with a `where` clause on that method:

```
fn headline(&self) -> String
where
    Self: Display,           // only Display implementors can call headline
{
    format!("** {self} **")
}
```

```
error[E0277]: `Post` doesn't implement `std::fmt::Display`
```

That error appears where someone calls `post.headline()` on a type that is not `Display`; the trait itself still compiles, and every other method stays available to `Post`.

## 6. Who may implement what: the orphan rule

`impl Trait for Type` is allowed only if something in it is local (defined in your crate):

- the trait is local, or

- the type is local, or

- a local type appears as one of the trait's type parameters, as in `impl From<Celsius> for f64`.

orphan-rule.png: local and foreign traits and types, and the one red cell.

A local type wrapped in a foreign generic does not count: `Vec<Celsius>` is a `Vec`, defined in std. A blanket `impl<T> ForeignTrait for T` is never allowed either, because `T` covers types from every crate.

```
error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate
 --> orphan.rs:2:1
  |
2 | impl fmt::Display for Vec<i32> { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^--------
  |                       |
  |                       `Vec` is not defined in the current crate
  = note: define and implement a trait or new type instead
```

Why the rule exists. If two libraries could both write `impl Display for Vec<i32>`, a program using both would have two answers for one question, and nothing to pick between them. The rule makes sure every (trait, type) pair has at most one possible home. It also lets std add new impls without breaking your crate.

Workarounds. Wrap the foreign type in a local newtype, `struct List(Vec<i32>);`, and implement the trait for that (a newtype costs nothing at run time). Or define a local trait and implement it for the foreign type. `orphan.rs` shows all three allowed shapes.

## 7. Blanket impls

A blanket impl implements a trait for every type that meets a bound:

```
trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}
impl<T: Debug> Describe for T {
    fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("<{self:?}>") }
}
// 5.describe(), "hi".describe(), vec![1, 2].describe() all work
```

std uses this pattern: every type that implements `Display` gets `to_string()` through `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`. The blanket covers types written later too, so you never write that impl yourself.

The cost: once a blanket impl covers a type, no other impl of the same trait may cover it. Stable Rust has no "the more specific impl wins" rule, so overlap is an error:

```
error[E0119]: conflicting implementations of trait `Label` for type `u8`
3 | impl<T: Display> Label for T { ... }
  | ---------------------------- first implementation here
4 | impl Label for u8 { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ conflicting implementation for `u8`
```

The order of the impls does not matter, and there is no way to mark one as preferred on stable Rust. (A feature called specialization exists only on nightly.)

## 8. Bounds in signatures and `impl Trait`

Three ways to say "any type that implements `Summary`":

```
fn notify(item: &impl Summary) { ... }           // short form
fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T) { ... }          // generic parameter
fn notify_both<T, U>(a: &T, b: &U)
where
    T: Summary,
    U: Summary + Display,                         // two bounds with +
{ ... }
```

With a named `T` you can force two arguments to have the same type (`fn pair<T: Summary>(a: &T, b: &T)`); `impl Summary` twice allows two different types.

### Argument position vs return position

Who picks the concrete typeHow many types

`fn f(x: impl Trait)`the caller, at each callone per call site (each gets its own monomorphized copy)

`fn f() -> impl Trait`the function bodyexactly one for the whole function; callers only see "some `Trait`"

Return-position `impl Trait` hides the type's name, but there is still exactly one type, fixed at compile time. Returning different types from different branches is an error:

```
error[E0308]: `if` and `else` have incompatible types
3 |     if flag { "yes" } else { 1 }
  |               -----          ^ expected `&str`, found integer
help: you could change the return type to be a boxed trait object
```

To return "one of several kinds" while keeping `-> impl Trait`, make the branches one type: convert them to the same type (for example both to `String`), or define an enum with one variant per kind and implement the trait for the enum. The compiler's suggestion, `Box<dyn Trait>`, is a different trade (a heap allocation and dynamic dispatch) covered in 12.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct Pair<T> {
    pub a: T,
    pub b: T,
}

impl<T> Pair<T> {
    pub fn swap(self) -> Pair<T> {
        Pair { a: self.b, b: self.a }
    }
}

impl<T: PartialOrd> Pair<T> {
    pub fn larger(&self) -> &T {
        if self.b > self.a { &self.b } else { &self.a }
    }
}

pub fn first_or<T: Clone>(items: &[T], fallback: T) -> T {
    if items.is_empty() { fallback } else { items[0].clone() }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn swap_any_type() {
        let p = Pair { a: String::from("x"), b: String::from("y") };
        assert_eq!(p.swap(), Pair { a: String::from("y"), b: String::from("x") });
        assert_eq!(Pair { a: 1, b: 2 }.swap(), Pair { a: 2, b: 1 });
    }

    #[test]
    fn larger_numbers_and_strings() {
        assert_eq!(*Pair { a: 3, b: 9 }.larger(), 9);
        assert_eq!(Pair { a: String::from("pear"), b: String::from("apple") }.larger(), "pear");
        assert_eq!(*Pair { a: 4.5, b: 4.5 }.larger(), 4.5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_or_fallback() {
        assert_eq!(first_or(&[7, 8], 0), 7);
        assert_eq!(first_or(&[], 0), 0);
        let words = vec![String::from("hi")];
        assert_eq!(first_or(&words, String::from("none")), "hi");
        assert_eq!(words.len(), 1); // still ours
    }
}

use std::fmt::{Debug, Display};

pub fn count_equal<T: PartialEq>(items: &[T], target: &T) -> usize {
    let mut n = 0;
    for item in items {
        if item == target {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    n
}

pub fn join_all(items: &[impl Display], sep: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    let mut first = true;
    for item in items {
        if !first {
            out.push_str(sep);
        }
        first = false;
        out.push_str(&item.to_string());
    }
    out
}

pub fn show_pair<L, V>(label: L, value: V) -> String
where
    L: Display,
    V: Debug,
{
    format!("{label}: {value:?}")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn counts() {
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&[1, 2, 1, 1], &1), 3);
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&["a", "b"], &"c"), 0);
        let words = vec![String::from("x"), String::from("x")];
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&words, &String::from("x")), 2);
    }

    #[test]
    fn joins() {
        assert_eq!(join_all(&[1, 2, 3], ", "), "1, 2, 3");
        assert_eq!(join_all(&["a"], "-"), "a");
        let empty: [i32; 0] = [];
        assert_eq!(join_all(&empty, "-"), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn pairs() {
        assert_eq!(show_pair("ids", vec![1, 2]), "ids: [1, 2]");
        assert_eq!(show_pair(5, "five"), "5: \"five\"");
    }
}

# schema_migrate/runner.py (v2.3), excerpt
# schema_migrations: filename text PRIMARY KEY, version text NOT NULL,
#                    applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL, applied_by text NOT NULL

def pending(conn, directory):
    applied = {r.filename for r in conn.execute("SELECT filename FROM schema_migrations")}
    return [f for f in sorted(directory.glob("*.sql")) if f.name not in applied]

def apply(conn, path, applied_by):
    conn.execute(path.read_text())          # the file controls its own transaction
    conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO schema_migrations (version, filename, applied_at, applied_by) "
        "VALUES (%s, %s, now(), %s)",
        (path.name[:4], path.name, applied_by),

- it should use guards like `IF NOT EXISTS` / `IF EXISTS`, check current schema state, or versioned migration bookkeeping,
- it should avoid data-changing steps that assume it is the only actor unless those steps are protected by locks or transactional checks,

Not by itself. A lease-based queue delivers at least once: a lease can expire while its holder is still alive (a long pause, a network split, a pod draining past its lease) and the task goes to a second worker. Duplicate deliveries are normal; duplicate effects are the bug. Why this effect doubled: schema-migrate decides what is applied by filename (filename is the primary key, and apply() records it only after running the file), and the model named the same change differently each time, so both 0147 files ran: version 0147 twice, 148 applied against 146 in the repository. Model output is not deterministic, so you cannot dedupe on output, and 'Safe to re-run' with IF NOT EXISTS makes one file rerunnable, not the task. Make the effect safe, keyed on intent: an idempotency key per task and effect (T-882:migrate) under a unique constraint, written in the same transaction as the DDL (Postgres DDL is transactional; the second file has no BEGIN), so a second apply is refused and says who applied the first. Pass the lease's fencing token with every effect and reject stale ones: qx2lm applied at 14:03:12, after h8vtn had claimed. Key schema_migrations on version and have CI refuse duplicate versions. Better, take the effect away from builders: they produce a PR, verification applies migrations to a throwaway database, and shared staging changes only from main, once, after the orders-db review. Exactly-once: not available across a queue, a model call and an outside database; systems that offer it do so within one transactional store. What you build is effectively once: at-least-once delivery, idempotent effects, fencing. And compare the costs: the duplicate session was about $2.92 of tokens; the duplicate effect blocked staging deploys for 19 h 40 min. Spend the engineering on the effect.

  - inside the sandbox
  - applied by filename
  - fencing token
  - effectively once

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

For the second apply to have been refused, the migration runner would have needed a durable uniqueness check on the migration identity, not just the filename. In practice that means the applied-migrations table would have to already contain `0147` for that database, and the runner would have to treat that as authoritative before running the file. If it only keys off a per-process cache or a per-session view, the second pod can still race through and apply it.

On the delivery side, I don’t think you can honestly promise true exactly-once across a queue and a database you don’t own. The realistic target is at-least-once delivery with idempotent handlers and deduplication at the boundaries. So the harness should make duplicate execution safe and detectable, but not pretend it can eliminate duplicates everywhere just by orchestration.

## 1. Defining and creating structs

A struct groups related values under one name, and gives each value a field name. Where a tuple says "an `(String, String, bool, u64)`", a struct says what each part means.

```
struct Profile {
    name: String,
    email: String,
    active: bool,
    visits: u64,
}
```

The definition is a template. To make a value, write the struct name and a value for every field, in any order. Read a field with a dot.

```
let mut first = Profile {
    email: String::from("a@example.com"),
    name: String::from("a"),
    active: true,
    visits: 0,
};
first.visits += 1;
println!("{} has {} visits", first.name, first.visits);
```

Mutability belongs to the binding, not to fields. To change any field, the whole value must be `let mut`. There is no way to mark one field `mut`.

A struct owns its fields. When the struct goes out of scope, every field is dropped with it. Fields of type `String` or `Vec` follow the move rules you saw in 02.

This lesson adapts The Rust Programming Language, chapter 5 and Rust by Example (MIT/Apache-2.0). Open `define.rs` and `methods.rs` alongside it.

## 2. Shorthand and update syntax

Field init shorthand. When a variable has the same name as the field, write the name once:

```
fn build_profile(name: String, email: String) -> Profile {
    Profile { name, email, active: true, visits: 0 } // name: name, email: email
}
```

Struct update syntax. `..other` at the end of a struct literal means "every field I did not write out comes from `other`".

```
let second = Profile {
    email: String::from("b@example.com"),
    ..first
};
```

Update syntax is not a special copy. It is a set of ordinary field assignments, so each field follows its own rule:

FieldWhere it comes fromWhat happens to `first`'s field

`email`written outuntouched, still usable

`name` (`String`)`..first`moved into `second`; `first.name` is unusable

`active` (`bool`)`..first`copied; still usable

`visits` (`u64`)`..first`copied; still usable

After this, `first.visits` and `first.email` still work, but `first.name` and `first` as a whole do not:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `first.name`
```

Ask per field: did I write it out? If not, is its type Copy? Copy fields are copied, everything else moves. To keep a non-Copy field, write it out (for example `tags: base.tags.clone()`).

## 3. Tuple structs and unit structs

A tuple struct has a name but no field names. Fields are read by position: `.0`, `.1`.

```
struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);
struct Meters(f64);

let red = Rgb(255, 0, 0);
let run = Meters(5.5);
println!("{} {}", red.0, run.0);
```

Two tuple structs with the same field types are still different types. A function that takes `Meters` will not accept a plain `f64` or some other one-field struct. A one-field tuple struct used this way is called a newtype: it gives a plain number its own meaning, so the compiler stops you mixing metres with seconds.

A unit struct has no fields at all: `struct Marker;`. It is useful later, when a type matters but carries no data (for example, to implement a trait on it in 09).

## 4. Methods

A method is a function defined inside an `impl` block whose first parameter is `self` in some form. It is called with dot syntax on a value.

```
struct Rectangle { width: u32, height: u32 }

impl Rectangle {
    fn area(&self) -> u32 {
        self.width * self.height
    }
    fn scale(&mut self, factor: u32) {
        self.width *= factor;
        self.height *= factor;
    }
}
```

`&self` is short for `self: &Self`, and `Self` is the type the `impl` is for. A method call is plain function call syntax in disguise:

You writeThe compiler calls

`big.area()``Rectangle::area(&big)`

`big.scale(2)``Rectangle::scale(&mut big, 2)`

`big.into_pair()``Rectangle::into_pair(big)`

The compiler adds the `&` or `&mut` for you (automatic referencing). Because `big.scale(2)` really takes `&mut big`, `big` must be declared `let mut`, exactly as if you had written the borrow yourself.

## 5. Associated functions

A function in an `impl` block without `self` is an associated function. It belongs to the type, not to a value, so it is called with `::`.

```
impl Rectangle {
    fn square(size: u32) -> Self {
        Self { width: size, height: size }
    }
}

let small = Rectangle::square(3);
```

- Constructors are usually associated functions. `new` is a convention, not a keyword: name them for what they build (`square`, `empty`, `with_limit`).

- Inside an `impl`, `Self` names the type, so `Self { .. }` and `Rectangle { .. }` mean the same.

- A type can have many `impl` blocks; they all add to the same type.

You will often build text inside methods. `format!` takes the same arguments as `println!` but returns the text as a `String` instead of printing it:

```
fn label(&self) -> String {
    format!("{}x{}", self.width, self.height)
}
```

## 6. Receivers and borrows

The first parameter of a method is its receiver. It is the same choice you make for any function parameter in 02 and 03: borrow, borrow mutably, or take ownership.

ReceiverThe method getsThe caller needsValue usable afterwards?Typical use

`&self`a read-only viewany bindingyes`area`, `len`, `is_empty`

`&mut self`exclusive write accessa `let mut` binding and no other live borrowyes`scale`, `push`, `record`

`self`ownershipany bindingno, it moved (unless the type is Copy)`into_pair`, `build`, `close`

Pick the weakest receiver that works. Reading needs `&self`. Changing needs `&mut self`. Only take `self` when the method uses the value up or turns it into something else.

A method that takes `self` may also change it before handing it back. Write `mut self`: the method owns the value, so it may mutate it.

```
fn doubled(mut self) -> Self {
    self.width *= 2;
    self   // ownership goes back to the caller
}

let r = Rectangle::square(2).doubled(); // calls chain, each one takes and returns
```

### Fields versus methods

Inside one function, the borrow checker tracks fields separately. Holding `&mut s.items` while reading `s.limit` is fine: they are different places in memory.

A method call is different. The checker looks only at the method's signature, never its body. A method `fn items_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Vec<i32>` borrows all of `self` mutably, for as long as the returned reference is in use. While that reference lives, calling even a `&self` method on the same value is a conflict, because the signature does not say which field it touches.

Checking only signatures is deliberate: a library can change a method body without breaking any caller. The price is that the checker cannot see that two methods use different fields.

## 7. Derive: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default

A new struct can do almost nothing: you cannot print it with `{:?}`, compare it with `==` or `clone()` it. The `#[derive(...)]` attribute asks the compiler to write the code for common traits (shared behaviour) for you.

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
```

DeriveGives youDerived behaviour

`Debug``{:?}`, `{:#?}` (pretty), `dbg!`prints the type name and each field

`Clone``.clone()`clones each field

`Copy`implicit copies instead of movesbitwise copy; needs `Clone` too, and every field must be Copy

`PartialEq``==`, `!=`equal when every field is equal

`PartialOrd``<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`compares fields in declaration order: the first field decides unless equal, then the next; needs `PartialEq`

`Default``T::default()`each field's own default: 0, `false`, empty `String`/`Vec`

So for `Point`, `Point { x: 1, y: 9 } < Point { x: 2, y: 0 }` is `true`: `x` is compared first and decides. Field order is part of the meaning of a derived ordering.

`dbg!(expr)` prints the file, line, expression and value to stderr, then returns the value, so you can wrap it around any expression.

A derive works only if every field's type has that trait. Deriving `Default` on a struct with a field of a type that has no `Default` fails with `error[E0277]: the trait bound ... is not satisfied`. Same for `Copy` with a `String` field.

### Why nothing is derived automatically

- The derived meaning can be wrong. Field-by-field `==` is wrong if a field is a cache or a counter that should not affect equality. Declaration-order `<` is wrong if "smaller" means smaller area.

- It can leak. `Debug` prints every field, including a password or token.

- It changes cost and rules. `Clone` makes deep copies easy to write; `Copy` changes moves into copies everywhere.

- It is a promise. Once callers rely on `==` or `Copy`, removing it breaks them.

## 8. Writing Default by hand

When zero values are wrong defaults (a retry count of 0, a timeout of 0 seconds), write `Default` yourself instead of deriving it:

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Settings {
    name: String,
    retries: u32,
    verbose: bool,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Settings { name: String::from("main"), retries: 3, verbose: false }
    }
}

let s = Settings { verbose: true, ..Settings::default() };
```

Traits in general are covered in 09. This one shape, `impl Default for T { fn default() -> Self { ... } }`, is all you need now. It combines well with update syntax: `..Settings::default()` fills every field you did not write.

If a type has both `new()` and `Default`, make them agree. A `default()` that quietly gives different values from `new()` surprises every caller.

## 9. Check yourself

Answer these out loud or ask the Tutor about them. Then try the exercises.

- Why must I write `let mut` to call a `&mut self` method?

- When should a method take `self` by value?

- After `let b = Config { name: x, ..a };`, which fields of `a` can I still use?

- Why doesn't Rust derive `Debug` and `PartialEq` for every struct?

- Two fields of a struct, `width` then `height`, with derived `PartialOrd`: which field decides `a < b`?

Exercises: `ex1_steps.rs` (methods and receivers), `ex2_wallet.rs` (a type that guards its own rules), `ex3_version.rs` (derive order and a hand-written `Default`).

// Exercise 1: methods, associated functions and receivers.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_steps.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A StepLog keeps a daily step goal and the steps recorded so far.
// Reference solution.
// The receivers below are placeholders: if a method has to change the log,
// change its receiver too.

struct StepLog {
    goal: u32,
    days: u32,
    total: u32,
}

impl StepLog {
    /// A new log with a daily goal and nothing recorded.
    fn new(goal: u32) -> Self {
        StepLog { goal, days: 0, total: 0 }
    }

    /// Record one day's steps.
    fn record(&mut self, steps: u32) {
        self.days += 1;
        self.total += steps;
    }

    /// Average steps per recorded day. 0 when nothing is recorded yet.
    fn average(&self) -> u32 {
        if self.days == 0 {
            return 0;
        }
        self.total / self.days
    }

    /// True when the average reaches the goal.
    fn on_track(&self) -> bool {
        self.average() >= self.goal
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn new_log_is_empty() {
        let log = StepLog::new(8000);
        assert_eq!((log.goal, log.days, log.total), (8000, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn average_of_an_empty_log_is_zero() {
        assert_eq!(StepLog::new(10).average(), 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn records_and_averages() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(5000);
        log.record(4000);
        log.record(7000);
        assert_eq!(log.days, 2);
        assert_eq!(log.average(), 5500);
        assert!(log.on_track());
    }

    #[test]
    fn below_goal_is_not_on_track() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(9000);
        log.record(3000);
        assert!(!log.on_track());
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a type that keeps its own rules.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_wallet.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Wallet holds money in cents (whole numbers, so no rounding errors).
// Reference solution.
// Tip: format!("{:02}", 5) gives "05".

struct Wallet {
    owner: String,
    cents: u64,
}

impl Wallet {
    /// A new, empty wallet.
    fn open(owner: &str) -> Wallet {
        Wallet { owner: owner.to_string(), cents: 0 }
    }

    /// Add money.
    fn deposit(&mut self, cents: u64) {
        self.cents += cents;
    }

    /// Take money out. If there is not enough, return false and change nothing.
    fn spend(&mut self, cents: u64) -> bool {
        if cents > self.cents {
            return false;
        }
        self.cents -= cents;
        true
    }

    /// The balance as text, for example "ada: $12.05".
    fn balance_text(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}: ${}.{:02}", self.owner, self.cents / 100, self.cents % 100)
    }

    /// Close the wallet: give back the owner's name and the remaining cents.
    fn close(self) -> (String, u64) {
        (self.owner, self.cents)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn opens_empty() {
        let w = Wallet::open("ada");
        assert_eq!(w.owner, "ada");
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn deposit_and_spend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1500);
        assert!(w.spend(295));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 1205);
    }

    #[test]
    fn refuses_to_overspend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(100);
        assert!(!w.spend(101));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 100);
    }

    #[test]
    fn formats_dollars_and_cents() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1205);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $12.05");
        w.spend(1200);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $0.05");
    }

    #[test]
    fn close_gives_everything_back() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("bo");
        w.deposit(42);
        let (owner, left) = w.close();
        assert_eq!(owner, "bo");
        assert_eq!(left, 42);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: what derive gives you, and Default by hand.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_version.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Version like 1.4.2 must compare the usual way: major first, then minor,
// then patch. So 1.4.2 < 1.10.0 < 2.0.0.
//
// TODO 1: the derive list is right, but comparisons come out wrong.
//         Fix it without writing any comparison code yourself.
// TODO 2: the default version is 0.1.0, not 0.0.0. Write Default by hand.
// TODO 3: write bump_minor: 1.4.2 becomes 1.5.0.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]
struct Version {
    major: u32, // derived PartialOrd compares fields in declaration order
    minor: u32,
    patch: u32,
}

impl Version {
    fn new(major: u32, minor: u32, patch: u32) -> Version {
        Version { major, minor, patch }
    }

    fn bump_minor(self) -> Version {
        Version { minor: self.minor + 1, patch: 0, ..self }
    }
}

impl Default for Version {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Version::new(0, 1, 0)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn major_decides_first() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 2) < Version::new(2, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn minor_decides_before_patch() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 9) < Version::new(1, 10, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_is_0_1_0() {
        assert_eq!(Version::default(), Version::new(0, 1, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn bump_minor_resets_patch() {
        assert_eq!(Version::new(1, 4, 2).bump_minor(), Version::new(1, 5, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn versions_are_copy() {
        let v = Version::new(1, 0, 0);
        let w = v;
        assert_eq!(v, w);
        assert_eq!(format!("{w:?}").contains("major: 1"), true);
    }
}

## 1. Two kinds of failure

Things go wrong in every program, and Rust makes you say which kind of wrong you mean. There are two kinds:

A bugAn expected problem

Examplesan index your own code computed is out of range; an invariant you promised is brokena user typed letters where a number belongs; a file is missing; a network call timed out

Can the program sensibly carry on?no: it would work on wrong datayes: ask again, use a default, skip, report

Rust toolpanic (`panic!`, `expect`, `assert!`)`Result<T, E>` (or `Option<T>` when there is nothing to say)

Which kind a failure is depends on the function's contract: what it promises and what it asks of its callers. Write the contract down in a doc comment. "An empty list is normal" makes an empty list an expected case, so the function must handle it. "Every caller checks `whole > 0` first" makes a zero a caller bug, so a panic is fair.

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 9 "Error Handling", and Rust by Example, "Defining an error type" and "Wrapping errors" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

Choosing how to fail: a bug panics; an expected problem returns `Result`, with an error enum if the caller can act on the cause, or `Box<dyn Error>` if it can only report it.

## 2. What a panic does

When code panics, Rust prints a message to stderr, then unwinds the stack: it walks back up through the calling functions and drops every value on the way, running their `Drop` code (11). Then the thread ends; if it was the main thread, the program exits with code 101. `panic.rs` shows all of this:

```
2
thread 'main' panicked at panic.rs:18:5:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 7
cleanup ran during unwinding
```

The first and last lines are stdout; the panic message is stderr. Set the environment variable `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` and the panic also prints a backtrace: the list of functions that were running, innermost first. Look for your own function names in it (`pick`, then `main`).

Some arithmetic panics too, and some does not:

OperationResult

integer division by zero, `5 / 0`always panics: "attempt to divide by zero"

float division by zero, `1.0 / 0.0`, `0.0 / 0.0`no panic: `inf` and `NaN`, which then spread silently

integer overflow, `u32::MAX + 1`panics in a debug build; wraps around in a release build by default

`a.checked_add(b)`, `checked_mul`, `checked_div` ...never panic: `None` on overflow or division by zero

Panics in Rust are not exceptions to be caught higher up. Treat a panic as "this program has a bug". Expected problems travel as values, in a `Result`.

## 3. `Result` is an enum

`Result` is an ordinary enum from the standard library:

```
enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),   // success, carrying the value
    Err(E),  // failure, carrying an error value
}
```

Functions that can fail return it, and the caller decides what to do. The caller must deal with both cases before it can use the value, because the value sits inside `Ok`. `match` works as with any enum (05), and many error types let you look deeper: `ParseIntError` has a `kind()` you can match on. `result.rs`:

```
match text.parse::<i32>() {
    Ok(n) => println!("{text:?}: number {n}"),
    Err(e) => match e.kind() {
        IntErrorKind::Empty => eprintln!("{text:?}: empty input"),
        IntErrorKind::PosOverflow => eprintln!("{text:?}: too big"),
        _ => eprintln!("{text:?}: {e}"),
    },
}
```

`eprintln!` is `println!` for stderr. Report problems there, so that the normal output on stdout stays clean for whoever reads or pipes it.

## 4. Shortcuts: `unwrap`, `expect` and friends

Writing a full `match` every time is long. `Result` and `Option` have methods for the common cases:

MethodOn `Err` / `None`Use when

`unwrap()`panics with a generic messagequick experiments; failure is a bug

`expect("msg")`panics with your messagefailure is a bug; the message states the invariant you relied on

`unwrap_or(v)`, `unwrap_or_else(|| ..)`gives a fallback valuea default makes sense

`opt.ok_or(e)`, `ok_or_else(|| ..)`turns `None` into `Err(e)`an `Option` inside a function that returns `Result`

`res.map_err(|e| ..)`changes the error into another value or typeadding context, or matching the function's error type

`res.ok()`turns `Err` into `None`, dropping the erroryou really do not care why

```
let m: i32 = "8".parse().expect("a literal we wrote ourselves is always valid");
let pair = "w=40".split_once('=').ok_or(String::from("no '='"));
let width = "4o".parse::<u32>().map_err(|e| format!("bad width: {e}"));
```

Write `expect` messages as the reason it cannot fail ("config was validated at startup"), not as a description of the failure ("parse failed"). If it ever fires, the message tells the reader which assumption broke.

## 5. The `?` operator

Most of the time a function that cannot handle an error should pass it to its caller. The `?` operator does exactly that. After an expression that is a `Result`:

- on `Ok(v)`, the whole expression becomes `v` and the function carries on;

- on `Err(e)`, it returns early with `Err(From::from(e))`.

The two paths through `expr?`. The error goes through `From::from` before the early return.

That `From::from(e)` step converts the error into the error type of the function you are in. It is why one function can use `?` on several different error types, as long as each converts. Without a matching `From` impl the compiler stops you:

```
error[E0277]: `?` couldn't convert the error to `ConfigError`
  --> custom_error.rs:43:28
   |
38 | fn get_number(config: &[(&str, &str)], key: &str) -> Result<u32, ConfigError> {
   |                                                      ------------------------ expected `ConfigError` because of this
...
43 |     Ok(value.parse::<u32>()?)
   |              --------------^ the trait `From<ParseIntError>` is not implemented for `ConfigError`
```

Three rules to remember:

- `?` returns from the nearest function or closure, which must itself return `Result` (or `Option`).

- `?` on an `Option` returns `None` early; it works only in a function that returns `Option`. In a function returning `Result`, convert first: `opt.ok_or(e)?`.

- Inside a closure passed to `map`, a `?` would leave the closure, not your function. Instead let the closure return the `Result` and `collect` into `Result<Vec<_>, _>` (10). That collect stops at the first `Err` and returns it; then use `?` once on the whole thing. A plain `for` loop with `?` inside also works.

```
fn parse_all(items: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<i32>, ParseIntError> {
    items.iter().map(|s| s.parse::<i32>()).collect()
}
```

## 6. `main` can return `Result`

`main` may be declared `fn main() -> Result<(), E>` for an error type `E` that implements `Debug`. Then `?` works in `main` too. If `main` returns `Err`, Rust prints it with `{:?}` to stderr, prefixed with `Error: `, and the exit code is 1 (not 101: nothing panicked). `question_mark.rs` ends this way:

```
Error: "empty line"
```

Use `?` in a `main` that returns `()` and you get:

```
error[E0277]: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option` (or another type that implements `FromResidual`)
   |
30 | fn main() {
   | --------- this function should return `Result` or `Option` to accept `?`
```

## 7. Conversions that can fail: `FromStr` and `TryFrom`

Two standard traits describe conversions that might not work. Implement them and your types join in with the rest of the language.

TraitYou writeYou get

`FromStr``type Err` and `fn from_str(s: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err>``text.parse::<YourType>()`

`TryFrom<U>``type Error` and `fn try_from(u: U) -> Result<Self, Self::Error>``YourType::try_from(u)` and `u.try_into()`

```
impl FromStr for Point {
    type Err = String; // the error type parse() will return
    fn from_str(s: &str) -> Result<Point, String> {
        let (a, b) = s.split_once(',').ok_or(format!("no comma in {s:?}"))?;
        let x = a.trim().parse::<i32>().map_err(|e| format!("x: {e}"))?;
        let y = b.trim().parse::<i32>().map_err(|e| format!("y: {e}"))?;
        Ok(Point { x, y })
    }
}
```

Note that `?` inside `from_str` converts errors into `Self::Err`, the type you declared. The standard library implements `TryFrom` between integer types: `u8::try_from(300_i32)` is an `Err(TryFromIntError)`. `TryFrom` and `TryInto` are in the prelude, so no `use` is needed.

## 8. Custom error types

A library function usually fails for several distinct reasons, and callers need to tell them apart. Give them an enum, one variant per cause. To be a proper error, the type implements three things:

- `Debug` (derive it), so it can be printed with `{:?}` and returned from `main`;

- `Display`, the human message;

- `std::error::Error`, the marker trait for errors, whose one useful method is `source()`.

When a cause comes from a lower layer (a `ParseIntError` inside your config error), keep that lower error inside the variant and hand it back from `source()`. A report can then walk the whole chain. `custom_error.rs`, adapted from Rust by Example:

```
#[derive(Debug)]
enum ConfigError {
    Missing(String),
    BadNumber(ParseIntError),
}

impl Error for ConfigError {
    fn source(&self) -> Option<&(dyn Error + 'static)> {
        match self {
            ConfigError::BadNumber(e) => Some(e),
            ConfigError::Missing(_) => None,
        }
    }
}

impl From<ParseIntError> for ConfigError {
    fn from(e: ParseIntError) -> Self { ConfigError::BadNumber(e) }
}
```

The `From` impl is what lets `value.parse::<u32>()?` work in a function returning `Result<u32, ConfigError>`. And `report` walks the chain with `source()`:

```
height: value is not a number (caused by: invalid digit found in string)
```

Converting withGood for

`impl From<Low> for High`every `?` on a `Low` converts the same way, with no extra code at the call site

`.map_err(|e| High::Variant { context, source: e })?`adding context only the call site knows (a line number, a file name)

Keep each layer's message about its own layer. If `Display` already prints the inner error and `source()` also returns it, a report that walks the chain prints the cause twice. Either show it in the message or return it from `source()`, not both.

Mapping a lower error into an unrelated variant (`.map_err(|_| SizeError::BadUnit(..))`) compiles, but it reports the wrong cause and throws the real one away.

## 9. `Box<dyn Error>`

`Box<dyn Error>` is a trait object (12): "some error, of a type decided at run time". Every error type converts into it through `?`, and so does plain text: `"empty line".into()` or `.ok_or("empty line")?`. That makes it convenient:

```
fn first_number(line: &str) -> Result<i64, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let first = line.split_whitespace().next().ok_or("empty line")?; // &str into Box<dyn Error>
    let n: i64 = first.parse()?;                                     // ParseIntError into Box<dyn Error>
    Ok(n)
}
```

The price is that the concrete type is hidden. A caller holding a `Box<dyn Error>` can print it, walk `source()`, or ask "are you this type?" with `downcast_ref::<ParseIntError>()`, which returns an `Option`. It cannot `match` on causes, and an error made from a `&str` has no public type to downcast to. Comparing message text breaks the day someone rewords the message.

WhereError type

a library, or any function whose caller may react differently per causean error enum

`main`, a script, top-level glue that only reports and exits`Box<dyn Error>`

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- How do I choose between `expect` and returning a `Result`? Where does the doc comment come in?

- What exactly does `?` do with the error before returning, and from which function does it return?

- Why does `?` inside a `map` closure not return from the outer function?

- Why does `source()` matter if `Display` already prints a message?

- When is `Box<dyn Error>` the right error type, and when is it not?

Sources: The Rust Programming Language, ch. 9; Rust by Example, "Defining an error type" and "Wrapping errors" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

Diagram: what `expr?` does.

At the top, `expr?`. Two arrows leave it.
- Left arrow, labelled `Ok(v) / Some(v)`: the whole expression becomes `v` and the function carries on.
- Right arrow, labelled `Err(e) / None`: first "convert: From::from(e)" (into the function's error type), then a red box "return Err(From::from(e))" from the NEAREST function or closure.

Footnotes: the nearest function or closure must itself return Result (or Option, for `?` on an Option). With no From impl for the conversion you get error[E0277] "? couldn't convert the error".

1. Decision "Is the failure a bug?" Yes leads to a red box "panic (expect / assert!): a broken invariant; continuing is wrong".

// Exercise 1: an order total that reports what went wrong
// Practise Option -> Result with ok_or_else, changing errors with map_err,
// and passing them up with ?. (reference solution)
//
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_order.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
// Run builds and runs the tests at the bottom. Replace every todo!() until
// all tests pass. Do not change the tests.

fn price_of(prices: &[(&str, u32)], name: &str) -> Option<u32> {
    prices.iter().find(|(n, _)| *n == name).map(|(_, p)| *p)
}

fn parse_qty(text: &str) -> Result<u32, String> {
    text.parse::<u32>().map_err(|e| format!("bad quantity {text:?}: {e}"))
}

fn order_total(prices: &[(&str, u32)], lines: &[&str]) -> Result<u32, String> {
    let mut total = 0;
    for line in lines {
        let (name, qty) = line.split_once(" x").ok_or_else(|| format!("no quantity in {line:?}"))?;
        let price = price_of(prices, name).ok_or_else(|| format!("unknown item {name:?}"))?;
        total += price * parse_qty(qty)?;
    }
    Ok(total)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    const PRICES: [(&str, u32); 2] = [("tea", 3), ("cake", 5)];

    #[test]
    fn lookups() {
        assert_eq!(price_of(&PRICES, "cake"), Some(5));
        assert_eq!(price_of(&PRICES, "pie"), None);
        assert_eq!(parse_qty("12"), Ok(12));
        assert_eq!(parse_qty("x"), Err(String::from("bad quantity \"x\": invalid digit found in string")));
    }

    #[test]
    fn good_order() {
        assert_eq!(order_total(&PRICES, &["tea x3", "cake x1"]), Ok(14));
        assert_eq!(order_total(&PRICES, &[]), Ok(0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_error_wins() {
        assert_eq!(order_total(&PRICES, &["tea x1", "tea"]), Err(String::from("no quantity in \"tea\"")));
        assert_eq!(order_total(&PRICES, &["pie x2", "tea"]), Err(String::from("unknown item \"pie\"")));
        assert_eq!(
            order_total(&PRICES, &["cake x-1"]),
            Err(String::from("bad quantity \"-1\": invalid digit found in string"))
        );
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a conversion that can fail
// Implement TryFrom<u32> for Month with your own small error type, then use
// it from a parser. TryFrom and TryInto are in the prelude. (reference solution)
//
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_month.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
// Run builds and runs the tests at the bottom. Replace every todo!() until
// all tests pass. Do not change the tests.

use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Month(u8);

// The value that was not a month.
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct NotAMonth(u32);

impl fmt::Display for NotAMonth {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "{} is not a month (1-12)", self.0)
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for NotAMonth {}

impl TryFrom<u32> for Month {
    type Error = NotAMonth;
    fn try_from(n: u32) -> Result<Month, NotAMonth> {
        if (1..=12).contains(&n) { Ok(Month(n as u8)) } else { Err(NotAMonth(n)) }
    }
}

fn parse_month(text: &str) -> Result<Month, String> {
    let n: u32 = text.trim().parse().map_err(|e| format!("not a number: {e}"))?;
    let m = Month::try_from(n).map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
    Ok(m)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn try_from_checks_the_range() {
        assert_eq!(Month::try_from(1), Ok(Month(1)));
        assert_eq!(Month::try_from(12), Ok(Month(12)));
        assert_eq!(Month::try_from(0), Err(NotAMonth(0)));
        assert_eq!(Month::try_from(13), Err(NotAMonth(13)));
        let m: Result<Month, NotAMonth> = 5_u32.try_into(); // the other direction, for free
        assert_eq!(m, Ok(Month(5)));
    }

    #[test]
    fn error_message() {
        assert_eq!(NotAMonth(13).to_string(), "13 is not a month (1-12)");
        let boxed: Box<dyn std::error::Error> = Box::new(NotAMonth(40));
        assert_eq!(boxed.to_string(), "40 is not a month (1-12)");
    }

    #[test]
    fn parse_month_reports_both_kinds() {
        assert_eq!(parse_month(" 7 "), Ok(Month(7)));
        assert_eq!(parse_month("13"), Err(String::from("13 is not a month (1-12)")));
        assert_eq!(parse_month("may"), Err(String::from("not a number: invalid digit found in string")));
    }
}

// Exercise 3: Box<dyn Error> at the top of a program
// A small adder for lines like "2+3". Any error type can go into a
// Box<dyn Error>, including a plain message ("...".into()). (reference solution)
//
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_adder.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
// Run builds and runs the tests at the bottom. Replace every todo!() until
// all tests pass. Do not change the tests.

use std::error::Error;

fn add_line(line: &str) -> Result<i64, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let (a, b) = line.split_once('+').ok_or("missing +")?;
    let a: i64 = a.trim().parse()?;
    let b: i64 = b.trim().parse()?;
    Ok(a + b)
}

fn add_all(text: &str) -> Result<i64, Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut sum = 0;
    for line in text.lines().filter(|l| !l.trim().is_empty()) {
        sum += add_line(line)?;
    }
    Ok(sum)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use std::num::ParseIntError;

    #[test]
    fn adds() {
        assert_eq!(add_line("2+3").unwrap(), 5);
        assert_eq!(add_line(" 10 + -4 ").unwrap(), 6);
    }

    #[test]
    fn errors_keep_their_type_inside_the_box() {
        let e = add_line("2-3").unwrap_err();
        assert_eq!(e.to_string(), "missing +");
        assert!(e.downcast_ref::<ParseIntError>().is_none());
        let e = add_line("2+x").unwrap_err();
        assert_eq!(e.to_string(), "invalid digit found in string");
        assert!(e.downcast_ref::<ParseIntError>().is_some());
    }

    #[test]
    fn add_all_stops_at_the_first_error() {
        assert_eq!(add_all("1+1\n\n2+2\n").unwrap(), 6);
        assert_eq!(add_all("").unwrap(), 0);
        assert_eq!(add_all("1+1\noops\n2+x").unwrap_err().to_string(), "missing +");
    }
}
