## 1. Why generics

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 10.1-10.2, and Rust by Example (Generics, Bounds, Traits, impl Trait), MIT/Apache-2.0.

Suppose you wrote a function that finds the largest `i32` in a slice, then needed the same for `char`. The two bodies would be identical; only the type differs. A type parameter lets you write the body once:

```
fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T {
    let mut largest = &list[0];
    for item in list {
        if item > largest {
            largest = item;
        }
    }
    largest
}
```

Read `<T: PartialOrd>` as "for any type `T` that can be compared with `<` and `>`". The caller picks `T` at each call (`largest(&[34, 50])` uses `i32`, `largest(&['y', 'm'])` uses `char`). The body must compile for every `T` the bounds allow, not just the ones you happen to call it with. `largest.rs` runs this on numbers, chars and Strings.

## 2. Bounds unlock operations

Inside a generic body, the compiler knows nothing about `T` except what the bounds promise. Remove `: PartialOrd` from `largest` and the comparison is refused, even though every type you call it with could be compared:

```
error[E0369]: binary operation `>` cannot be applied to type `&T`
 --> largest.rs:4:17
  |
4 |         if item > largest {
  |            ---- ^ ------- &T
  |            |
  |            &T
help: consider restricting type parameter `T` with trait `PartialOrd`
```

Each operation you want needs its trait:

You want to writeBoundNotes

`a > b`, `a <= b``T: PartialOrd`

`a == b``T: PartialEq`

`a - b` giving a `T``T: Sub<Output = T>`from `std::ops`; same idea for `Add`, `Mul`

`println!("{x}")``T: Display``{x:?}` needs `Debug`

`let x = slice[0];` (an owned copy)`T: Copy`or `T: Clone` and write `slice[0].clone()`

`T::default()``T: Default`0 for numbers, empty for String and Vec

Two of these need a closer look.

The `Output` of an operator trait. `Sub` is declared as `trait Sub<Rhs = Self> { type Output; fn sub(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self::Output; }`. The result type is a separate choice of each implementor, so `T: Sub` alone says "`a - b` is allowed and produces something". If you need the result to be a `T` again (to store it back in a `T` variable or return it), say so: `T: Sub<Output = T>`.

Copying out of a borrowed slice. A `&[T]` lets you look at elements, not take them. `let x = list[0];` would move the element out of a slice you only borrowed, so it is allowed only when `T: Copy` (then it is a copy, not a move). With `T: Clone` you can write `list[0].clone()`; returning `&T` (as `largest` does) needs neither.

```
use std::ops::Mul;

// x * x for any type that can be multiplied by itself, giving the same type back.
fn square<T>(x: T) -> T
where
    T: Mul<Output = T> + Copy,   // Copy: x is used twice, so it must not move
{
    x * x
}
// square(3) == 9, square(1.5) == 2.25
```

Without `Copy`, the first use of `x` in `x * x` moves it (operators take their operands by value), and the second use is E0382. Without `Output = T`, the result is "some type" and cannot be returned as a `T`.

A `where` clause says the same thing as bounds in the angle brackets; it is just easier to read when there are several.

## 3. Generic types and conditional methods

Structs and enums take type parameters too. You already use two: `Option<T>` and `Vec<T>`.

```
struct Point<T> {
    x: T,
    y: T,          // both fields are the same T
}

impl<T> Point<T> {              // for every Point<T>
    fn x(&self) -> &T { &self.x }
}

impl Point<f64> {               // only for Point<f64>
    fn distance_from_origin(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.x.powi(2) + self.y.powi(2)).sqrt()
    }
}
```

The header of each `impl` block decides which types get its methods.

HeaderMethods exist for

`impl<T> Point<T>`every `Point`

`impl Point<f64>`only `Point<f64>`

`impl<T: Display + PartialOrd> Duo<T>`only when `T` meets the bound

Calling a method on a type its impl does not cover is a compile error (E0599), and when the method exists but a bound is unmet, the message says "its trait bounds were not satisfied". A type cannot get the same method name from two impl blocks that overlap (E0592). A method can also have its own type parameters, separate from the struct's: `fn with_y<U>(&self, y: U) -> (T, U)` in `point.rs`.

## 4. What generics cost: monomorphization

The compiler turns generic code into ordinary code by making one concrete copy for each type it is used with. This is called monomorphization.

monomorphization.png: one generic function, one generated copy per type.

- At run time there is no lookup and no boxing: `largest::<i32>` runs exactly like a hand-written `largest_i32`.

- The price is paid at compile time: more code to compile, and a larger binary.

- The body is type-checked once, against the bounds. That is why a missing bound is an error even if every call would work.

Sub-module 12 shows the other approach, trait objects (`dyn Trait`), which keeps one copy and decides at run time.

## 5. Traits, default methods and overrides

A trait is a named set of methods a type can promise to have. A method without a body is required; a method with a body is a default that implementors get for free and may override.

```
trait Summary {
    fn author(&self) -> String;                      // required
    fn summarize(&self) -> String {                  // default
        format!("(Read more from {}...)", self.author())
    }
}

struct Post { author: String }
impl Summary for Post {
    fn author(&self) -> String { format!("@{}", self.author) }
    // summarize: uses the default
}
```

A default method may call any other method of the trait. When it calls `self.author()`, the implementing type's own `author` runs. The same is true for other default methods: if a type overrides one default, every other default that calls it uses the override. In `traits.rs`, `Reply` overrides `summarize`, so `notify(&reply)` prints the reply's version.

A default method can only use what the trait promises about `Self`. It cannot read the implementor's fields (it does not know them), and it cannot use `{self}` unless `Self: Display` is promised. You can require more for one method only with a `where` clause on that method:

```
fn headline(&self) -> String
where
    Self: Display,           // only Display implementors can call headline
{
    format!("** {self} **")
}
```

```
error[E0277]: `Post` doesn't implement `std::fmt::Display`
```

That error appears where someone calls `post.headline()` on a type that is not `Display`; the trait itself still compiles, and every other method stays available to `Post`.

## 6. Who may implement what: the orphan rule

`impl Trait for Type` is allowed only if something in it is local (defined in your crate):

- the trait is local, or

- the type is local, or

- a local type appears as one of the trait's type parameters, as in `impl From<Celsius> for f64`.

orphan-rule.png: local and foreign traits and types, and the one red cell.

A local type wrapped in a foreign generic does not count: `Vec<Celsius>` is a `Vec`, defined in std. A blanket `impl<T> ForeignTrait for T` is never allowed either, because `T` covers types from every crate.

```
error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate
 --> orphan.rs:2:1
  |
2 | impl fmt::Display for Vec<i32> { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^--------
  |                       |
  |                       `Vec` is not defined in the current crate
  = note: define and implement a trait or new type instead
```

Why the rule exists. If two libraries could both write `impl Display for Vec<i32>`, a program using both would have two answers for one question, and nothing to pick between them. The rule makes sure every (trait, type) pair has at most one possible home. It also lets std add new impls without breaking your crate.

Workarounds. Wrap the foreign type in a local newtype, `struct List(Vec<i32>);`, and implement the trait for that (a newtype costs nothing at run time). Or define a local trait and implement it for the foreign type. `orphan.rs` shows all three allowed shapes.

## 7. Blanket impls

A blanket impl implements a trait for every type that meets a bound:

```
trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}
impl<T: Debug> Describe for T {
    fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("<{self:?}>") }
}
// 5.describe(), "hi".describe(), vec![1, 2].describe() all work
```

std uses this pattern: every type that implements `Display` gets `to_string()` through `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`. The blanket covers types written later too, so you never write that impl yourself.

The cost: once a blanket impl covers a type, no other impl of the same trait may cover it. Stable Rust has no "the more specific impl wins" rule, so overlap is an error:

```
error[E0119]: conflicting implementations of trait `Label` for type `u8`
3 | impl<T: Display> Label for T { ... }
  | ---------------------------- first implementation here
4 | impl Label for u8 { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ conflicting implementation for `u8`
```

The order of the impls does not matter, and there is no way to mark one as preferred on stable Rust. (A feature called specialization exists only on nightly.)

## 8. Bounds in signatures and `impl Trait`

Three ways to say "any type that implements `Summary`":

```
fn notify(item: &impl Summary) { ... }           // short form
fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T) { ... }          // generic parameter
fn notify_both<T, U>(a: &T, b: &U)
where
    T: Summary,
    U: Summary + Display,                         // two bounds with +
{ ... }
```

With a named `T` you can force two arguments to have the same type (`fn pair<T: Summary>(a: &T, b: &T)`); `impl Summary` twice allows two different types.

### Argument position vs return position

Who picks the concrete typeHow many types

`fn f(x: impl Trait)`the caller, at each callone per call site (each gets its own monomorphized copy)

`fn f() -> impl Trait`the function bodyexactly one for the whole function; callers only see "some `Trait`"

Return-position `impl Trait` hides the type's name, but there is still exactly one type, fixed at compile time. Returning different types from different branches is an error:

```
error[E0308]: `if` and `else` have incompatible types
3 |     if flag { "yes" } else { 1 }
  |               -----          ^ expected `&str`, found integer
help: you could change the return type to be a boxed trait object
```

To return "one of several kinds" while keeping `-> impl Trait`, make the branches one type: convert them to the same type (for example both to `String`), or define an enum with one variant per kind and implement the trait for the enum. The compiler's suggestion, `Box<dyn Trait>`, is a different trade (a heap allocation and dynamic dispatch) covered in 12.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct Pair<T> {
    pub a: T,
    pub b: T,
}

impl<T> Pair<T> {
    pub fn swap(self) -> Pair<T> {
        Pair { a: self.b, b: self.a }
    }
}

impl<T: PartialOrd> Pair<T> {
    pub fn larger(&self) -> &T {
        if self.b > self.a { &self.b } else { &self.a }
    }
}

pub fn first_or<T: Clone>(items: &[T], fallback: T) -> T {
    if items.is_empty() { fallback } else { items[0].clone() }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn swap_any_type() {
        let p = Pair { a: String::from("x"), b: String::from("y") };
        assert_eq!(p.swap(), Pair { a: String::from("y"), b: String::from("x") });
        assert_eq!(Pair { a: 1, b: 2 }.swap(), Pair { a: 2, b: 1 });
    }

    #[test]
    fn larger_numbers_and_strings() {
        assert_eq!(*Pair { a: 3, b: 9 }.larger(), 9);
        assert_eq!(Pair { a: String::from("pear"), b: String::from("apple") }.larger(), "pear");
        assert_eq!(*Pair { a: 4.5, b: 4.5 }.larger(), 4.5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_or_fallback() {
        assert_eq!(first_or(&[7, 8], 0), 7);
        assert_eq!(first_or(&[], 0), 0);
        let words = vec![String::from("hi")];
        assert_eq!(first_or(&words, String::from("none")), "hi");
        assert_eq!(words.len(), 1); // still ours
    }
}

## 1. Defining and creating structs

A struct groups related values under one name, and gives each value a field name. Where a tuple says "an `(String, String, bool, u64)`", a struct says what each part means.

```
struct Profile {
    name: String,
    email: String,
    active: bool,
    visits: u64,
}
```

The definition is a template. To make a value, write the struct name and a value for every field, in any order. Read a field with a dot.

```
let mut first = Profile {
    email: String::from("a@example.com"),
    name: String::from("a"),
    active: true,
    visits: 0,
};
first.visits += 1;
println!("{} has {} visits", first.name, first.visits);
```

Mutability belongs to the binding, not to fields. To change any field, the whole value must be `let mut`. There is no way to mark one field `mut`.

A struct owns its fields. When the struct goes out of scope, every field is dropped with it. Fields of type `String` or `Vec` follow the move rules you saw in 02.

This lesson adapts The Rust Programming Language, chapter 5 and Rust by Example (MIT/Apache-2.0). Open `define.rs` and `methods.rs` alongside it.

## 2. Shorthand and update syntax

Field init shorthand. When a variable has the same name as the field, write the name once:

```
fn build_profile(name: String, email: String) -> Profile {
    Profile { name, email, active: true, visits: 0 } // name: name, email: email
}
```

Struct update syntax. `..other` at the end of a struct literal means "every field I did not write out comes from `other`".

```
let second = Profile {
    email: String::from("b@example.com"),
    ..first
};
```

Update syntax is not a special copy. It is a set of ordinary field assignments, so each field follows its own rule:

FieldWhere it comes fromWhat happens to `first`'s field

`email`written outuntouched, still usable

`name` (`String`)`..first`moved into `second`; `first.name` is unusable

`active` (`bool`)`..first`copied; still usable

`visits` (`u64`)`..first`copied; still usable

After this, `first.visits` and `first.email` still work, but `first.name` and `first` as a whole do not:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `first.name`
```

Ask per field: did I write it out? If not, is its type Copy? Copy fields are copied, everything else moves. To keep a non-Copy field, write it out (for example `tags: base.tags.clone()`).

## 3. Tuple structs and unit structs

A tuple struct has a name but no field names. Fields are read by position: `.0`, `.1`.

```
struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);
struct Meters(f64);

let red = Rgb(255, 0, 0);
let run = Meters(5.5);
println!("{} {}", red.0, run.0);
```

Two tuple structs with the same field types are still different types. A function that takes `Meters` will not accept a plain `f64` or some other one-field struct. A one-field tuple struct used this way is called a newtype: it gives a plain number its own meaning, so the compiler stops you mixing metres with seconds.

A unit struct has no fields at all: `struct Marker;`. It is useful later, when a type matters but carries no data (for example, to implement a trait on it in 09).

## 4. Methods

A method is a function defined inside an `impl` block whose first parameter is `self` in some form. It is called with dot syntax on a value.

```
struct Rectangle { width: u32, height: u32 }

impl Rectangle {
    fn area(&self) -> u32 {
        self.width * self.height
    }
    fn scale(&mut self, factor: u32) {
        self.width *= factor;
        self.height *= factor;
    }
}
```

`&self` is short for `self: &Self`, and `Self` is the type the `impl` is for. A method call is plain function call syntax in disguise:

You writeThe compiler calls

`big.area()``Rectangle::area(&big)`

`big.scale(2)``Rectangle::scale(&mut big, 2)`

`big.into_pair()``Rectangle::into_pair(big)`

The compiler adds the `&` or `&mut` for you (automatic referencing). Because `big.scale(2)` really takes `&mut big`, `big` must be declared `let mut`, exactly as if you had written the borrow yourself.

## 5. Associated functions

A function in an `impl` block without `self` is an associated function. It belongs to the type, not to a value, so it is called with `::`.

```
impl Rectangle {
    fn square(size: u32) -> Self {
        Self { width: size, height: size }
    }
}

let small = Rectangle::square(3);
```

- Constructors are usually associated functions. `new` is a convention, not a keyword: name them for what they build (`square`, `empty`, `with_limit`).

- Inside an `impl`, `Self` names the type, so `Self { .. }` and `Rectangle { .. }` mean the same.

- A type can have many `impl` blocks; they all add to the same type.

You will often build text inside methods. `format!` takes the same arguments as `println!` but returns the text as a `String` instead of printing it:

```
fn label(&self) -> String {
    format!("{}x{}", self.width, self.height)
}
```

## 6. Receivers and borrows

The first parameter of a method is its receiver. It is the same choice you make for any function parameter in 02 and 03: borrow, borrow mutably, or take ownership.

ReceiverThe method getsThe caller needsValue usable afterwards?Typical use

`&self`a read-only viewany bindingyes`area`, `len`, `is_empty`

`&mut self`exclusive write accessa `let mut` binding and no other live borrowyes`scale`, `push`, `record`

`self`ownershipany bindingno, it moved (unless the type is Copy)`into_pair`, `build`, `close`

Pick the weakest receiver that works. Reading needs `&self`. Changing needs `&mut self`. Only take `self` when the method uses the value up or turns it into something else.

A method that takes `self` may also change it before handing it back. Write `mut self`: the method owns the value, so it may mutate it.

```
fn doubled(mut self) -> Self {
    self.width *= 2;
    self   // ownership goes back to the caller
}

let r = Rectangle::square(2).doubled(); // calls chain, each one takes and returns
```

### Fields versus methods

Inside one function, the borrow checker tracks fields separately. Holding `&mut s.items` while reading `s.limit` is fine: they are different places in memory.

A method call is different. The checker looks only at the method's signature, never its body. A method `fn items_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Vec<i32>` borrows all of `self` mutably, for as long as the returned reference is in use. While that reference lives, calling even a `&self` method on the same value is a conflict, because the signature does not say which field it touches.

Checking only signatures is deliberate: a library can change a method body without breaking any caller. The price is that the checker cannot see that two methods use different fields.

## 7. Derive: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default

A new struct can do almost nothing: you cannot print it with `{:?}`, compare it with `==` or `clone()` it. The `#[derive(...)]` attribute asks the compiler to write the code for common traits (shared behaviour) for you.

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
```

DeriveGives youDerived behaviour

`Debug``{:?}`, `{:#?}` (pretty), `dbg!`prints the type name and each field

`Clone``.clone()`clones each field

`Copy`implicit copies instead of movesbitwise copy; needs `Clone` too, and every field must be Copy

`PartialEq``==`, `!=`equal when every field is equal

`PartialOrd``<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`compares fields in declaration order: the first field decides unless equal, then the next; needs `PartialEq`

`Default``T::default()`each field's own default: 0, `false`, empty `String`/`Vec`

So for `Point`, `Point { x: 1, y: 9 } < Point { x: 2, y: 0 }` is `true`: `x` is compared first and decides. Field order is part of the meaning of a derived ordering.

`dbg!(expr)` prints the file, line, expression and value to stderr, then returns the value, so you can wrap it around any expression.

A derive works only if every field's type has that trait. Deriving `Default` on a struct with a field of a type that has no `Default` fails with `error[E0277]: the trait bound ... is not satisfied`. Same for `Copy` with a `String` field.

### Why nothing is derived automatically

- The derived meaning can be wrong. Field-by-field `==` is wrong if a field is a cache or a counter that should not affect equality. Declaration-order `<` is wrong if "smaller" means smaller area.

- It can leak. `Debug` prints every field, including a password or token.

- It changes cost and rules. `Clone` makes deep copies easy to write; `Copy` changes moves into copies everywhere.

- It is a promise. Once callers rely on `==` or `Copy`, removing it breaks them.

## 8. Writing Default by hand

When zero values are wrong defaults (a retry count of 0, a timeout of 0 seconds), write `Default` yourself instead of deriving it:

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Settings {
    name: String,
    retries: u32,
    verbose: bool,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Settings { name: String::from("main"), retries: 3, verbose: false }
    }
}

let s = Settings { verbose: true, ..Settings::default() };
```

Traits in general are covered in 09. This one shape, `impl Default for T { fn default() -> Self { ... } }`, is all you need now. It combines well with update syntax: `..Settings::default()` fills every field you did not write.

If a type has both `new()` and `Default`, make them agree. A `default()` that quietly gives different values from `new()` surprises every caller.

## 9. Check yourself

Answer these out loud or ask the Tutor about them. Then try the exercises.

- Why must I write `let mut` to call a `&mut self` method?

- When should a method take `self` by value?

- After `let b = Config { name: x, ..a };`, which fields of `a` can I still use?

- Why doesn't Rust derive `Debug` and `PartialEq` for every struct?

- Two fields of a struct, `width` then `height`, with derived `PartialOrd`: which field decides `a < b`?

Exercises: `ex1_steps.rs` (methods and receivers), `ex2_wallet.rs` (a type that guards its own rules), `ex3_version.rs` (derive order and a hand-written `Default`).

// Exercise 1: methods, associated functions and receivers.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_steps.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A StepLog keeps a daily step goal and the steps recorded so far.
// Reference solution.
// The receivers below are placeholders: if a method has to change the log,
// change its receiver too.

struct StepLog {
    goal: u32,
    days: u32,
    total: u32,
}

impl StepLog {
    /// A new log with a daily goal and nothing recorded.
    fn new(goal: u32) -> Self {
        StepLog { goal, days: 0, total: 0 }
    }

    /// Record one day's steps.
    fn record(&mut self, steps: u32) {
        self.days += 1;
        self.total += steps;
    }

    /// Average steps per recorded day. 0 when nothing is recorded yet.
    fn average(&self) -> u32 {
        if self.days == 0 {
            return 0;
        }
        self.total / self.days
    }

    /// True when the average reaches the goal.
    fn on_track(&self) -> bool {
        self.average() >= self.goal
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn new_log_is_empty() {
        let log = StepLog::new(8000);
        assert_eq!((log.goal, log.days, log.total), (8000, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn average_of_an_empty_log_is_zero() {
        assert_eq!(StepLog::new(10).average(), 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn records_and_averages() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(5000);
        log.record(4000);
        log.record(7000);
        assert_eq!(log.days, 2);
        assert_eq!(log.average(), 5500);
        assert!(log.on_track());
    }

    #[test]
    fn below_goal_is_not_on_track() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(9000);
        log.record(3000);
        assert!(!log.on_track());
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a type that keeps its own rules.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_wallet.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Wallet holds money in cents (whole numbers, so no rounding errors).
// Reference solution.
// Tip: format!("{:02}", 5) gives "05".

struct Wallet {
    owner: String,
    cents: u64,
}

impl Wallet {
    /// A new, empty wallet.
    fn open(owner: &str) -> Wallet {
        Wallet { owner: owner.to_string(), cents: 0 }
    }

    /// Add money.
    fn deposit(&mut self, cents: u64) {
        self.cents += cents;
    }

    /// Take money out. If there is not enough, return false and change nothing.
    fn spend(&mut self, cents: u64) -> bool {
        if cents > self.cents {
            return false;
        }
        self.cents -= cents;
        true
    }

    /// The balance as text, for example "ada: $12.05".
    fn balance_text(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}: ${}.{:02}", self.owner, self.cents / 100, self.cents % 100)
    }

    /// Close the wallet: give back the owner's name and the remaining cents.
    fn close(self) -> (String, u64) {
        (self.owner, self.cents)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn opens_empty() {
        let w = Wallet::open("ada");
        assert_eq!(w.owner, "ada");
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn deposit_and_spend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1500);
        assert!(w.spend(295));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 1205);
    }

    #[test]
    fn refuses_to_overspend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(100);
        assert!(!w.spend(101));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 100);
    }

    #[test]
    fn formats_dollars_and_cents() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1205);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $12.05");
        w.spend(1200);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $0.05");
    }

    #[test]
    fn close_gives_everything_back() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("bo");
        w.deposit(42);
        let (owner, left) = w.close();
        assert_eq!(owner, "bo");
        assert_eq!(left, 42);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: what derive gives you, and Default by hand.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_version.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Version like 1.4.2 must compare the usual way: major first, then minor,
// then patch. So 1.4.2 < 1.10.0 < 2.0.0.
//
// TODO 1: the derive list is right, but comparisons come out wrong.
//         Fix it without writing any comparison code yourself.
// TODO 2: the default version is 0.1.0, not 0.0.0. Write Default by hand.
// TODO 3: write bump_minor: 1.4.2 becomes 1.5.0.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]
struct Version {
    major: u32, // derived PartialOrd compares fields in declaration order
    minor: u32,
    patch: u32,
}

impl Version {
    fn new(major: u32, minor: u32, patch: u32) -> Version {
        Version { major, minor, patch }
    }

    fn bump_minor(self) -> Version {
        Version { minor: self.minor + 1, patch: 0, ..self }
    }
}

impl Default for Version {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Version::new(0, 1, 0)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn major_decides_first() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 2) < Version::new(2, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn minor_decides_before_patch() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 9) < Version::new(1, 10, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_is_0_1_0() {
        assert_eq!(Version::default(), Version::new(0, 1, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn bump_minor_resets_patch() {
        assert_eq!(Version::new(1, 4, 2).bump_minor(), Version::new(1, 5, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn versions_are_copy() {
        let v = Version::new(1, 0, 0);
        let w = v;
        assert_eq!(v, w);
        assert_eq!(format!("{w:?}").contains("major: 1"), true);
    }
}

### can_hold and receivers · 2 Nov

## `can_hold` and receivers (methods.rs lines 22-24, 42)

- `fn can_hold(&self, other: &Rectangle) -> bool` returns true only when `self` is strictly bigger in both dimensions.
- `&&` means both sides must be true, so one failing side makes the whole expression false.
- `>` is strict, not `>=`. So a 4x5 holds a 3x3, but a 5x4 does NOT hold a 4x5 (height 4 is not > 5).
- What the body computes and what the method needs from each value are two separate questions.
- If the parameter were `other: Rectangle` instead of `&Rectangle`, the call `big.can_hold(&small)` on line 42 would not compile: it passes a reference where a whole value is expected. Dropping the `&` at the call site would move `small` into the method, so `small` could not be used again.
- `can_hold` only reads `other`'s two fields to compare them, so `&Rectangle` is enough. Pick the weakest receiver that works: `&self` to read, `&mut self` to change, `self` only when the value is used up.

### Receivers: area vs into_pair, record · 2 Nov

## Receivers: reading vs using up, and `&mut self`

- `area` (`methods.rs` lines 18-20) only reads `self.width` and `self.height`. It leaves the value alone, so `&self` is enough.
- `into_pair` (lines 33-35) uses the value up: it hands back `(self.width, self.height)` and the original rectangle is consumed. That need forces `self`.
- Same struct, two different needs. Pick the weakest receiver that works.
- The body and the receiver are separate questions: what the body computes is one thing, what the method needs from each value is another.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { searchProducts, type Product } from "../api/search";

export function useSearch(query: string, inStockOnly: boolean) {
  const [results, setResults] = useState<Product[]>([]);
  const [total, setTotal] = useState(0);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (query.trim().length < 2) {
      setResults([]);
      setTotal(0);
      return;
    }
    setLoading(true);
    setError(null);
    searchProducts(query, inStockOnly)
      .then((res) => {
        setResults(res.items);
        setTotal(res.total);
      })
      .catch(() => setError("Search failed. Try again."))
      .finally(() => setLoading(false));
  }, [query, inStockOnly]);

  return { results, total, loading, error };
}

Two problems in the blocking path. poll: sensfifo_poll builds the mask from kfifo_is_empty but never calls poll_wait(filp, &dev->readq, wait). poll_wait is what adds the caller to the device's wait queue so the poll syscall is woken when data arrives; without it the write's wake_up_interruptible never reaches the poller, so the syscall sleeps for the whole timeout and only re-checks the device when the timeout expires (do_poll polls every fd once more after timing out): it returns 1 with POLLIN at 2000 ms although the sample arrived at 300 ms, and with an infinite timeout it would never return. The fix is to call poll_wait before testing the fifo and then OR in EPOLLIN | EPOLLRDNORM when non-empty (EPOLLOUT | EPOLLWRNORM too, since the device is writable). Blocking read and signals: the loop calls wait_event_interruptible(dev->readq, !kfifo_is_empty(&dev->fifo)) but ignores its return. wait_event_interruptible returns -ERESTARTSYS when a signal is delivered; the code discards that and loops. The signal stays pending (it is only handled on the way back to user space), so every later wait_event_interruptible returns -ERESTARTSYS at once and the reader spins in the kernel: the sig test shows the child still in read() 4500 ms after the signal with 4.49 s of system CPU time, its handler running only after a write released the read, which then returned 4096. The fix is `if (wait_event_interruptible(...)) { mutex is not held here; return -ERESTARTSYS; }`, which the kernel turns into -EINTR for user space. The locking around the wait is actually correct: the loop unlocks before sleeping and re-checks the condition after re-locking, so there is no lost wakeup; wake_up_interruptible is called from write after kfifo_put. read still returns 4096 here because of the seed bug.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - returns count
  - stale kernel stack
  - no .owner
  - never calls poll_wait
  - returns -ERESTARTSYS
  - ignores its return

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

# Proposal: agent-pipeline for every backend team

**Author:** Head of Platform
**Date:** 10 Sep 2026, for decision at Engineering leads on Tuesday 15 Sep

## Why

agent-pipeline has taken small backend tickets since 2 June: 488 runs so far. An agent-ok ticket goes
from label to PR in about 20 minutes, and every backend team has asked for it. Splitting the work between
agents is what makes it reliable: no single agent could hold the research, the code and the review for a
ticket like TRK-1482 in one context.

## What we fixed after INC-4417

| PR | Change | Deployed |
|---|---|---|
| #214 (pipeline owner) | `handoff.maxWords` from 120 to 400 | 2 Sep |
| #219 (on-call engineer) | The reviewer also receives the summarizer's brief; the revision limit is one counter instead of one per message | 8 Sep |
| #217 (pipeline owner) | Summarizer prompt: "Always keep every constraint, limit and caveat from the notes, word for word." | 9 Sep, 09:40 |
| | model-3 for the coder and the reviewer | from 21 Sep |

PR #219 changes two places in `src/pipeline.ts`:

```ts
// One count of revision rounds for the pipeline, instead of one per message.
let revisionRounds = 0;

export async function runPipeline(
```

```ts
      case "reviewer": {
        // The reviewer also gets the brief, so it knows what the change is for.
        const reviewerInput = messages
          .filter((m) => m.from === "coder" || m.from === "summarizer")
          .map((m) => `[From ${m.from}]: ${m.content}`)
          .join("\n\n");
        const res = await agents.reviewer.run(reviewerInput);

        if (verdict(res.content) === "APPROVED") { ... }

        if (revisionRounds >= config.review.maxRevisionRounds) {
          status = "escalated";
          send("reviewer", "orchestrator", `ESCALATED after ${revisionRounds} revision rounds.\n\n${res.content}`, { ... });
          break;
        }
        revisionRounds += 1;
```

## Evidence that it works

**1. TRK-1482 now comes out right.** I re-ran it three times on 9 Sep, right after #217 went out:

| Run | Revision rounds | Verdict | The limiter it built |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3188 | 1 | approved | express-rate-limit, Redis store, key `"tax-api:prod"`, 540 per 60 s window |
| 3190 | 1 | approved | the same |
| 3191 | 0 | approved | the same, with the limit read from `TAX_API_RATE_LIMIT` (default 540) |

All three count against the tax API key with a shared store, which is exactly what INC-4417 needed.

**2. The tests pass.** `npm test`: 2 passed, 1 skipped.

**3. The revision cap works now.**

| | Runs | Approved | Escalated to a human | Stopped by the 20-minute timeout |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 Jun to 7 Sep | 476 | 439 | 0 | 37 |
| 8 Sep to 10 Sep (after #219) | 12 | 7 | 5 | 0 |

## Proposal

- From 1 October any backend team (11 teams) can label tickets `agent-ok`. Worker concurrency from 4 to 8,
  still one process.
- Two more agents in the same pattern: a **tester** that writes tests from the brief, and a **security
  reviewer** that reviews the coder's messages for security issues.
- Merge rule: the reviewer agent's APPROVED plus one human approval.
- Quality: we report the approval rate per team every month. Today it is 91% (446 of 488 runs).
- Cost: about $1.10 a run in llm-gw charges today; about $1.60 with five agents.

# Request approval app

An Oracle APEX app where managers review and approve purchase requests.

- Page 10 lists purchase requests in an Interactive Report. Filters: status, and a search box on the title.
- A manager picks a request and presses Approve.
- Files here are readable summaries of the app's settings with the real code in them.
- `db/` is the schema and the PL/SQL package. `apex/` is the app-level setup and page 10.

--- apex/app_setup.sql ---
-- Application: Request approval
-- Authentication scheme: Oracle APEX accounts
-- Maximum session length: 28800 seconds

-- Application item: G_BU_LIST
--   Session state protection: Restricted, may not be set from the browser


-- Application process: Load access list
--   Point: After authentication
begin
  select listagg(bu_id, ',') within group (order by bu_id)
    into :G_BU_LIST
    from user_access
   where app_user = :APP_USER;
end;


-- Authorization scheme: IS_MANAGER
--   Type: Exists SQL query
--   Evaluation point: Once per session
--   Error message: Only managers can do this.
select 1
  from user_access
 where app_user    = :APP_USER
   and access_role = 'MANAGER'

--- apex/page_10_processes.sql ---
-- Page 10: Purchase requests

-- Button: APPROVE
--   Action: Submit page
--   Authorization scheme: IS_MANAGER


-- Validation: Request selected
--   Type: Item is not null (P10_REQUEST_ID)
--   Error message: Select a request first.


-- Process: Approve request
--   Point: Processing
--   When button pressed: APPROVE
begin
  request_api.approve_request(p_request_id => :P10_REQUEST_ID);

--- apex/page_10_report.sql ---
-- Page 10: Purchase requests

-- Items
--   P10_STATUS      Select list (DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED, REJECTED)   Session state protection: Unrestricted
--   P10_SEARCH      Text field                                           Session state protection: Unrestricted
--   P10_REQUEST_ID  Hidden, set by the "Select" link column               Session state protection: Checksum required, session level


-- Region: Requests
--   Type: Interactive Report
--   Source: PL/SQL function body returning SQL query
--   Page items to submit: P10_STATUS, P10_SEARCH
--   Cache: enabled, by user, 600 seconds
--   Rows per page: 15
--   Column TITLE: Escape special characters: Yes
declare
  l_sql varchar2(4000);
begin
  l_sql := 'select request_id, bu_id, requester, title, amount, status, created_on '
        || 'from purchase_requests '
        || 'where instr('','' || :G_BU_LIST || '','', '','' || bu_id || '','') > 0 ';

  if :P10_STATUS is not null then
    l_sql := l_sql || 'and status = ''' || :P10_STATUS || ''' ';
  end if;

  if :P10_SEARCH is not null then
    l_sql := l_sql || 'and upper(title) like ''%' || upper(:P10_SEARCH) || '%'' ';
  end if;

  l_sql := l_sql || 'order by created_on desc';
  return l_sql;
end;


-- Dynamic action: Refresh requests
--   Event: Change
--   Items: P10_STATUS, P10_SEARCH
--   True action: Refresh region "Requests"

--- db/request_api.pkb ---
create or replace package body request_api as

  function can_see_bu (p_bu_id in number) return boolean is
  begin
    return instr(',' || v('G_BU_LIST') || ',', ',' || p_bu_id || ',') > 0;
  end can_see_bu;


  procedure approve_request (p_request_id in number) is
    l_bu_id purchase_requests.bu_id%type;
  begin
    select bu_id
      into l_bu_id
      from purchase_requests
     where request_id = p_request_id;

    if not can_see_bu(l_bu_id) then
      raise_application_error(-20001, 'You do not have access to this business unit');
    end if;

    update purchase_requests
       set status      = 'APPROVED',
           approved_by = v('APP_USER'),
           approved_on = sysdate
     where request_id  = p_request_id;

    commit;
  end approve_request;

end request_api;
/

At a high level, the click submits Page 10, APEX enforces the button’s authorization and validation, then the page process calls the PL/SQL package to do the actual update and commit.

Flow from click to approved:
1. The manager clicks **Approve** on Page 10.
2. The button is configured as **Submit page** and has the **IS_MANAGER** authorization scheme, so only users who pass that check can use it.
3. On submit, APEX runs the validation **Request selected**. That checks `P10_REQUEST_ID` is not null, so a request has to be chosen first.
4. If validation passes, the page process **Approve request** runs.
5. That process calls `request_api.approve_request(p_request_id => :P10_REQUEST_ID);`.
6. Inside `request_api.approve_request`, the package looks up the request’s `bu_id` from `purchase_requests`.
7. It then calls `can_see_bu` to verify the signed-in user can access that business unit. If not, it raises an application error.
8. If allowed, it updates the row in `purchase_requests`, setting:
   - `status = 'APPROVED'`
   - `approved_by = v('APP_USER')`
   - `approved_on = sysdate`
9. The procedure commits, so the change is saved immediately.
10. After the page processes finish, APEX shows the success message: `Request <id> approved`.

Where each rule is decided:
- **Who is a manager:** the application authorization scheme `IS_MANAGER` in `apex/app_setup.sql`.
- **Whether a request must be selected:** the page validation in `apex/page_10_processes.sql`.
- **Whether the user may approve that specific request’s BU:** `request_api.approve_request` and `can_see_bu` in `db/request_api.pkb`.
- **What rows appear on the report:** the Page 10 report query filters `purchase_requests` by the user’s `G_BU_LIST`, plus optional status/search filters from page items.
- **How `G_BU_LIST` gets set:** the application process **Load access list** after authentication, from `user_access` for the current `APP_USER`.

So the UI and APEX rules decide who can click and submit; the package decides whether that specific request can be approved and performs the database update. If you want, I can also trace the exact sequence of APEX page events and item/session-state handling.

{"move_object":{"move":"REDIRECT","confusion":"The 'Drop only runs once and won't care' belief and the 'take is same as replace' belief","confusion_skill":"G3","note":"","response":"You have a confusion about what `std::mem::take` does. It does leave the field uninitialized after moving the String out, which would cause undefined behavior if Drop tries to access it later. The Drop impl for Holder needs to be able to run `self.label` safely, and it expects every field to still have a value to read.

Specifically, `std::mem::take(&mut h.label)` works differently from a simple move:
1. It moves the current String value OUT (`let label = ...`)
2. It REPLACES the field with `String::new()` which is an empty string ""
3. This keeps `h.label` in a valid state when Drop runs

Compare this to `std::mem::replace(&mut h.label, String::from("new"))` (line 52 in raii.rs) - this is different because it specifies what replacement value to use. Take always uses `Default::default()`

So `take` isn't the same as `replace` - `take` is a convenience wrapper that uses `replace` with `Default::default()` as the new value.

Since you can't move fields out directly from types with `Drop` (lines 29-31 of the lesson), `take` provides a safe way to extract a field while preserving the Drop-correct state. It's not redundant; it's the only safe way to do this specific pattern."}}

# Email drafter benchmark: how we evaluate

Care AI team | 25 September 2026 | method behind the design note, Table 1

## Eval set

150 customer emails from the Care queue, received 1 to 14 September 2026, each with a snapshot
of the account data as it was when the email arrived.

- 100 drawn at random from the queue.
- 50 added by hand: emails that care agents flagged in #care-ai-feedback as poor v1 drafts, so
  the set covers the emails that matter most.

| Category | Random | Flagged | Eval set |
|---|---|---|---|
| document_request | 24 | 0 | 24 |
| billing_payment | 21 | 4 | 25 |
| policy_change | 17 | 0 | 17 |
| claim_status | 14 | 0 | 14 |
| cancellation_renewal | 6 | 0 | 6 |
| refund_dispute | 7 | 21 | 28 |
| coverage_question | 11 | 25 | 36 |
| All | 100 | 50 | 150 |

The same 150 emails were our development set for v2: we ran each prompt version from v2.0
(26 Aug) to v2.7 (18 Sep) on them and kept the best, v2.7.

## Systems

- v1: the production agent and prompt as of 18 Sep.
- v2: v2.7, four agents.
- v2 without the reviewer (ablation): v2.7 with the first draft taken as final.

One draft per email per system, at the production temperature (0.7). Runs 22 to 24 Sep.

## Judge

- Model: llm-pro, temperature 0, one call per draft.
- Input: the customer's email thread and the draft. The judge does not see the account data,
  the ledger or the policy wording (keeps the judge fast and cheap).
- Rubric R-3, the same checklist the reviewer agent uses, so the judge and the reviewer agree:

| Criterion | 0 to 20 points for |
|---|---|
| Accuracy | facts and amounts are consistent with the information given |
| Completeness | every question in the email is answered |
| Resolution | the customer gets a clear resolution or next step |
| Tone | warm, empathetic, on brand |
| Policy | nothing is promised outside company policy |

The five scores are summed to a score from 0 to 100. Each draft is scored on its own; v1's
drafts were scored on 23 Sep and v2's on 24 Sep.

## What we report

- The mean judge score per system. v2 is better if its mean is higher.
- No confidence intervals: 150 emails is a good-sized set.
- Mean draft length: v1 159 words, v2 221 words.

## Human check

The Care QA lead read 20 v2 drafts picked at random on 24 Sep. 18 were fine. 2 stated
a wrong amount: E-20122 (a refund amount) and E-20116 (a deductible). The judge scored those
two 88 and 85.

Measured in the same runs and reported in the design note, Table 1. Not part of the pass or fail.

uplink_send ignores the return value of sem_wait(&u->slots). When a signal handler runs in a thread blocked in sem_wait, glibc returns -1 with errno EINTR (the handlers are installed without SA_RESTART, and this behaviour is documented in sem_wait(3) and signal(7)). The worker then uploads without a permit, and its sem_post at the end adds a permit that was never taken: the semaphore now holds 3. The chart shows exactly that: in_flight max at most 2 until the health agent starts at minute 4, then 3 from minute 4.0 on, slots + in_flight stuck at 3, and 429 answers every minute after that (none before), each one a failed upload retried after a backoff. The collector's own count agrees: 3 concurrent uploads from this device in every minute from minute 5. Why workers see SIGUSR1 at all: main.c installs the handlers, creates the workers, and only then blocks SIGHUP and SIGUSR1 with pthread_sigmask, so the workers inherited an empty mask. That is what main's comment intends ('HUP and USR1 go to the other threads'), without seeing that those threads block in sem_wait. The kernel delivers the process-directed SIGUSR1 to a thread that does not block it, wk0. It only matters when wk0 happens to be waiting for a slot, which is why the count stepped once. It went no further because with 3 permits wk0 rarely waits: a third upload gets 429 at once and frees its permit. SIGHUP from the daily logrotate adds to it the same way. Fix: retry, `while (sem_wait(&u->slots) != 0) { if (errno != EINTR) ...error... }`, as the sem_timedwait example in the man page does; and block SIGHUP, SIGUSR1 and SIGTERM in main before pthread_create, handling them in one place (sigwait or signalfd in one thread). Check sem_getvalue in the stats against GW_UPLINK_SLOTS so a drift shows up as an alarm.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - the same condition variable
  - another worker instead
  - two condition variables
  - inherited an empty mask
  - never taken
  - returns -1 with errno EINTR

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I’d start by assuming `uplink_send()` is failing to enforce the slot limit atomically. If `in_flight` is checked and incremented separately, two workers can race and both decide a slot is available, which would let `in_flight` exceed `GW_UPLINK_SLOTS`.

So the lines I’d focus on are the ones that:
- read `in_flight` or available slots,
- decide whether to wait or proceed,
- increment `in_flight`,
- and enqueue the request without holding the same lock through all of that.

That kind of gap would fit the chart: once SIGUSR1 starts, the extra stats logging adds scheduling noise, and if `uplink_send()` is using a mutex/condvar incorrectly, the workers can slip past the limit and stack up more than `GW_UPLINK_SLOTS` uploads in flight.

What I’d change is to make slot acquisition a single critical section: hold the uplink mutex, wait in a `while (in_flight == GW_UPLINK_SLOTS)` loop, increment `in_flight` before dropping the lock, and only decrement it when the upload completes or is cancelled. If there’s already a separate state machine around retries, I’d keep the slot reserved across retries too, otherwise a retry storm can also make the accounting look like the limit is being exceeded.

If you want, I can also trace the specific `uplink_send()` call flow from the code and point out where I’d expect the race to be.

{"move_object":{"move":"EXPLAIN","confusion":"","confusion_skill":"","note":"Learner asked why Rust cannot copy ptr/len/cap and keep both names for a String. Aiming at B2 (move semantics) and B3 (Copy vs Clone). They are at step 5 of 15, moves.rs not yet run. Next turn: check they can say what a move actually copies (the three stack fields) and why two owners would free the buffer twice.","response":"Good question, and the sneaky part is this: Rust *does* copy those three fields. The pointer, length and capacity get copied bit for bit. What it refuses to do is leave both names usable.

Think about what the heap buffer actually is. That is the data. The three fields are only a note saying where the data lives. If `s1` and `s2` both held that same note, then at the closing `}` both would run `String`'s destructor on the same buffer. It would be freed twice. The second free is a double free, the bug the lesson opens with.

So a move is: copy the three fields, then mark the old name dead. One note, one owner.

`clone()` copies those same three fields too, but it also allocates a second buffer and copies every byte into it. Now each name points at its own buffer, so both can own theirs.

So: if both names kept the same pointer, which one frees the buffer at the end, and what would the other one be freeing?","topic":"why moves, not copies"}}

When you write `let s2 = s1;` for a `String`:
- Rust copies the stack fields (pointer, length, capacity) - cheap.
- Then `s1` is marked as moved: unusable.

- A `String` cannot have two owners because each would try to free the heap buffer at scope end - that would be a double free bug.
Comparing to `i32` which implements `Copy`:
- The whole value is on the stack (just the number itself).
- No heap memory to free.
- Copying it is as cheap as moving it.

Reference: section 4. Moves and section 7. Copy and Clone.","confusion":"strong; wrong belief: a String could be copied by letting two owners exist. double free happens when both try to free the same heap buffer","topic":"why String is not Copy","response":"You noticed a real tension the compiler is solving. the move copies only the stack fields, then marks `s1` as unusable. Only the new owner can free. Compare this to `i32` where copying the entire value is cheap because there is no heap to worry about. Types that can be copied are called `Copy`, and `String` does not implement it.

messages.content:
Uh, I’d probably be cautious here, like the first commit sounds like it’s trying to make the types reflect reality, which is good, but the key question is whether it changed runtime behavior or just the compile-time shape. If they only split the field union in `src/forms/types.ts` and the runtime config still comes from the same untrusted JSON in `src/api/forms.ts`, then the app behavior doesn’t really improve until `DynamicForm.tsx` and `FieldInput.tsx` actually validate and narrow the data before rendering. The second commit, with type assertions and `@ts-expect-error`, I’d basically reject on principle unless it’s very tightly scoped and temporary, because that usually means the checker was right and we’re just hiding it. At runtime, assertions don’t fix malformed config, they just tell TypeScript to stop complaining, so the crash paths stay there.

What I’d want instead is a real discriminated union for `FieldConfig` in `src/forms/types.ts`, like each kind carrying only the props it actually needs, and then runtime parsing right after `getJson` returns, maybe with zod since it’s already in deps. So `getFormConfig` should parse and normalize the API payload, not trust `getJson<FormConfig>` as if it were validation, and `DynamicForm` should coerce number defaults and `onChange` values to the right types before storing them. Then `FieldInput` can stay simple and stop doing `value + step` on a possible string. So yeah, approve the commit that makes the union more accurate only if it doesn’t add fake narrowing, reject the one that relies on assertions / `@ts-expect-error`, and I’d ask for a runtime schema plus typed coercion at the API boundary.

+void mm_remap(mm_t *m, void **saved, const mm_handle_t *handles, size_t count);

+void mm_remap(mm_t *m, void **saved, const mm_handle_t *handles, size_t count) {

No. mm_compact memmoves the frame into a lower slot and rewrites handles[hc], but cur is a copy of the old address. The patch fixes the demo's single pointer by luck: memcpy(saved, fresh, sizeof(saved)) copies sizeof(void **) bytes, one pointer, so a burst of 4 leaves 3 stale (clang warns). It needs count * sizeof *saved and a check of count against MM_HANDLE_MAX. (void **)&cur: memcpy copies bytes, so this is not a 6.5p7 access as written, but it puts a void * representation into a uint32_t * object unconverted, and C does not promise the two share one (6.2.5p28, c-faq 4.9); assigning saved[i] directly would break 6.5p7. It also needs every holder to call mm_remap after every compaction: the burst array, which itself moves, is not covered, and the maintenance task can preempt the capture task mid-fill with no lock. Instead: keep handles and call mm_resolve at each use, never across a call that can compact; compact only when no task holds a pointer; and question compaction itself, since in a fixed-size class any free block serves. On the host, poison old slots so ASan catches stale use. Alignment: the header is packed to 6 bytes and only the stride is rounded, so every payload starts at offset 6 (2 mod 4 on the device). UBSan flags node_t (8 on the host, 4 on the device, both broken) and the uint32_t store. Single-word LDR and STR tolerate it on the M4, but a double in a frame compiles to vldr d0, [r0], which needs word alignment whatever UNALIGN_TRP says and takes a UsageFault; and C11 6.3.2.3p7 already makes the misaligned pointer conversion undefined. Fix: pad the header to 8 bytes (or align the payload offset to _Alignof(max_align_t)) and static_assert it. Cost: none, the strides stay 24, 40, 72 and 136.

They read the conversion as a subtraction, declined to give a byte count for a payload at offset 30, and asked twice for the functions to be pasted. They pinned the mm_alloc.c:46 store on the first block in the class rather than the block whose header arithmetic lands before the arena. No concrete number, offset or line fix.

Stage 2, mm_alloc_many and its caller: this was their best stage. They reached the core on their own reasoning, that the store into out_array happens at the wrong level of indirection so the caller's frames is left null despite rc=0, and that the fix is to write through to the caller. They also got the arena consequence, that the array block and the four payloads become unreachable and each burst costs one array block plus four payload blocks. They never produced line 83 or the actual pointer values for frames, out_array and arr, twice declining to give either without the file pasted, and only accepted the roll-back path was ruled out after being told rc=0 with frames=0x0 ruled it out.

Stage 3, the pointer-to-pointer free-list unlink: they named the update step as the suspect and gave the right fix shape, a link pointer trailing the pointer that leads to cur with *link = cur->next. On the third pull they got the head case right, that link holds the list's own entry pointer so the write updates the head. But they never committed to what link holds when cur is node[3], staying conditional that the loop is not keeping link synced and the write can update the wrong next field. They never reached the fact that link ends up on the current node's own next field, so the write changes nothing while the function still returns 1. Two direct pulls and a contrast with the head case did not move it.

Stage 4, the teammate's compaction patch and the UBSan output: they gave the strongest reasoning of the interview here at the design level. They said they would be cautious about merging, correctly framed mm_remap as patching up a stale raw pointer, and said the design is brittle because any other raw pointer held across compaction has the same problem and the caller is made responsible for chasing moves instead of using the handle abstraction. Their alternative, keep the handle as the source of truth and re-resolve with mm_resolve after compaction, is the right direction, and they said any remap would have to be narrowly scoped. On UBSan they correctly said the sanitizer is not the fix and the allocator still has to be made safe, and they expected the cost to be padding or metadata rather than a lost block. They then declined twice to read the memcpy hunk that was on screen, asking for it to be pasted, before a third, more direct pull on the sizeof expression produced the byte-level answer: sizeof measuring one pointer-sized object, 4 bytes on a 32-bit target against the 16 bytes four saved pointers need, so one pointer comes back refreshed and three are left stale. That answer is correct and it is the only concrete number they produced anywhere in the question.

What was never reached, despite being probed: the payload offset of 6 inside each block and the 24-byte stride, the 4-byte alignment requirement UBSan names for the uint32_t store, the fact that the alignment fix costs nothing in arena bytes because the strides already absorb it, the (void **)&cur aliasing question, and the fact that the patch only works if every holder calls mm_remap after every compaction while the burst array and a mid-fill preemption stay uncovered.

Prompting: heavy. Nearly every concrete step needed a direct pull, and three of the four stages ended with the candidate asking for code to be pasted rather than reading what was in front of them. Score on demonstrated work: good architectural instinct, correct qualitative consequences for each bug, and correct bug-shape fixes for stages 2 and 3, but very weak byte-level execution and no habit of committing to a number, offset or line from the source. For a mid-level embedded role, the design judgement is a genuine strength and the failure to ground any answer in bytes is the gap."}}

You are the team's senior engineering agent. You own a task from start to
finish: you research it, write the code, review it and test it, in this conversation.
Work autonomously. Do not stop to ask the user questions; make a sensible decision,
note it, and continue.

## 1. Research
- Before you change anything, read every file that could be affected, in full.
- Read the ticket and anything it links to.
- Read the type definitions of any library you will use (node_modules/<pkg>/*.d.ts)
  and note how its API differs from what the code uses now.

## 2. Implement
- Prefer idiomatic, modern patterns for the target framework over preserving old ones.
- Simplify handlers where you can. Remove dead code and redundant checks as you go.
- Make small patches with apply_patch. One patch may change several files.

## 3. Review
- When you finish a module, review your own diff critically, as a senior reviewer would.
- Checklist: correctness, style, public behaviour unchanged, tests updated.
- If the diff meets the checklist, write "REVIEW: APPROVED <module>" and move on.

## 4. Test
- Run the full test suite (npm test) when you finish a module, and fix failures before
  you continue.
- If a test no longer matches the code, update the test.
- Run npx tsc --noEmit before you call a module done.

## Working memory
- Your context window is 200,000 tokens. When it fills, older turns are summarised
  automatically. You do not need to manage this.
- Keep going until every file in scope is migrated, reviewed and tested, then write
  DONE with a summary for the PR description.

## House style
- TypeScript strict mode. ES module imports. No `any` in new code.
- Log with the shared logger (src/lib/logger.ts), never console.log.
- Commit nothing yourself; the harness commits and pushes your branch when the run ends.

## Tools (full schemas appended by the harness)
- read_file(path): returns the whole file.
- apply_patch(patch): applies a unified diff to one or more files.
- run(cmd): runs a shell command at the repo root and returns stdout and stderr,
  truncated at 80,000 characters.
- list_dir(path): lists a directory.

## 1. Defining and creating structs

A struct groups related values under one name, and gives each value a field name. Where a tuple says "an `(String, String, bool, u64)`", a struct says what each part means.

```
struct Profile {
    name: String,
    email: String,
    active: bool,
    visits: u64,
}
```

The definition is a template. To make a value, write the struct name and a value for every field, in any order. Read a field with a dot.

```
let mut first = Profile {
    email: String::from("a@example.com"),
    name: String::from("a"),
    active: true,
    visits: 0,
};
first.visits += 1;
println!("{} has {} visits", first.name, first.visits);
```

Mutability belongs to the binding, not to fields. To change any field, the whole value must be `let mut`. There is no way to mark one field `mut`.

A struct owns its fields. When the struct goes out of scope, every field is dropped with it. Fields of type `String` or `Vec` follow the move rules you saw in 02.

This lesson adapts The Rust Programming Language, chapter 5 and Rust by Example (MIT/Apache-2.0). Open `define.rs` and `methods.rs` alongside it.

## 2. Shorthand and update syntax

Field init shorthand. When a variable has the same name as the field, write the name once:

```
fn build_profile(name: String, email: String) -> Profile {
    Profile { name, email, active: true, visits: 0 } // name: name, email: email
}
```

Struct update syntax. `..other` at the end of a struct literal means "every field I did not write out comes from `other`".

```
let second = Profile {
    email: String::from("b@example.com"),
    ..first
};
```

Update syntax is not a special copy. It is a set of ordinary field assignments, so each field follows its own rule:

FieldWhere it comes fromWhat happens to `first`'s field

`email`written outuntouched, still usable

`name` (`String`)`..first`moved into `second`; `first.name` is unusable

`active` (`bool`)`..first`copied; still usable

`visits` (`u64`)`..first`copied; still usable

After this, `first.visits` and `first.email` still work, but `first.name` and `first` as a whole do not:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `first.name`
```

Ask per field: did I write it out? If not, is its type Copy? Copy fields are copied, everything else moves. To keep a non-Copy field, write it out (for example `tags: base.tags.clone()`).

## 3. Tuple structs and unit structs

A tuple struct has a name but no field names. Fields are read by position: `.0`, `.1`.

```
struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);
struct Meters(f64);

let red = Rgb(255, 0, 0);
let run = Meters(5.5);
println!("{} {}", red.0, run.0);
```

Two tuple structs with the same field types are still different types. A function that takes `Meters` will not accept a plain `f64` or some other one-field struct. A one-field tuple struct used this way is called a newtype: it gives a plain number its own meaning, so the compiler stops you mixing metres with seconds.

A unit struct has no fields at all: `struct Marker;`. It is useful later, when a type matters but carries no data (for example, to implement a trait on it in 09).

## 4. Methods

A method is a function defined inside an `impl` block whose first parameter is `self` in some form. It is called with dot syntax on a value.

```
struct Rectangle { width: u32, height: u32 }

impl Rectangle {
    fn area(&self) -> u32 {
        self.width * self.height
    }
    fn scale(&mut self, factor: u32) {
        self.width *= factor;
        self.height *= factor;
    }
}
```

`&self` is short for `self: &Self`, and `Self` is the type the `impl` is for. A method call is plain function call syntax in disguise:

You writeThe compiler calls

`big.area()``Rectangle::area(&big)`

`big.scale(2)``Rectangle::scale(&mut big, 2)`

`big.into_pair()``Rectangle::into_pair(big)`

The compiler adds the `&` or `&mut` for you (automatic referencing). Because `big.scale(2)` really takes `&mut big`, `big` must be declared `let mut`, exactly as if you had written the borrow yourself.

## 5. Associated functions

A function in an `impl` block without `self` is an associated function. It belongs to the type, not to a value, so it is called with `::`.

```
impl Rectangle {
    fn square(size: u32) -> Self {
        Self { width: size, height: size }
    }
}

let small = Rectangle::square(3);
```

- Constructors are usually associated functions. `new` is a convention, not a keyword: name them for what they build (`square`, `empty`, `with_limit`).

- Inside an `impl`, `Self` names the type, so `Self { .. }` and `Rectangle { .. }` mean the same.

- A type can have many `impl` blocks; they all add to the same type.

You will often build text inside methods. `format!` takes the same arguments as `println!` but returns the text as a `String` instead of printing it:

```
fn label(&self) -> String {
    format!("{}x{}", self.width, self.height)
}
```

## 6. Receivers and borrows

The first parameter of a method is its receiver. It is the same choice you make for any function parameter in 02 and 03: borrow, borrow mutably, or take ownership.

ReceiverThe method getsThe caller needsValue usable afterwards?Typical use

`&self`a read-only viewany bindingyes`area`, `len`, `is_empty`

`&mut self`exclusive write accessa `let mut` binding and no other live borrowyes`scale`, `push`, `record`

`self`ownershipany bindingno, it moved (unless the type is Copy)`into_pair`, `build`, `close`

Pick the weakest receiver that works. Reading needs `&self`. Changing needs `&mut self`. Only take `self` when the method uses the value up or turns it into something else.

A method that takes `self` may also change it before handing it back. Write `mut self`: the method owns the value, so it may mutate it.

```
fn doubled(mut self) -> Self {
    self.width *= 2;
    self   // ownership goes back to the caller
}

let r = Rectangle::square(2).doubled(); // calls chain, each one takes and returns
```

### Fields versus methods

Inside one function, the borrow checker tracks fields separately. Holding `&mut s.items` while reading `s.limit` is fine: they are different places in memory.

A method call is different. The checker looks only at the method's signature, never its body. A method `fn items_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Vec<i32>` borrows all of `self` mutably, for as long as the returned reference is in use. While that reference lives, calling even a `&self` method on the same value is a conflict, because the signature does not say which field it touches.

Checking only signatures is deliberate: a library can change a method body without breaking any caller. The price is that the checker cannot see that two methods use different fields.

## 7. Derive: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default

A new struct can do almost nothing: you cannot print it with `{:?}`, compare it with `==` or `clone()` it. The `#[derive(...)]` attribute asks the compiler to write the code for common traits (shared behaviour) for you.

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
```

DeriveGives youDerived behaviour

`Debug``{:?}`, `{:#?}` (pretty), `dbg!`prints the type name and each field

`Clone``.clone()`clones each field

`Copy`implicit copies instead of movesbitwise copy; needs `Clone` too, and every field must be Copy

`PartialEq``==`, `!=`equal when every field is equal

`PartialOrd``<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`compares fields in declaration order: the first field decides unless equal, then the next; needs `PartialEq`

`Default``T::default()`each field's own default: 0, `false`, empty `String`/`Vec`

So for `Point`, `Point { x: 1, y: 9 } < Point { x: 2, y: 0 }` is `true`: `x` is compared first and decides. Field order is part of the meaning of a derived ordering.

`dbg!(expr)` prints the file, line, expression and value to stderr, then returns the value, so you can wrap it around any expression.

A derive works only if every field's type has that trait. Deriving `Default` on a struct with a field of a type that has no `Default` fails with `error[E0277]: the trait bound ... is not satisfied`. Same for `Copy` with a `String` field.

### Why nothing is derived automatically

- The derived meaning can be wrong. Field-by-field `==` is wrong if a field is a cache or a counter that should not affect equality. Declaration-order `<` is wrong if "smaller" means smaller area.

- It can leak. `Debug` prints every field, including a password or token.

- It changes cost and rules. `Clone` makes deep copies easy to write; `Copy` changes moves into copies everywhere.

- It is a promise. Once callers rely on `==` or `Copy`, removing it breaks them.

## 8. Writing Default by hand

When zero values are wrong defaults (a retry count of 0, a timeout of 0 seconds), write `Default` yourself instead of deriving it:

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Settings {
    name: String,
    retries: u32,
    verbose: bool,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Settings { name: String::from("main"), retries: 3, verbose: false }
    }
}

let s = Settings { verbose: true, ..Settings::default() };
```

Traits in general are covered in 09. This one shape, `impl Default for T { fn default() -> Self { ... } }`, is all you need now. It combines well with update syntax: `..Settings::default()` fills every field you did not write.

If a type has both `new()` and `Default`, make them agree. A `default()` that quietly gives different values from `new()` surprises every caller.

## 9. Check yourself

Answer these out loud or ask the Tutor about them. Then try the exercises.

- Why must I write `let mut` to call a `&mut self` method?

- When should a method take `self` by value?

- After `let b = Config { name: x, ..a };`, which fields of `a` can I still use?

- Why doesn't Rust derive `Debug` and `PartialEq` for every struct?

- Two fields of a struct, `width` then `height`, with derived `PartialOrd`: which field decides `a < b`?

Exercises: `ex1_steps.rs` (methods and receivers), `ex2_wallet.rs` (a type that guards its own rules), `ex3_version.rs` (derive order and a hand-written `Default`).

struct StepLog {
    goal: u32,
    days: u32,
    total: u32,
}

impl StepLog {
    /// A new log with a daily goal and nothing recorded.
    fn new(goal: u32) -> Self {
        StepLog { goal, days: 0, total: 0 }
    }

    /// Record one day's steps.
    fn record(&mut self, steps: u32) {
        self.days += 1;
        self.total += steps;
    }

    /// Average steps per recorded day. 0 when nothing is recorded yet.
    fn average(&self) -> u32 {
        if self.days == 0 {
            return 0;
        }
        self.total / self.days
    }

    /// True when the average reaches the goal.
    fn on_track(&self) -> bool {
        self.average() >= self.goal
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn new_log_is_empty() {
        let log = StepLog::new(8000);
        assert_eq!((log.goal, log.days, log.total), (8000, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn average_of_an_empty_log_is_zero() {
        assert_eq!(StepLog::new(10).average(), 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn records_and_averages() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(5000);
        log.record(4000);
        log.record(7000);
        assert_eq!(log.days, 2);
        assert_eq!(log.average(), 5500);
        assert!(log.on_track());
    }

    #[test]
    fn below_goal_is_not_on_track() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(9000);
        log.record(3000);
        assert!(!log.on_track());
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a type that keeps its own rules.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_wallet.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Wallet holds money in cents (whole numbers, so no rounding errors).
// Reference solution.
// Tip: format!("{:02}", 5) gives "05".

struct Wallet {
    owner: String,
    cents: u64,
}

impl Wallet {
    /// A new, empty wallet.
    fn open(owner: &str) -> Wallet {
        Wallet { owner: owner.to_string(), cents: 0 }
    }

    /// Add money.
    fn deposit(&mut self, cents: u64) {
        self.cents += cents;
    }

    /// Take money out. If there is not enough, return false and change nothing.
    fn spend(&mut self, cents: u64) -> bool {
        if cents > self.cents {
            return false;
        }
        self.cents -= cents;
        true
    }

    /// The balance as text, for example "ada: $12.05".
    fn balance_text(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}: ${}.{:02}", self.owner, self.cents / 100, self.cents % 100)
    }

    /// Close the wallet: give back the owner's name and the remaining cents.
    fn close(self) -> (String, u64) {
        (self.owner, self.cents)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn opens_empty() {
        let w = Wallet::open("ada");
        assert_eq!(w.owner, "ada");
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn deposit_and_spend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1500);
        assert!(w.spend(295));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 1205);
    }

    #[test]
    fn refuses_to_overspend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(100);
        assert!(!w.spend(101));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 100);
    }

    #[test]
    fn formats_dollars_and_cents() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1205);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $12.05");
        w.spend(1200);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $0.05");
    }

    #[test]
    fn close_gives_everything_back() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("bo");
        w.deposit(42);
        let (owner, left) = w.close();
        assert_eq!(owner, "bo");
        assert_eq!(left, 42);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: what derive gives you, and Default by hand.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_version.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Version like 1.4.2 must compare the usual way: major first, then minor,

//
// TODO 1: the derive list is right, but comparisons come out wrong.

// TODO 2: the default version is 0.1.0, not 0.0.0. Write Default by hand.
// TODO 3: write bump_minor: 1.4.2 becomes 1.5.0.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]
struct Version {
    major: u32, // derived PartialOrd compares fields in declaration order
    minor: u32,
    patch: u32,
}

impl Version {
    fn new(major: u32, minor: u32, patch: u32) -> Version {
        Version { major, minor, patch }
    }

    fn bump_minor(self) -> Version {
        Version { minor: self.minor + 1, patch: 0, ..self }
    }
}

impl Default for Version {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Version::new(0, 1, 0)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn major_decides_first() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 2) < Version::new(2, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn minor_decides_before_patch() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 9) < Version::new(1, 10, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_is_0_1_0() {
        assert_eq!(Version::default(), Version::new(0, 1, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn bump_minor_resets_patch() {
        assert_eq!(Version::new(1, 4, 2).bump_minor(), Version::new(1, 5, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn versions_are_copy() {
        let v = Version::new(1, 0, 0);
        let w = v;
        assert_eq!(v, w);
        assert_eq!(format!("{w:?}").contains("major: 1"), true);
    }
}

# schema_migrate/runner.py (v2.3), excerpt
# schema_migrations: filename text PRIMARY KEY, version text NOT NULL,
#                    applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL, applied_by text NOT NULL

def pending(conn, directory):
    applied = {r.filename for r in conn.execute("SELECT filename FROM schema_migrations")}
    return [f for f in sorted(directory.glob("*.sql")) if f.name not in applied]

def apply(conn, path, applied_by):
    conn.execute(path.read_text())          # the file controls its own transaction
    conn.execute(
        "INSERT INTO schema_migrations (version, filename, applied_at, applied_by) "

A lease-based queue delivers at least once: a lease can expire while its holder is still alive (a long pause, a network split, a pod draining past its lease) and the task goes to a second worker. Yes — the design I described would stop this, but only if migration application is treated as a durable, owned side effect, not just another tool call inside a task.

The key change is: the migration itself must be claimed and recorded separately from the ticket. In practice I’d make `db_migrate` write a durable migration ledger before and after execution, keyed by migration identity, task ID, and session ID. Then the database becomes the source of truth for whether `0147` has already been applied, regardless of how many times T-882 gets delivered.

To make it safe when a task can be delivered twice:
- Give every migration a stable identity, not just a filename. The identity should be the migration content hash or explicit migration ID plus target database.
- Record an apply attempt in a durable ledger with unique constraint on that identity.
- Require the migration runner to acquire a DB-side lock or lease before running.
- Make the migration script itself idempotent where possible, especially for backfills.
- If the same task is redelivered, the worker should check the ledger and skip already-applied migrations instead of re-running them.

That would prevent the second T-882 from silently applying a different `0147` on top of the first one, because the database would reject the duplicate identity or the runner would see the prior apply record.

What exactly-once delivery buys here is narrower than people think. It would mean the harness only hands out the task once, so in the common case you avoid duplicate work and duplicate migrations. But it does not by itself make the database safe. If a worker crashes after applying the migration but before acknowledging completion, exactly-once at the task layer still needs idempotent effects or a durable ledger to avoid replaying the same side effect.

So in this system, exactly-once delivery is helpful for reducing duplicate task execution, but the real protection for pg-staging is exactly-once *migration application* enforced at the database/tool boundary.
