// Exercise 1: say which input the result borrows from (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_tie.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

fn after<'a>(text: &'a str, marker: &str) -> &'a str {
    match text.find(marker) {
        Some(i) => &text[i + marker.len()..],
        None => "",
    }
}

fn first_with<'a>(items: &'a [String], needle: &str) -> Option<&'a str> {
    for s in items {
        if s.contains(needle) {
            return Some(s.as_str());
        }
    }
    None
}

fn shorter<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if b.len() < a.len() { b } else { a }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn after_finds_the_rest() {
        assert_eq!(after("key=value", "="), "value");
        assert_eq!(after("a::b::c", "::"), "b::c");
        assert_eq!(after("no marker", "#"), "");
        assert_eq!(after("ends=", "="), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn result_outlives_the_marker() {
        let text = String::from("name: Ada");
        let rest;
        {
            let marker = String::from(": ");
            rest = after(&text, &marker);
        } // marker is dropped here; rest borrows only from text
        assert_eq!(rest, "Ada");
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_with_outlives_the_needle() {
        let items = vec![String::from("red apple"), String::from("green pear")];
        let found;
        {
            let needle = String::from("pear");
            found = first_with(&items, &needle);
        }
        assert_eq!(found, Some("green pear"));
        assert_eq!(first_with(&items, "plum"), None);
        assert_eq!(first_with(&[], "x"), None);
    }

    #[test]
    fn shorter_picks_either_input() {
        assert_eq!(shorter("abc", "de"), "de");
        assert_eq!(shorter("ab", "cde"), "ab");
        assert_eq!(shorter("ab", "cd"), "ab");
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a record that borrows its line (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_record.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

struct Record<'a> {
    line: &'a str,
}

impl<'a> Record<'a> {
    fn field(&self, i: usize) -> Option<&'a str> {
        // self.line is a &'a str (Copy), so the slices borrow the line, not self.
        self.line.split(',').nth(i).map(|f| f.trim())
    }

    fn fields(&self) -> Vec<&'a str> {
        self.line.split(',').map(|f| f.trim()).collect()
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &'a str {
        self.field(0).unwrap_or("")
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn fields_are_trimmed() {
        let r = Record { line: "ada, 36 ,london" };
        assert_eq!(r.field(0), Some("ada"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(1), Some("36"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(2), Some("london"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(3), None);
        assert_eq!(r.fields(), ["ada", "36", "london"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn name_of_empty_line() {
        assert_eq!(Record { line: "" }.name(), "");
        assert_eq!(Record { line: "solo" }.name(), "solo");
    }

    #[test]
    fn fields_outlive_the_record() {
        let line = String::from("grace, 45, nyc");
        let (name, all);
        {
            let r = Record { line: &line };
            name = r.name();
            all = r.fields();
        } // r is dropped here; name and all borrow from `line`
        assert_eq!(name, "grace");
        assert_eq!(all.len(), 3);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: boxes that own, and boxes that borrow (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_boxes.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

fn greeter(name: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn() -> String> {
    let name = name.to_string(); // owned copy: the box is 'static
    Box::new(move || format!("hello, {name}"))
}

fn checker<'a>(allowed: &'a [&'a str]) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool + 'a> {
    Box::new(move |w| allowed.contains(&w)) // moves the reference in; borrows the slice
}

fn counter(words: Vec<String>) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> usize> {
    Box::new(move |w| words.iter().filter(|x| x.as_str() == w).count()) // the Vec is moved in
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn greeter_owns_its_name() {
        let g = {
            let temp = String::from("Ada");
            greeter(&temp)
        }; // temp is gone; the greeter must still work
        assert_eq!(g(), "hello, Ada");
        assert_eq!(g(), "hello, Ada");
    }

    #[test]
    fn checker_borrows_the_list() {
        let words = ["red", "green"];
        let ok = checker(&words);
        assert!(ok("red"));
        assert!(!ok("blue"));
        assert!(!checker(&[])("red"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn counter_owns_its_words() {
        let count = {
            let words = vec![String::from("a"), String::from("b"), String::from("a")];
            counter(words)
        }; // the Vec was moved into the box
        assert_eq!(count("a"), 2);
        assert_eq!(count("b"), 1);
        assert_eq!(count("z"), 0);
    }
}

From 7876b0add8419708e39ef4cdf610cf6848212db0 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: firmware team <firmware-team@example.com>
Date: Wed, 30 Sep 2026 16:41:00 +0000
Subject: [PATCH] ring: publish head with a release store

ring_stress fails on arm64 (records with the wrong seq or a bad CRC) and
passes on x86-64. The writer can see the new head before it sees the bytes
of the record: make the head store in ring_commit() a release store, so the
record is written before head moves.

ring_stress on the arm64 laptop now passes, 5 runs of 20M records.
---
 src/ring.c | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/src/ring.c b/src/ring.c
index 219b76e..ca7bbf1 100644
--- a/src/ring.c
+++ b/src/ring.c
@@ -27,7 +27,7 @@ void ring_commit(struct ring *r)
 {
 	uint32_t head = atomic_load_explicit(&r->head, memory_order_relaxed);
 
-	atomic_store_explicit(&r->head, head + 1, memory_order_relaxed);
+	atomic_store_explicit(&r->head, head + 1, memory_order_release);
 }
 
 const struct tlm_rec *ring_peek(struct ring *r)
--

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
Not as it stands: the patch fixes one of the four index accesses. The board's compiler output changes in one line, str w8, [x0] to stlr w8, [x0] in ring_commit; ring_peek still loads head with a plain ldr w9, [x0]. A release store synchronizes only with an acquire load that reads it, so there is still no happens-before from the record's stores to the writer's reads, and ThreadSanitizer still reports both pairs (10 reports). Five passes prove little: here ring_peek returns the slot pointer through a csel on the loaded head, an address dependency arm64 does order, which most likely hid the bug. The compiler happens to emit it; C11 does not promise it, and inlining or a refactor can turn it into a branch, which orders no later load. On x86-64 the patch changes no instruction ('no difference'), so the x86 pass never tested anything. The orders: ring_commit stores head with release (the record before the index); ring_peek loads head with acquire (the slot after the index); ring_pop stores tail with release (the writer's reads of the slot finish before the slot is handed back); ring_reserve loads tail with acquire (the producer refills a slot only after seeing it freed: ThreadSanitizer's write-after-read report). Each thread's load of its own index stays relaxed (one writer, program order is enough), and ring_count can stay relaxed (a status snapshot). On the A72 that is stlr and ldar, no dmb. seq_cst is not needed: nothing here must order a store before a later load of another variable; it costs nothing more for these on the A72 but makes each store an xchg on x86-64. Layout: head, tail and slot[0] share one 64-byte line (offsets 0, 4 and 8), and each side writes its own index and reads the other's on every call, so the line moves between the cores on every record. Give head and tail their own lines (64 bytes on the A72, 128 on the M1), and let each side cache the other's index and reload it only when the ring looks full or empty, as Rigtorp's SPSCQueue does.

NEVER say any of these, in any wording::
  - orders nothing around it
  - previous lap
  - works by accident
  - one of the four
  - happens to emit
  - never tested anything

You may point at where to look. You may not name the mechanism or the fix. If your sentence would let them answer without thinking, rewrite it.

I wouldn’t merge it yet. That sounds like it may have fixed the producer publication on arm64, but the ThreadSanitizer report still bothers me: if it’s still flagging a read in `crc32` against the write at `ring_stress.c:50`, I’d want to understand whether the test is still exposing an unsynchronized data race or whether that’s just the expected read of the payload after the ring index publication.

I’m not confident enough to prescribe the exact memory orders access-by-access without seeing `src/ring.c`. My guess would be that the producer’s store to `head` in `ring_commit` needs release semantics, and the consumer’s load of `head` in `ring_peek` needs acquire semantics. But I’d want you to confirm the current code shape before I say what `tail` should be on each side.

## 1. The problem lifetimes solve

A reference must never outlive the value it points to. If it did, it would point at memory that has already been freed: a dangling reference. Rust rules these out at compile time. The part of the compiler that does it, the borrow checker, compares two spans for every borrow:

- how long the value lives (from where it is created to where it is dropped, usually the end of its scope), and

- how long the reference is used (from where it is created to its last use).

The second span must fit inside the first. That span of validity is the reference's lifetime. Inside one function the compiler works lifetimes out on its own; you have done this since 03 without writing a single one. Lifetimes need writing only where the compiler cannot see across a boundary: a function signature, or a struct that holds a reference.

```
let r;
{
    let x = 5;
    r = &x;          // r borrows x
}                    // x is dropped here
println!("{r}");     // r is used after x is gone: error[E0597]
```

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 10.3 "Validating References with Lifetimes", and Rust by Example, "Lifetimes" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

## 2. Annotations describe, they do not extend

A lifetime annotation is a name that starts with an apostrophe, usually short: `'a`, `'b`. It goes after the `&`:

```
&i32        // a reference
&'a i32     // a reference with an explicit lifetime 'a
&'a mut i32 // a mutable reference with an explicit lifetime 'a
```

`x: &'a str` means "`x` is valid for at least the span called `'a`". On its own a single annotation says little. Its power is in relating several references: two parameters and a return value that share `'a` are tied together.

An annotation never changes how long any value lives. Values are still dropped at the end of their scope. Writing `'a` cannot keep a `String` alive; it can only describe a relationship the compiler then checks. If the relationship is false, the code is rejected.

## 3. Connecting inputs to outputs

Here is the Book's example, in `longest.rs`. It returns whichever of two string slices is longer:

```
fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if x.len() > y.len() { x } else { y }
}
```

Read the signature as a contract: "for some span `'a` during which both `x` and `y` are valid, the result is valid for `'a` too." In practice `'a` becomes the overlap of the two inputs, so the result may be used only while the shorter-lived input is still alive.

The compiler checks the two sides of the contract separately:

- The body is checked against the signature: returning `x` or `y` is allowed, both are `'a`.

- Each caller is checked against the signature only. The caller never looks inside the body.

That second point explains `longest_scope.rs`. We can see that the result is `string1`, which is still alive. But the signature says "as long as the shorter of the two", and `string2` dies first:

```
error[E0597]: `string2` does not live long enough
  --> longest_scope.rs:19:44
   |
18 |         let string2 = String::from("xyz");
   |             ------- binding `string2` declared here
19 |         result = longest(string1.as_str(), string2.as_str());
   |                                            ^^^^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
20 |     } // string2 is dropped here
   |     - `string2` dropped here while still borrowed
...
23 |     println!("The longest string is {result}");
   |                                      ------ borrow later used here
```

How long each value in longest_scope.rs lives. `'a` covers only the overlap of the two inputs, so using `result` after the inner block breaks the contract.

Why can't the compiler just read the body? Because the signature is the function's public promise. If callers depended on the body, changing the body (say, sometimes returning `y`) could break code in other files and crates. Checking against the signature keeps every function checkable on its own.

## 4. Tie only the inputs the output can come from

A lifetime parameter on an input is a demand on callers: "keep this alive as long as you use the result". So give the output's lifetime only to the inputs the result can actually point into. An input that is only read (a search pattern, a length limit, a flag) should keep its own, unnamed lifetime.

```
// The result is always `line` or a slice of it. `tag` is only compared.
fn strip_tag<'a>(line: &'a str, tag: &str) -> &'a str {
    line.strip_prefix(tag).unwrap_or(line)
}
```

If `tag` were also `&'a str`, the function would still compile, but every caller would have to keep `tag` alive as long as the result, for no reason. A caller that builds the tag in a short block would then get E0597 naming the tag, even though the result never points into it.

A string literal such as `""` has type `&'static str`, which can stand in for any shorter lifetime. So a function declared to return `&'a str` may also return `""`.

## 5. The three elision rules

Early Rust needed annotations on every signature with references. The patterns were so regular that the compiler now fills them in. These are the lifetime elision rules. A lifetime on a parameter is an input lifetime; on the return type, an output lifetime.

RuleSaysExample, written and inferred

1Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime.`fn f(a: &str, b: &str)` becomes `fn f<'a, 'b>(a: &'a str, b: &'b str)`

2If there is exactly one input lifetime, every output gets it.`fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` becomes `fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str`

3If one input is `&self` or `&mut self`, every output gets self's lifetime.`fn name(&self, p: &str) -> &str` becomes `fn name<'s, 'p>(&'s self, p: &'p str) -> &'s str`

Non-reference parameters (`usize`, `bool`, an owned `String`) have no lifetime and do not count. A function whose output holds no reference needs no output lifetime at all, whatever its inputs.

The rules as a flowchart. If no rule decides the output lifetime, you get E0106 and must write it.

When no rule decides, the compiler refuses to guess. `elision_fail.rs` has two reference inputs and no `self`:

```
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> elision_fail.rs:9:30
  |
9 | fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
  |            ----     ----     ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `a` or `b`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
9 | fn pick<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
  |        ++++     ++          ++          ++
```

There is a second, different failure. Sometimes a rule does decide, but the body returns something the decided signature does not allow. Then the error is not E0106 but "lifetime may not live long enough": elision wrote a contract and the body broke it. The fix is to write the signature you meant.

The compiler's `help:` suggestion is a guess that makes the signature well formed. It is not always what the body needs, and it may tie more inputs than necessary (section 4). Read it, then decide which inputs the result can really come from.

## 6. Structs that hold references

A struct may hold a reference if it declares a lifetime parameter for it. `excerpt.rs`, adapted from the Book:

```
struct Excerpt<'a> {
    part: &'a str,
}
```

This says: an `Excerpt<'a>` cannot outlive the text its `part` borrows. The lifetime parameter is declared again on the `impl`, `impl<'a> Excerpt<'a>`, and is then available to every method.

Methods can return two different kinds of borrow, and the difference matters:

SignatureResult is tied toCan the result outlive the struct?

`fn announce(&self, note: &str) -> &str`the borrow of `self` (rule 3)no

`fn part(&self) -> &'a str`the text the struct borrows (`'a`)yes, as long as the text lives

In `excerpt.rs`, `kept = short_lived.part()` outlives `short_lived` because `part` returns `&'a str`. Change the return type to `&str` and rule 3 ties the result to `&self` instead:

```
error[E0597]: `short_lived` does not live long enough
  --> excerpt.rs:40:16
   |
39 |         let short_lived = Excerpt { part: &text[0..9] };
   |             ----------- binding `short_lived` declared here
40 |         kept = short_lived.part(); // fine: tied to text, not to short_lived
   |                ^^^^^^^^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
41 |     }
   |     - `short_lived` dropped here while still borrowed
42 |     println!("kept: {kept}");
   |                      ---- borrow later used here
```

The same applies to `&mut self` methods: an elided output keeps the struct mutably borrowed for as long as the result is used, so you cannot call the method again meanwhile. Returning `&'a str` instead says the result points into the underlying data, not into the struct.

### Two fields, two lifetimes

If one lifetime `'a` covers two reference fields, both borrows must be valid for the same `'a`, so `'a` shrinks to the shorter of the two. Anything a method returns as `&'a str` is then tied to the shorter-lived field too, even if it points into the longer one. When the fields come from places with different lifetimes, give each its own parameter (`more_lifetimes.rs`):

```
struct Tagged<'v, 'n> {
    value: &'v str,
    note: &'n str,
}
impl<'v, 'n> Tagged<'v, 'n> {
    fn value(&self) -> &'v str { self.value } // not tied to `note`
}
```

## 7. `'static`, owned returns and `T: 'static`

`'static` is the lifetime of the whole program. String literals are `&'static str`: their bytes are stored in the program binary and never freed.

A function can never return a reference to something it created itself: the value is dropped when the function returns, and no annotation changes that.

```
fn make_greeting(name: &str) -> &str {
    let s = format!("hello, {name}");
    &s
}
```

```
error[E0515]: cannot return reference to local variable `s`
 --> d.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     &s
  |     ^^ returns a reference to data owned by the current function
```

The fix is to return an owned value. When some results are fixed text and others are built at run time, `Cow<'static, str>` (08) carries either: `Cow::Borrowed("fixed")` costs nothing, `Cow::Owned(format!(..))` allocates only when needed. The type also tells the caller "sometimes owned".

`'static` also appears as a bound: `T: 'static` means "`T` holds no borrow shorter than the whole program". Every owned type satisfies it (`String`, `Vec<i32>`), and so does `&'static str`. It does not mean the value lives forever: a `String` passed to such a function is still dropped normally.

```
fn store<T: Debug + 'static>(item: T) -> Box<dyn Debug> { Box::new(item) }
fn store_borrowed<'a, T: Debug + 'a>(item: T) -> Box<dyn Debug + 'a> { Box::new(item) }
```

You met the second use in 12: `Box<dyn Trait>` in a signature means `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. Write `+ 'a` to box something that borrows. Passing `&local` to `store` fails, and the note points at the bound:

```
error[E0597]: `local` does not live long enough
   |               argument requires that `local` is borrowed for `'static`
note: requirement that the value outlives `'static` introduced here
   |
26 | fn store<T: Debug + 'static>(item: T) -> Box<dyn Debug> {
   |                     ^^^^^^^
```

## 8. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- If a function takes two `&str` and returns `&str`, why can't the compiler just read the body?

- For `fn f(v: &[i32], n: usize) -> &[i32]`, which elision rules apply, and what is the full signature?

- In `impl<'a> Excerpt<'a>`, what is the difference between returning `&str` and `&'a str` from `&self`?

- Why can tying an extra input to `'a` break a caller, even though the function compiles?

- Does `T: 'static` mean a `String` passed in is never freed?

Sources: The Rust Programming Language, ch. 10.3; Rust by Example, "Lifetimes", "Structs", "Elision" and "Static" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

Diagram: a flowchart of the lifetime elision rules.

1. Start: "Rule 1: each reference input gets its own lifetime."
2. Decision: "exactly one input lifetime?" Yes leads to "Rule 2: outputs get that lifetime". No leads to the next decision.
3. Decision: "an input is &self or &mut self?" Yes leads to "Rule 3: outputs get self's lifetime". No leads to a red box "error[E0106] missing lifetime specifier: write it yourself".

// Exercise 1: say which input the result borrows from (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_tie.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

fn after<'a>(text: &'a str, marker: &str) -> &'a str {
    match text.find(marker) {
        Some(i) => &text[i + marker.len()..],
        None => "",
    }
}

fn first_with<'a>(items: &'a [String], needle: &str) -> Option<&'a str> {
    for s in items {
        if s.contains(needle) {
            return Some(s.as_str());
        }
    }
    None
}

fn shorter<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if b.len() < a.len() { b } else { a }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn after_finds_the_rest() {
        assert_eq!(after("key=value", "="), "value");
        assert_eq!(after("a::b::c", "::"), "b::c");
        assert_eq!(after("no marker", "#"), "");
        assert_eq!(after("ends=", "="), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn result_outlives_the_marker() {
        let text = String::from("name: Ada");
        let rest;
        {
            let marker = String::from(": ");
            rest = after(&text, &marker);
        } // marker is dropped here; rest borrows only from text
        assert_eq!(rest, "Ada");
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_with_outlives_the_needle() {
        let items = vec![String::from("red apple"), String::from("green pear")];
        let found;
        {
            let needle = String::from("pear");
            found = first_with(&items, &needle);
        }
        assert_eq!(found, Some("green pear"));
        assert_eq!(first_with(&items, "plum"), None);
        assert_eq!(first_with(&[], "x"), None);
    }

        assert_eq!(shorter("abc", "de"), "de");
        assert_eq!(shorter("ab", "cde"), "ab");
        assert_eq!(shorter("ab", "cd"), "ab");
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a record that borrows its line (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_record.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

struct Record<'a> {
    line: &'a str,
}

impl<'a> Record<'a> {
    fn field(&self, i: usize) -> Option<&'a str> {
        // self.line is a &'a str (Copy), so the slices borrow the line, not self.
        self.line.split(',').nth(i).map(|f| f.trim())
    }

    fn fields(&self) -> Vec<&'a str> {
        self.line.split(',').map(|f| f.trim()).collect()
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &'a str {
        self.field(0).unwrap_or("")
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn fields_are_trimmed() {
        let r = Record { line: "ada, 36 ,london" };
        assert_eq!(r.field(0), Some("ada"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(1), Some("36"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(2), Some("london"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(3), None);
        assert_eq!(r.fields(), ["ada", "36", "london"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn name_of_empty_line() {
        assert_eq!(Record { line: "" }.name(), "");
        assert_eq!(Record { line: "solo" }.name(), "solo");
    }

    #[test]
    fn fields_outlive_the_record() {
        let line = String::from("grace, 45, nyc");
        let (name, all);
        {
            let r = Record { line: &line };
            name = r.name();
            all = r.fields();
        } // r is dropped here; name and all borrow from `line`
        assert_eq!(name, "grace");
        assert_eq!(all.len(), 3);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: boxes that own, and boxes that borrow (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_boxes.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

fn greeter(name: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn() -> String> {
    let name = name.to_string(); // owned copy: the box is 'static
    Box::new(move || format!("hello, {name}"))
}

fn checker<'a>(allowed: &'a [&'a str]) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool + 'a> {
    Box::new(move |w| allowed.contains(&w)) // moves the reference in; borrows the slice
}

fn counter(words: Vec<String>) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> usize> {
    Box::new(move |w| words.iter().filter(|x| x.as_str() == w).count()) // the Vec is moved in
}

#[cfg(test)]

    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn greeter_owns_its_name() {
        let g = {
            let temp = String::from("Ada");
            greeter(&temp)
        }; // temp is gone; the greeter must still work
        assert_eq!(g(), "hello, Ada");
        assert_eq!(g(), "hello, Ada");

## 1. Box: one owner, value on the heap

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 15.1-15.3, and Rust by Example (Box, stack and heap; RAII), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A smart pointer is a value that acts like a reference but also owns what it points to, and has extra behaviour. You have already used two: `String` and `Vec`. `Box<T>` is the simplest one: it puts one value of type `T` on the heap and keeps a pointer to it.

```
let b = Box::new(5);        // the 5 lives on the heap; b is a pointer on the stack
println!("b = {b}");       // prints 5: Box displays its contents
let c = b;                  // moving a Box moves only the pointer
// when c goes out of scope: the i32 is dropped, then the heap slot is freed
```

PropertyBox<T>

Ownersexactly one, like any value; moving the Box moves ownership

Size on the stackone pointer, whatever `T` is

Freedwhen the Box is dropped, decided at compile time (no garbage collector, no reference count)

Main usesa type whose size is not known at compile time (recursive types, section 2); a large value you want to move without copying it; trait objects (12)

## 2. Recursive types need a pointer

Rust must know the size of every type at compile time. A type that contains itself directly has no finite size:

```
enum List {
    Cons(i32, List),   // a List holds a List holds a List ...
    Nil,
}
```

```
error[E0072]: recursive type `List` has infinite size
 --> box_list.rs:1:1
  |
1 | enum List { Cons(i32, List), Nil }
  | ^^^^^^^^^             ---- recursive without indirection
help: insert some indirection (e.g., a `Box`, `Rc`, or `&`) to break the cycle
```

Replace the inner `List` with `Box<List>`: a pointer has a fixed size, and the next node lives on the heap.

box-layout.png: the infinite inline version next to the boxed chain.

- The cycle can also pass through other types: `A` holds a `B` that holds an `A`. The compiler reports both types. One pointer anywhere on the cycle is enough, because it gives the whole loop a fixed size.

- `Vec<T>` already is an owning pointer: its value is pointer, length and capacity, with the elements on the heap. `enum Tree { Leaf, Node(Vec<Tree>) }` compiles without any Box.

- `Option<T>` is not a pointer: it holds its `T` inline, so `next: Option<Node>` still has infinite size. Write `Option<Box<Node>>`.

Sizes printed by `box_list.rs` (`size_of::<Box<List>>() = 8` and so on) are layout facts for a 64-bit target, not language rules. Read them as illustration only.

## 3. The `*` operator and moving out

On a reference, `*r` follows the pointer. A type can make `*` work on itself by implementing `Deref` (section 4). Then `*x` means `*Deref::deref(&x)`: call `deref` to get a `&Target`, then follow that reference.

That result is a place behind a shared reference. You can read it, compare it, or borrow it again, but you cannot move out of it:

```
error[E0507]: cannot move out of dereference of `MyBox<String>`
  |     let taken: String = *name;
  |                         ^^^^^ move occurs because value has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
```

`Box` is the exception. The compiler knows `Box` specially, so `*boxed` is the value itself, owned by you, and you may move it out. The Box is used up by the move:

```
let name = Box::new(String::from("heap"));
let moved: String = *name;     // allowed only for Box
// println!("{name}");         // error[E0382]: the Box was consumed
```

With your own wrapper, move a field out instead (`let taken = name.0;`), which works when you own the wrapper and it has no `Drop` impl (section 8).

## 4. Deref and DerefMut

```
use std::ops::{Deref, DerefMut};

struct MyBox<T>(T);

impl<T> Deref for MyBox<T> {
    type Target = T;                  // what *x and coercion lead to
    fn deref(&self) -> &T {
        &self.0
    }
}

impl<T> DerefMut for MyBox<T> {
    fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T {
        &mut self.0
    }
}
```

`Deref` gives shared access: `*x`, and calling `&self` methods of the target. `DerefMut` gives mutable access: calling `&mut self` methods (like `push_str`) and assigning through `*x = ...`. Without `DerefMut`:

```
error[E0596]: cannot borrow data in dereference of `MyBox<String>` as mutable
```

The compiler picks one or the other per use: a method that takes `&self` goes through `deref`, a method that takes `&mut self` goes through `deref_mut`.

## 5. Deref coercion

When you pass a `&T` where a `&U` is expected and `T: Deref<Target = U>`, the compiler inserts the `deref` calls for you, as many steps as needed:

```
fn hello(name: &str) { println!("Hello, {name}!"); }

let name = MyBox(String::from("Rust"));
hello(&name);            // &MyBox<String> -> &String -> &str
hello(&(*name)[..]);     // what you would have to write without coercion
```

deref-chain.png: each step uses one Deref impl until the types match.

FromToNeeds

`&T``&U``T: Deref<Target = U>`

`&mut T``&mut U``T: DerefMut<Target = U>`

`&mut T``&U``T: Deref<Target = U>`

`&T``&mut U`never: it would break the borrowing rules

Coercion only converts one reference into another. Passing a value (`hello(name)`) is a type mismatch, not a coercion. Method calls auto-deref the same way: `name.len()` tries `MyBox`, then `String`, and finds `String::len`. All of this is resolved at compile time; nothing is copied.

## 6. When values are dropped

A type can run code when a value of it goes away by implementing `Drop`:

```
struct Loud { name: &'static str }
impl Drop for Loud {
    fn drop(&mut self) { println!("  drop {}", self.name); }
}
```

The rules for when are fixed and predictable:

SituationDropped

Locals at the end of a scopein reverse order of declaration

Fields of a struct, elements of a tuple, array or Vecin declaration order (first field first), after the owner's own `drop`

A value moved into a functionwhen that function's parameter goes out of scope, unless it moves it on again

A variable assigned a new valuethe old value is dropped at that assignment

A value that was moved awaynot dropped here at all: its new owner drops it

`drop.rs` exercises every row. Predict its 15 lines before running it.

## 7. Ending a value early

You may not call the `drop` method yourself:

```
error[E0040]: explicit use of destructor method
  |     early.drop();
  |           ^^^^ explicit destructor calls not allowed
help: consider using `drop` function
```

If you could, Rust would still drop the value again at the end of the scope: a double drop. Use the free function `drop(x)` (from `std::mem`, always in scope) instead. It takes `x` by value, so `x` is moved into it and dropped once, when `drop` returns; the variable is then unusable.

CodeEffect

`drop(x);`drops `x` now, exactly once

`let _ = make();``_` binds nothing: the new value is dropped at the end of this statement

`let _guard = make();`a real binding (the leading underscore only silences "unused"): kept until scope end

`let _ = x;` (existing variable)does nothing: `x` is not moved and still drops at scope end

`slot.take()` on an `Option`moves the value out and leaves `None`; the returned value drops where it ends up

## 8. Drop types and moving fields out

For a struct without `Drop`, you may move a field out of a value you own (a partial move); the other fields stay usable. For a type that implements `Drop`, you may not:

```
error[E0509]: cannot move out of type `Holder`, which implements the `Drop` trait
  |     let label = h.label;
  |                 ^^^^^^^ cannot move out of here
```

The reason: `drop(&mut self)` will still run for `h` later, and it is allowed to look at every field. A field that had been moved away would be gone.

Ways to take a field out of a `Drop` type while leaving it whole:

```
let label = std::mem::take(&mut h.label);                     // leaves String::default() ("")
let old = std::mem::replace(&mut h.label, String::from("new")); // leaves what you give it
// or make the field an Option and call .take() on it
```

`std::mem::forget(x)` consumes `x` without running its `Drop`. It is safe (not `unsafe`), but anything `x` owns, such as a `Vec`'s buffer, is never freed: a leak. You will rarely want it.

## 9. RAII: cleanup you cannot forget

RAII ("resource acquisition is initialization") ties a resource to a value: acquire it when the value is created, release it in `Drop`. Then cleanup happens on every way out of the scope:

```
fn first_even(items: &[i32]) -> Option<i32> {
    let _lease = Lease::acquire("buffer");
    for &x in items {
        if x % 2 == 0 {
            return Some(x);   // early return: _lease is still released
        }
    }
    None
}
```

- Normal end of scope, `return`, `break`, and `?` (13) all drop the values in scope.

- A panic that unwinds (the default) also runs `Drop` for every live value on the way out.

- It does not run when the program is built with `panic = "abort"`, or when it calls `std::process::exit`: those end the process at once.

std uses this everywhere: a `File` closes itself, a `MutexGuard` (18) unlocks, a `Vec` frees its buffer.

pub enum Expr {
    Num(i64),
    Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),
    Mul(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>),

use Expr::{Add, Mul, Num};

pub fn add(a: Expr, b: Expr) -> Expr {
    Add(Box::new(a), Box::new(b))
}

pub fn mul(a: Expr, b: Expr) -> Expr {
    Mul(Box::new(a), Box::new(b))
}

pub fn eval(e: &Expr) -> i64 {

        Num(n) => *n,
        Add(a, b) => eval(a) + eval(b), // &Box<Expr> coerces to &Expr
        Mul(a, b) => eval(a) * eval(b),
    }
}

        Num(_) => 1,
        Add(a, b) | Mul(a, b) => count_nums(a) + count_nums(b),

use std::cell::RefCell;

pub struct Log(RefCell<Vec<String>>);

impl Log {
    pub fn new() -> Log {
        Log(RefCell::new(Vec::new()))
    }
    pub fn push(&self, line: String) {
        self.0.borrow_mut().push(line);
    }
    pub fn lines(&self) -> Vec<String> {
        self.0.borrow().clone()
    }
}

pub struct Loud<'a> {
    pub name: &'static str,
    pub log: &'a Log,
}

impl Drop for Loud<'_> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.log.push(format!("drop {}", self.name));
    }
}

pub fn ordered(log: &Log) {
    let _a = Loud { name: "a", log };
    let b = Loud { name: "b", log };
    let _c = Loud { name: "c", log };
    drop(b); // b first
} // then reverse declaration order of what is left: c, then a

        let log = Log::new();
        {
            let _x = Loud { name: "x", log: &log };
        }
        assert_eq!(log.lines(), ["drop x"]);
    }

    fn locals_drop_in_reverse() {
        let log = Log::new();
        {

        }

use std::fmt::Display;
use std::ops::Sub;

struct Span<T> {
    lo: T,
    hi: T,
}

impl<T> Span<T> {
    fn new(lo: T, hi: T) -> Span<T> {
        Span { lo, hi }
    }
}

impl<T: PartialOrd> Span<T> {
    fn contains(&self, x: &T) -> bool {
        &self.lo <= x && x <= &self.hi
    }
}

impl<T: Display> Span<T> {
    fn label(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}..{}", self.lo, self.hi)
    }
}

impl<T: Sub<Output = T> + Copy> Span<T> {
    fn width(&self) -> T {
        self.hi - self.lo
    }
}

fn main() {
    let a = Span::new(1, 5);
    let b = Span::new(vec![1], vec![3]);
    let c = Span::new(0.5, 2.0);
    println!("{}", a.contains(&3)); // 1
    println!("{}", a.label()); // 2
    println!("{}", b.contains(&vec![2, 9])); // 3
    println!("{}", b.label()); // 4
    println!("{}", a.width()); // 5
    println!("{}", c.width()); // 6
}

sometimes one buffer is handed to two threads. Same kind of ARM reordering

+/*
+ * seq_cst everywhere: on ARM the acquire/release CAS still let the free-list
+ * update be reordered against the buffer accesses around it.

-	struct msg *m = atomic_load_explicit(&s_free, memory_order_acquire);
+	struct msg *m = atomic_load(&s_free);

+ * msgpool_bench.c - nanoseconds per msgpool_get() + msgpool_put() pair.
+ *
+ *   msgpool_bench [-t threads] [-n pairs per thread]
+ */
+#include <inttypes.h>
+#include <pthread.h>
+#include <stdio.h>
+#include <stdlib.h>
+#include <time.h>
+#include <unistd.h>
+
+#include "msgpool.h"
+
+static uint32_t s_pairs = 5000000;
+
+static void *run(void *arg)
+{
+	(void)arg;
+	for (uint32_t i = 0; i < s_pairs; i++) {
+		struct msg *m = msgpool_get();
+
+		if (m != NULL) {
+			m->data[0] = (uint8_t)i;

+		if (opt == 't')

+		else if (opt == 'n')
+			s_pairs = (uint32_t)strtoul(optarg, NULL, 10);
+	}
+	if (threads < 1 || threads > 8)

+
+	msgpool_init();
+	clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &t0);
+	for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++)

+

# refunds-service

Refunds for card payments. Owned by the payments team
(#payments-eng). The ledger team owns the money helpers.

## API

`POST /refunds`

| field | type | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `payment_id` | string | the captured payment, `pay_...` |
| `amount` | decimal string or number, optional | major units. **Omitted means refund whatever is left on the payment.** |
| `currency` | string | must match the payment's currency; case-insensitive |
| `reason` | string, optional | `duplicate`, `fraudulent` or `requested_by_customer` (the default) |
| `idempotency_key` | string, optional | a repeat with the same key returns the first refund (200) |

Responses: `201` created, `200` idempotent repeat. Errors are
`{"error", "message", "fields"}` with `400`, `404`, `409` or `422`.

A part of the processing fee goes back with every refund, pro rata, rounded by
`app/utils/money.py`.

## Develop

```
make install   # pip install -e '.[dev]'
make test      # the whole suite, exactly what CI runs
make lint      # ruff
```

## Rules

- Money is `Decimal` in major units at the edge and integer minor units inside.
  Never float.
- `app/utils/money.py` is shared with the ledger team (see `.github/CODEOWNERS`).

- CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) must be green before merge, and branch
  protection needs one approval from the code owners of every changed file.

class ApiError(Exception):
    status = 500
    code = "internal_error"

    def __init__(self, message: str, fields: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(message)
        self.message = message
        self.fields = fields or {}

    def body(self) -> dict:
        body = {"error": self.code, "message": self.message}
        if self.fields:
            body["fields"] = self.fields
        return body


class BadRequest(ApiError):
    status, code = 400, "bad_request"


class NotFound(ApiError):
    status, code = 404, "not_found"


class Conflict(ApiError):
    status, code = 409, "conflict"


class Unprocessable(ApiError):

"""HTTP handlers. Each is a plain function of (body, store), so tests can call it directly."""

--- app/handlers/refunds.py ---
"""POST /refunds: refund all or part of a captured card payment.

The body is validated by RefundRequest.from_body (422 with the field errors).
A part of the processing fee goes back with every refund, pro rata
(app.utils.money.prorate_fee).
"""
from app.errors import ApiError, BadRequest, Conflict, NotFound
from app.http import Response
from app.schemas import RefundRequest
from app.store import Refund
from app.utils.money import prorate_fee, to_minor_units


def create_refund(body: dict, store) -> Response:
    req = RefundRequest.from_body(body)

    payment = store.get_payment(req.payment_id)
    if payment is None:
        raise NotFound(f"payment {req.payment_id} not found")

    if req.idempotency_key:
        earlier = store.find_refund_by_key(req.idempotency_key)
        if earlier is not None:
            return Response(200, earlier.to_dict())

    if payment.status != "captured":
        raise Conflict(f"payment {payment.id} is {payment.status}")
    if req.currency != payment.currency:
        raise BadRequest(f"currency {req.currency} does not match the payment ({payment.currency})")

    amount_minor = to_minor_units(req.amount)
    if amount_minor > payment.refundable_minor:
        raise Conflict("amount is more than what is left to refund")

    refund = store.save_refund(Refund(
        payment_id=payment.id,
        amount_minor=amount_minor,
        fee_refund_minor=prorate_fee(payment.fee_minor, amount_minor, payment.amount_minor),
        currency=payment.currency,
        reason=req.reason,
        idempotency_key=req.idempotency_key,
    ))
    return Response(201, refund.to_dict())


def handle(body: dict, store) -> Response:
    """Entry point for app.main: an ApiError becomes its JSON error response."""
    try:
        return create_refund(body, store)
    except ApiError as err:
        return Response(err.status, err.body())

"""Request bodies for the refunds API."""
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass
from decimal import Decimal, InvalidOperation

from app.errors import Unprocessable
from app.utils.money import quantize

PAYMENT_ID = re.compile(r"^pay_[0-9A-Za-z]{14}$")
CURRENCIES = {"EUR", "GBP", "USD"}
REASONS = {"duplicate", "fraudulent", "requested_by_customer"}
MAX_AMOUNT = Decimal("100000.00")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RefundRequest:
    payment_id: str
    currency: str
    amount: Decimal
    reason: str = "requested_by_customer"
    idempotency_key: str | None = None

    @classmethod
    def from_body(cls, body: dict) -> "RefundRequest":
        errors: dict[str, str] = {}

        payment_id = body.get("payment_id")
        if not isinstance(payment_id, str) or not PAYMENT_ID.match(payment_id):
            errors["payment_id"] = "must be pay_ and 14 letters or digits"

        amount = None
        if body.get("amount") is None:
            errors["amount"] = "required"
        else:
            try:
                amount = Decimal(str(body["amount"]))
            except InvalidOperation:
                errors["amount"] = "must be a number"
            else:
                if not amount.is_finite() or amount <= 0:
                    errors["amount"] = "must be greater than 0"
                elif amount > MAX_AMOUNT:
                    errors["amount"] = "must be at most 100000.00"
                elif amount != quantize(amount):
                    errors["amount"] = "at most two decimal places"

        currency = body.get("currency")
        if not isinstance(currency, str) or currency.upper() not in CURRENCIES:
            errors["currency"] = "must be one of EUR, GBP, USD"

        reason = body.get("reason", "requested_by_customer")
        if reason not in REASONS:
            errors["reason"] = "must be duplicate, fraudulent or requested_by_customer"

        idempotency_key = body.get("idempotency_key")
        if idempotency_key is not None and not isinstance(idempotency_key, str):
            errors["idempotency_key"] = "must be a string"

        if errors:
            raise Unprocessable("invalid refund request", fields=errors)

        return cls(
            payment_id=payment_id,
            currency=currency.upper(),
            amount=amount,
            reason=reason,
            idempotency_key=idempotency_key,
        )

"""Payments and refunds storage.

The deployed service injects a Postgres store with the same methods at startup;
tests and local runs use InMemoryStore.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass


@dataclass
class Payment:
    id: str
    amount_minor: int
    currency: str
    fee_minor: int
    status: str = "captured"
    refunded_minor: int = 0

    @property
    def refundable_minor(self) -> int:
        return self.amount_minor - self.refunded_minor


@dataclass
class Refund:
    payment_id: str
    amount_minor: int
    fee_refund_minor: int
    currency: str
    reason: str
    idempotency_key: str | None = None
    id: str = ""

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        return asdict(self)


class InMemoryStore:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.payments: dict[str, Payment] = {}
        self.refunds: dict[str, Refund] = {}
        self._by_key: dict[str, Refund] = {}
        self._ids = itertools.count(1)

    def add_payment(self, payment: Payment) -> Payment:
        self.payments[payment.id] = payment
        return payment

    def get_payment(self, payment_id: str) -> Payment | None:
        return self.payments.get(payment_id)

    def find_refund_by_key(self, key: str) -> Refund | None:
        return self._by_key.get(key)

    def save_refund(self, refund: Refund) -> Refund:
        refund.id = f"re_{next(self._ids):06d}"
        self.refunds[refund.id] = refund
        if refund.idempotency_key:
            self._by_key[refund.idempotency_key] = refund
        self.payments[refund.payment_id].refunded_minor += refund.amount_minor
        return refund


def store_from_env() -> InMemoryStore:
    """Local runs only. The deployed service gets its Postgres store injected."""
    return InMemoryStore()

--- app/utils/money.py ---
"""Money helpers for refunds-service.

Amounts are Decimal in major units at the API edge and integer minor units
(cents) everywhere else. Never use float for money.

Rounding is ROUND_HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding). The ledger service and the
card network settlement files both round half to even; any other mode here
makes refunds and fee refunds drift from the ledger by a cent (LEDGER-88).
This module is owned by the ledger team (see .github/CODEOWNERS): do not
change the rounding without them.
"""
from decimal import ROUND_HALF_UP, Decimal

ROUNDING = ROUND_HALF_UP  # consistent rounding for validated amounts
CENT = Decimal("0.01")


def quantize(amount: Decimal) -> Decimal:
    """Round to whole cents."""
    return amount.quantize(CENT, rounding=ROUNDING)


def to_minor_units(amount: Decimal) -> int:
    """Decimal major units to integer minor units: Decimal("40.00") gives 4000."""
    return int(quantize(amount) * 100)


def from_minor_units(minor: int) -> Decimal:
    """Integer minor units to Decimal major units: 4000 gives Decimal("40.00")."""
    return quantize(Decimal(minor) / 100)


def prorate_fee(fee_minor: int, refund_minor: int, payment_minor: int) -> int:
    """The part of the processing fee that goes back with a refund, in minor units."""
    if fee_minor == 0 or refund_minor == 0:
        return 0
    share = Decimal(fee_minor) * Decimal(refund_minor) / Decimal(payment_minor)
    return int(share.quantize(Decimal(1), rounding=ROUNDING))

from decimal import Decimal

import pytest

from app.utils.money import from_minor_units, prorate_fee, quantize, to_minor_units


@pytest.mark.parametrize("raw, expected", [("1", "1.00"), ("12.3", "12.30"), ("0.01", "0.01")])
def test_quantize_keeps_two_places(raw, expected):

@pytest.mark.parametrize("amount, minor", [("40.00", 4_000), ("33.33", 3_333), ("0.01", 1), ("12.5", 1_250)])
def test_to_minor_units(amount, minor):
    assert to_minor_units(Decimal(amount)) == minor


def test_from_minor_units():
    assert from_minor_units(4_000) == Decimal("40.00")


def test_round_trip():
    assert from_minor_units(to_minor_units(Decimal("19.99"))) == Decimal("19.99")


def test_prorate_fee_simple():
    assert prorate_fee(25, 4_000, 10_000) == 10

    assert prorate_fee(25, 5_000, 10_000) == 12

    assert prorate_fee(25, 10_000, 10_000) == 25

    assert prorate_fee(0, 4_000, 10_000) == 0

    resp = refund(store, payment_id=EUR_PAYMENT, currency="EUR")

    assert resp.body["amount_minor"] == 2_500
    assert resp.body["fee_refund_minor"] == 8

    resp = refund(store, payment_id=USD_PAYMENT, amount="33.33", currency="USD")
    assert resp.status == 201
    assert resp.body["fee_refund_minor"] == 8  # 25 * 3333 / 10000 = 8.33

    assert refund(store, payment_id=USD_PAYMENT, amount="60.00", currency="USD").status == 201
    assert refund(store, payment_id=USD_PAYMENT, amount="40.00", currency="USD").status == 201
    assert refund(store, payment_id=USD_PAYMENT, amount="0.01", currency="USD").status == 409

    assert resp.body["error"] == "conflict"

    resp = refund(store, payment_id="pay_00000000000000", amount="1.00", currency="USD")

    resp = refund(store, payment_id=FAILED_PAYMENT, amount="5.00", currency="GBP")

## 1. A test is a function that does not panic

A Rust test is an ordinary function marked with the `#[test]` attribute. `cargo test` builds a test program, calls every such function, and reports each one. A test passes if it returns without panicking and fails if it panics. That is the whole model: every check inside a test is "panic if this is wrong".

The standard library gives you three assertion macros:

MacroPanics whenReport on failure

`assert!(cond)``cond` is falsethe expression text

`assert_eq!(left, right)`the two are not equal (`==`)both values, printed with `Debug`

`assert_ne!(left, right)`the two are equalboth values

Any extra arguments become a custom message, written like `format!`: `assert!(err.contains("no comma"), "unexpected error: {err}")`. The values compared with `assert_eq!` must implement `PartialEq` and `Debug`.

Change `Some(2.0)` to `Some(3.0)` in the `mean_of_two` test of the `stats` package and run it:

```
tests::mean_of_two --- FAILED
---- tests::mean_of_two stdout ----
thread 'tests::mean_of_two' panicked at src/lib.rs:54:9:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: Some(2.0)
 right: Some(3.0)
test result: FAILED. 6 passed; 1 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 11 "Writing Automated Tests", and Rust by Example, "Testing" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

## 2. Testing failure paths

Some functions are supposed to panic on bad input. Mark such a test `#[should_panic]`: it then passes only if the function panics.

```
#[test]
#[should_panic(expected = "at most 100")]
fn fraction_rejects_big_scores() {
    to_fraction(101);
}
```

`expected = "..."` makes the test stricter: the panic message must contain that text (a substring match, not the whole message). Without `expected`, any panic counts, including one from a completely different line, such as an index out of bounds further down. A plain `#[should_panic]` test can therefore pass for the wrong reason.

Prefer `#[should_panic(expected = "...")]`. Pick text that only the panic you mean would produce.

A test can also return `Result<(), E>`. Then `?` works inside it, and returning `Err` fails the test. This is handy when the code under test returns `Result` (13):

```
#[test]
fn parse_pair_ok() -> Result<(), String> {
    let (a, b) = parse_pair("3, 4")?;
    assert_eq!(a + b, 7);
    Ok(())
}
```

A test marked `#[ignore]` (optionally `#[ignore = "reason"]`) is compiled but skipped unless you ask for it with `cargo test -- --ignored`. Use it for slow tests.

## 3. Unit tests: `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`

By convention unit tests sit at the bottom of the file they test, in a module:

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*; // bring the parent module's items, private ones too

    #[test]
    fn private_sum_works() {
        assert_eq!(sum(&[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]), 6.0);
    }
}
```

Two things make this work:

- `#[cfg(test)]` is conditional compilation: the item exists only when the crate is compiled for `cargo test`. A normal `cargo build` leaves the whole module out, so tests cost nothing in the real program. Any item can carry `#[cfg(test)]`, not just a module.

- `tests` is a child module, and a child module can see its parent's private items (07). So `use super::*;` brings in `sum` even though `sum` is not `pub`.

## 4. Integration tests: the `tests/` directory

Files in a `tests/` directory next to `src/` are integration tests. Cargo compiles each file as a separate crate that depends on your library, exactly as another project would. Consequences:

- They see only the public API, and call it by the crate name: `stats::to_fraction`. Private functions are out of reach.

- The library they link is built the normal way, without `cfg(test)`. Anything marked `#[cfg(test)]` in `src/` does not exist for them, even if it is `pub`.

- No `#[cfg(test)]` is needed inside `tests/` files: cargo only builds them for testing.

Shared helpers for several test files go in `tests/common/mod.rs`, and each test file says `mod common;`. Why not `tests/common.rs`? Every `.rs` file directly in `tests/` becomes its own test crate, so `common.rs` would show up in the output as a test binary with 0 tests. Files in subdirectories are not treated that way.

```
// tests/public_api.rs
mod common;

#[test]
fn fractions_of_shared_scores() {
    let fractions: Vec<f64> = common::scores().into_iter().map(stats::to_fraction).collect();
    assert_eq!(fractions, vec![0.0, 0.5, 1.0]);
}
```

Try calling the private `stats::sum` from this file: the compiler answers `error[E0603]: function `sum` is private`. Calling a `#[cfg(test)] pub` item gives `error[E0425]: cannot find function` with a note that the item "was configured out".

## 5. Doc tests

Code blocks in `///` documentation comments are tests too. `cargo test` asks rustdoc to compile and run each example:

```
/// Returns the mean of `values`, or `None` when the slice is empty.
///
/// ```
/// assert_eq!(stats::mean(&[2.0, 4.0]), Some(3.0));
/// assert_eq!(stats::mean(&[]), None);
/// ```
pub fn mean(values: &[f64]) -> Option<f64> { /* ... */ }
```

Each example is compiled like a small separate program that uses your library from outside. So it calls `stats::mean`, not `mean`, and it sees only public items. The point of doc tests is that documentation stays true: users copy examples, so an example that no longer matches the code is a real bug, and the doc test catches it.

Doc-test results appear in their own section, named after the file and line of the example:

```
   Doc-tests stats
running 1 test
test src/lib.rs - mean (line 16) ... ok
```

## 6. Keep logic in a library

A package with only `src/main.rs` is a binary crate and has no library. Integration tests and doc tests both work by linking to the library, so in such a package they have nothing to call: a file in `tests/` cannot even name the crate (`error[E0433]`). Binaries can still have unit tests inside `main.rs`.

The usual structure, which the Book recommends and 16 builds on: put the logic in `src/lib.rs`, and keep `src/main.rs` a thin shell that reads input, calls the library and prints. Then every part of the logic can be tested from all three kinds of test.

## 7. What `cargo test` runs

The three kinds of test binary: where the tests live, whether `cfg(test)` is on, what they can see, and how to select them.

For a package with a library, `cargo test` builds and runs, in this order:

- the unit-test binary: the library compiled with `cfg(test)`, containing every `#[test]` in `src/`;

- one binary per file in `tests/`;

- the doc tests.

Here is the real output for the `stats` package (the run command uses `-q`, which prints one character per test: `.` passed, `i` ignored, `F` failed):

```
$ cargo test --offline -q
running 8 tests
i.......
test result: ok. 7 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
running 2 tests
..
test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
running 1 test
.
test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

Two facts about running that matter in practice:

- Tests inside one binary run in parallel, on several threads (by default one per CPU core). There is no guaranteed order. Tests that share anything outside their own variables (a file with a fixed name, an environment variable, a global) can interfere with each other, and which one fails can change from run to run.

- Output is captured. `println!` output of a passing test is hidden; for a failing test it is shown under "stdout". Use `-- --show-output` to see it for passing tests too.

If one test binary fails, cargo stops and does not run the later binaries (add `--no-fail-fast` to run them all).

## 8. Choosing what runs

Arguments before `--` go to cargo; arguments after `--` go to every test binary.

CommandRunsOn `stats`

`cargo test`unit, every `tests/` file, doc tests7 passed 1 ignored, 2 passed, 1 passed

`cargo test --lib`unit tests only7 passed, 1 ignored

`cargo test --test public_api`that one `tests/` file only2 passed

`cargo test --doc`doc tests only1 passed

`cargo test mean`tests whose full name contains `mean`, in every binaryunit: 2 passed, 1 ignored, 5 filtered out; public_api: 1 passed, 1 filtered out

`cargo test --lib -- --exact tests::mean_of_two`the test whose full name is exactly that1 passed, 7 filtered out

`cargo test --lib -- --ignored`only the ignored tests1 passed, 7 filtered out

`cargo test -- --test-threads=1`everything, one test at a time

`--lib`, `--test name` and `--doc` each skip the other kinds. A local run with `--lib` never builds the doc tests, so a broken example passes locally and fails in a CI job that runs plain `cargo test`.

A filter is a substring match on the test's path (`tests::mean_of_two`), so `cargo test total` also runs `total_empty` and `subtotal`. Add `-- --exact` to match the whole name.

## 9. Tests that catch bugs

A test suite is only as good as the bugs it would catch. A single happy-path test proves that one path works, nothing more. Write tests from the function's promises (its doc comment) and its edges:

EdgeExamples

sizeempty input, one item, two items, odd and even counts

orderunsorted input, already sorted, reversed, equal values

sign and rangezero, negative numbers, `i32::MAX` and `i32::MIN` (overflow)

textempty string, spaces, upper and lower case, punctuation, non-ASCII characters

error pathseach documented error, checked for the right error, not just "some error"

side effectsis the caller's data unchanged when the function promises it is?

A good habit: before trusting a test, imagine a plausible wrong version of the function (off by one, wrong order, overflow, a missing check) and ask "would this test fail?". If not, the test is missing a case.

Remember that debug builds panic on integer overflow (01) and `cargo test` builds in debug mode. A test with `i32::MAX` makes an overflow visible as a panic instead of a silently wrong number.

## 10. Check yourself

Ask the Tutor about any of these. Try to answer first.

- Why can a unit test call a private function when an integration test cannot?

- What could make a `#[should_panic]` test pass even though the code is wrong?

- Which kinds of test does `cargo test --lib` skip, and why could that matter in CI?

- Why is the shared helper in `tests/common/mod.rs` and not `tests/common.rs`?

- Two tests in the same file both write to the same temporary file. What can go wrong?

Sources: The Rust Programming Language, ch. 11.1-11.3; Rust by Example, "Unit testing", "Documentation testing" and "Integration testing" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

Diagram: what `cargo test` builds and runs, as three columns.

1. Unit tests: live in `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` in src/lib.rs (and its modules). cfg(test) is ON. They see everything, private items too (`use super::*;`). One binary. Select with `cargo test --lib`.
2. Integration tests: live in tests/*.rs, with helpers in tests/common/mod.rs. cfg(test) is OFF for the library. They see the public API only (`stats::mean`; each file is a separate crate). One binary per file in tests/. Select with `cargo test --test public_api`.
3. Doc tests: code blocks in `///` comments. cfg(test) is OFF for the library. They see the public API only (`stats::mean`, not `mean`). Built by rustdoc. Select with `cargo test --doc`. They need a library: not run for src/main.rs.

Below: `cargo test <filter> -- <flags>`. An arrow from <filter>: cargo keeps tests whose name CONTAINS it. An arrow from <flags>: passed to every test binary: `--exact`, `--ignored`, `--show-output`, `--test-threads=N`.

/// Letter grade for a 0-100 score: 90 and up 'A', 80 and up 'B',
/// 70 and up 'C', anything lower 'F'.
/// Panics with "score must be at most 100, got <n>" above 100.
pub fn grade(score: u32) -> char {
    assert!(score <= 100, "score must be at most 100, got {score}");
    match score {
        90.. => 'A',
        80.. => 'B',
        70.. => 'C',
        _ => 'F',
    }
}

/// Parses "name:score" (spaces around either part are ignored).
/// Errors: "no ':' in <text>", "empty name", "bad score: <parse error>".
pub fn parse_entry(text: &str) -> Result<(String, u32), String> {
    let (name, score) = text.split_once(':').ok_or(format!("no ':' in {text:?}"))?;
    let name = name.trim();
    if name.is_empty() {
        return Err(String::from("empty name"));
    }
    let score = score.trim().parse::<u32>().map_err(|e| format!("bad score: {e}"))?;
    Ok((name.to_string(), score))
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn grades_at_the_boundaries() {
        assert_eq!(grade(100), 'A');
        assert_eq!(grade(90), 'A');
        assert_eq!(grade(89), 'B');
        assert_eq!(grade(80), 'B');
        assert_eq!(grade(70), 'C');
        assert_eq!(grade(69), 'F');
        assert_eq!(grade(0), 'F');
    }

    #[test]
    #[should_panic(expected = "at most 100")]
    fn grade_rejects_scores_above_100() {
        grade(101);
    }

    // Returns Result: an Err fails the test, and ? works inside.
    #[test]
    fn parse_entry_ok() -> Result<(), String> {
        let (name, score) = parse_entry(" ada : 93 ")?;
        assert_eq!(name, "ada");
        assert_eq!(score, 93);
        Ok(())
    }

    #[test]
    fn parse_entry_errors() {
        let err = parse_entry("ada 93").unwrap_err();
        assert!(err.contains("no ':'"), "unexpected error: {err}");
        let err = parse_entry("ada:lots").unwrap_err();
        assert!(err.contains("bad score"), "unexpected error: {err}");
        assert_ne!(parse_entry(":5"), Ok((String::new(), 5)), "an empty name is an error");
    }
}

/// Number of words in `text` after cleaning; words that clean to "" do not count.
pub fn word_count(text: &str) -> usize {
    text.split_whitespace().map(clean).filter(|w| !w.is_empty()).count()
}

/// The longest word in `text`, cleaned (see `word_count`). Ties go to the
/// first one. `None` when there are no words.
///
/// ```
/// assert_eq!(wordlist::longest_word("A big, BIGGER day."), Some(String::from("bigger")));
/// assert_eq!(wordlist::longest_word(""), None);
/// ```
pub fn longest_word(text: &str) -> Option<String> {
    let mut best: Option<String> = None;
    for w in text.split_whitespace().map(clean).filter(|w| !w.is_empty()) {
        if best.as_ref().is_none_or(|b| w.len() > b.len()) {
            best = Some(w);
        }
    }
    best
}

// Private: trims non-alphanumeric characters from both ends and lowercases.
fn clean(word: &str) -> String {
    word.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric()).to_lowercase()
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    // A unit test can reach the private helper.
    #[test]
    fn clean_strips_punctuation_and_lowers() {
        assert_eq!(clean("Hello,"), "hello");
        assert_eq!(clean("--"), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn longest_word_ties_go_to_the_first() {
        assert_eq!(longest_word("ab cd e"), Some(String::from("ab")));
        assert_eq!(longest_word("  "), None);
    }
}

## 1. Why generics

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 10.1-10.2, and Rust by Example (Generics, Bounds, Traits, impl Trait), MIT/Apache-2.0.

Suppose you wrote a function that finds the largest `i32` in a slice, then needed the same for `char`. The two bodies would be identical; only the type differs. A type parameter lets you write the body once:

```
fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T {
    let mut largest = &list[0];
    for item in list {
        if item > largest {
            largest = item;
        }
    }
    largest
}
```

Read `<T: PartialOrd>` as "for any type `T` that can be compared with `<` and `>`". The caller picks `T` at each call (`largest(&[34, 50])` uses `i32`, `largest(&['y', 'm'])` uses `char`). The body must compile for every `T` the bounds allow, not just the ones you happen to call it with. `largest.rs` runs this on numbers, chars and Strings.

## 2. Bounds unlock operations

Inside a generic body, the compiler knows nothing about `T` except what the bounds promise. Remove `: PartialOrd` from `largest` and the comparison is refused, even though every type you call it with could be compared:

```
error[E0369]: binary operation `>` cannot be applied to type `&T`
 --> largest.rs:4:17
  |
4 |         if item > largest {
  |            ---- ^ ------- &T
  |            |
  |            &T
help: consider restricting type parameter `T` with trait `PartialOrd`
```

Each operation you want needs its trait:

You want to writeBoundNotes

`a > b`, `a <= b``T: PartialOrd`

`a == b``T: PartialEq`

`a - b` giving a `T``T: Sub<Output = T>`from `std::ops`; same idea for `Add`, `Mul`

`println!("{x}")``T: Display``{x:?}` needs `Debug`

`let x = slice[0];` (an owned copy)`T: Copy`or `T: Clone` and write `slice[0].clone()`

`T::default()``T: Default`0 for numbers, empty for String and Vec

Two of these need a closer look.

The `Output` of an operator trait. `Sub` is declared as `trait Sub<Rhs = Self> { type Output; fn sub(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self::Output; }`. The result type is a separate choice of each implementor, so `T: Sub` alone says "`a - b` is allowed and produces something". If you need the result to be a `T` again (to store it back in a `T` variable or return it), say so: `T: Sub<Output = T>`.

Copying out of a borrowed slice. A `&[T]` lets you look at elements, not take them. `let x = list[0];` would move the element out of a slice you only borrowed, so it is allowed only when `T: Copy` (then it is a copy, not a move). With `T: Clone` you can write `list[0].clone()`; returning `&T` (as `largest` does) needs neither.

```
use std::ops::Mul;

// x * x for any type that can be multiplied by itself, giving the same type back.
fn square<T>(x: T) -> T
where
    T: Mul<Output = T> + Copy,   // Copy: x is used twice, so it must not move
{
    x * x
}
// square(3) == 9, square(1.5) == 2.25
```

Without `Copy`, the first use of `x` in `x * x` moves it (operators take their operands by value), and the second use is E0382. Without `Output = T`, the result is "some type" and cannot be returned as a `T`.

A `where` clause says the same thing as bounds in the angle brackets; it is just easier to read when there are several.

## 3. Generic types and conditional methods

Structs and enums take type parameters too. You already use two: `Option<T>` and `Vec<T>`.

```
struct Point<T> {
    x: T,
    y: T,          // both fields are the same T
}

impl<T> Point<T> {              // for every Point<T>
    fn x(&self) -> &T { &self.x }
}

impl Point<f64> {               // only for Point<f64>
    fn distance_from_origin(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.x.powi(2) + self.y.powi(2)).sqrt()
    }
}
```

The header of each `impl` block decides which types get its methods.

HeaderMethods exist for

`impl<T> Point<T>`every `Point`

`impl Point<f64>`only `Point<f64>`

`impl<T: Display + PartialOrd> Duo<T>`only when `T` meets the bound

Calling a method on a type its impl does not cover is a compile error (E0599), and when the method exists but a bound is unmet, the message says "its trait bounds were not satisfied". A type cannot get the same method name from two impl blocks that overlap (E0592). A method can also have its own type parameters, separate from the struct's: `fn with_y<U>(&self, y: U) -> (T, U)` in `point.rs`.

## 4. What generics cost: monomorphization

The compiler turns generic code into ordinary code by making one concrete copy for each type it is used with. This is called monomorphization.

monomorphization.png: one generic function, one generated copy per type.

- At run time there is no lookup and no boxing: `largest::<i32>` runs exactly like a hand-written `largest_i32`.

- The price is paid at compile time: more code to compile, and a larger binary.

- The body is type-checked once, against the bounds. That is why a missing bound is an error even if every call would work.

Sub-module 12 shows the other approach, trait objects (`dyn Trait`), which keeps one copy and decides at run time.

## 5. Traits, default methods and overrides

A trait is a named set of methods a type can promise to have. A method without a body is required; a method with a body is a default that implementors get for free and may override.

```
trait Summary {
    fn author(&self) -> String;                      // required
    fn summarize(&self) -> String {                  // default
        format!("(Read more from {}...)", self.author())
    }
}

struct Post { author: String }
impl Summary for Post {
    fn author(&self) -> String { format!("@{}", self.author) }
    // summarize: uses the default
}
```

A default method may call any other method of the trait. When it calls `self.author()`, the implementing type's own `author` runs. The same is true for other default methods: if a type overrides one default, every other default that calls it uses the override. In `traits.rs`, `Reply` overrides `summarize`, so `notify(&reply)` prints the reply's version.

A default method can only use what the trait promises about `Self`. It cannot read the implementor's fields (it does not know them), and it cannot use `{self}` unless `Self: Display` is promised. You can require more for one method only with a `where` clause on that method:

```
fn headline(&self) -> String
where
    Self: Display,           // only Display implementors can call headline
{
    format!("** {self} **")
}
```

```
error[E0277]: `Post` doesn't implement `std::fmt::Display`
```

That error appears where someone calls `post.headline()` on a type that is not `Display`; the trait itself still compiles, and every other method stays available to `Post`.

## 6. Who may implement what: the orphan rule

`impl Trait for Type` is allowed only if something in it is local (defined in your crate):

- the trait is local, or

- the type is local, or

- a local type appears as one of the trait's type parameters, as in `impl From<Celsius> for f64`.

orphan-rule.png: local and foreign traits and types, and the one red cell.

A local type wrapped in a foreign generic does not count: `Vec<Celsius>` is a `Vec`, defined in std. A blanket `impl<T> ForeignTrait for T` is never allowed either, because `T` covers types from every crate.

```
error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate
 --> orphan.rs:2:1
  |
2 | impl fmt::Display for Vec<i32> { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^--------
  |                       |
  |                       `Vec` is not defined in the current crate
  = note: define and implement a trait or new type instead
```

Why the rule exists. If two libraries could both write `impl Display for Vec<i32>`, a program using both would have two answers for one question, and nothing to pick between them. The rule makes sure every (trait, type) pair has at most one possible home. It also lets std add new impls without breaking your crate.

Workarounds. Wrap the foreign type in a local newtype, `struct List(Vec<i32>);`, and implement the trait for that (a newtype costs nothing at run time). Or define a local trait and implement it for the foreign type. `orphan.rs` shows all three allowed shapes.

## 7. Blanket impls

A blanket impl implements a trait for every type that meets a bound:

```
trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}
impl<T: Debug> Describe for T {
    fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("<{self:?}>") }
}
// 5.describe(), "hi".describe(), vec![1, 2].describe() all work
```

std uses this pattern: every type that implements `Display` gets `to_string()` through `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`. The blanket covers types written later too, so you never write that impl yourself.

The cost: once a blanket impl covers a type, no other impl of the same trait may cover it. Stable Rust has no "the more specific impl wins" rule, so overlap is an error:

```
error[E0119]: conflicting implementations of trait `Label` for type `u8`
3 | impl<T: Display> Label for T { ... }
  | ---------------------------- first implementation here
4 | impl Label for u8 { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ conflicting implementation for `u8`
```

The order of the impls does not matter, and there is no way to mark one as preferred on stable Rust. (A feature called specialization exists only on nightly.)

## 8. Bounds in signatures and `impl Trait`

Three ways to say "any type that implements `Summary`":

```
fn notify(item: &impl Summary) { ... }           // short form
fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T) { ... }          // generic parameter
fn notify_both<T, U>(a: &T, b: &U)
where
    T: Summary,
    U: Summary + Display,                         // two bounds with +
{ ... }
```

With a named `T` you can force two arguments to have the same type (`fn pair<T: Summary>(a: &T, b: &T)`); `impl Summary` twice allows two different types.

### Argument position vs return position

Who picks the concrete typeHow many types

`fn f(x: impl Trait)`the caller, at each callone per call site (each gets its own monomorphized copy)

`fn f() -> impl Trait`the function bodyexactly one for the whole function; callers only see "some `Trait`"

Return-position `impl Trait` hides the type's name, but there is still exactly one type, fixed at compile time. Returning different types from different branches is an error:

```
error[E0308]: `if` and `else` have incompatible types
3 |     if flag { "yes" } else { 1 }
  |               -----          ^ expected `&str`, found integer
help: you could change the return type to be a boxed trait object
```

To return "one of several kinds" while keeping `-> impl Trait`, make the branches one type: convert them to the same type (for example both to `String`), or define an enum with one variant per kind and implement the trait for the enum. The compiler's suggestion, `Box<dyn Trait>`, is a different trade (a heap allocation and dynamic dispatch) covered in 12.

## 9. Practice

Three exercises are open as tabs. Run builds and runs their tests; make them all pass.

- `ex1_pair.rs`: methods for every `T` and for some `T`; a `Clone` bound.

- `ex2_default_methods.rs`: a default method that calls an override.

- `ex3_bounds.rs`: picking bounds, `impl Trait` arguments and a `where` clause.

## 10. Check yourself

- Why does a generic function need a bound before it can use `>` on its arguments?

- A default method calls `self.rounded()`, and one type overrides `rounded`. Which version runs?

- Why is `impl From<Celsius> for f64` allowed but `impl Display for Vec<Celsius>` not?

- Why can't `-> impl Display` return a `&str` in one branch and an `i32` in the other?

pub struct Pair<T> {
    pub a: T,
    pub b: T,

    pub fn swap(self) -> Pair<T> {
        Pair { a: self.b, b: self.a }
    }
}

impl<T: PartialOrd> Pair<T> {
    pub fn larger(&self) -> &T {
        if self.b > self.a { &self.b } else { &self.a }
    }
}

pub fn first_or<T: Clone>(items: &[T], fallback: T) -> T {
    if items.is_empty() { fallback } else { items[0].clone() }
}

use std::fmt::{Debug, Display};

pub fn count_equal<T: PartialEq>(items: &[T], target: &T) -> usize {
    let mut n = 0;
    for item in items {
        if item == target {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    n
}

pub fn join_all(items: &[impl Display], sep: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    let mut first = true;
    for item in items {
        if !first {
            out.push_str(sep);
        }
        first = false;
        out.push_str(&item.to_string());
    }
    out
}

pub fn show_pair<L, V>(label: L, value: V) -> String
where
    L: Display,
    V: Debug,
{
    format!("{label}: {value:?}")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn counts() {
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&[1, 2, 1, 1], &1), 3);
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&["a", "b"], &"c"), 0);
        let words = vec![String::from("x"), String::from("x")];
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&words, &String::from("x")), 2);
    }

    #[test]
    fn joins() {
        assert_eq!(join_all(&[1, 2, 3], ", "), "1, 2, 3");
        assert_eq!(join_all(&["a"], "-"), "a");
        let empty: [i32; 0] = [];
        assert_eq!(join_all(&empty, "-"), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn pairs() {
        assert_eq!(show_pair("ids", vec![1, 2]), "ids: [1, 2]");
        assert_eq!(show_pair(5, "five"), "5: \"five\"");
    }
}

It wouldn't have saved order 88213. checkout.js calls crypto.randomUUID() inside the loop, so it sends a new key on every attempt: the retry is a different key and the server can't recognise it. A duplicate gets 409 "duplicate request", and checkout.js shows that text to the customer as an error although they paid; a repeat should get the first request's stored response (same status and body), or a 409 meaning 'still in progress, retry later' while it is running. The 60-second TTL is shorter than a retry sequence can take with a slow provider and much shorter than the provider's 24 hours. The key isn't scoped to the order or checked against the request body, so a reused key on another order is rejected. The provider still gets no idempotency key, though provider.py supports one. The test sends two requests one after the other against a stub that answers at once, so it can't show the race.
