## 1. The problem lifetimes solve

A reference must never outlive the value it points to. If it did, it would point at memory that has already been freed: a dangling reference. Rust rules these out at compile time. The part of the compiler that does it, the borrow checker, compares two spans for every borrow:

- how long the value lives (from where it is created to where it is dropped, usually the end of its scope), and

- how long the reference is used (from where it is created to its last use).

The second span must fit inside the first. That span of validity is the reference's lifetime. Inside one function the compiler works lifetimes out on its own; you have done this since 03 without writing a single one. Lifetimes need writing only where the compiler cannot see across a boundary: a function signature, or a struct that holds a reference.

```
let r;
{
    let x = 5;
    r = &x;          // r borrows x
}                    // x is dropped here
println!("{r}");     // r is used after x is gone: error[E0597]
```

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch. 10.3 "Validating References with Lifetimes", and Rust by Example, "Lifetimes" (MIT/Apache-2.0).

## 2. Annotations describe, they do not extend

A lifetime annotation is a name that starts with an apostrophe, usually short: `'a`, `'b`. It goes after the `&`:

```
&i32        // a reference
&'a i32     // a reference with an explicit lifetime 'a
&'a mut i32 // a mutable reference with an explicit lifetime 'a
```

`x: &'a str` means "`x` is valid for at least the span called `'a`". On its own a single annotation says little. Its power is in relating several references: two parameters and a return value that share `'a` are tied together.

An annotation never changes how long any value lives. Values are still dropped at the end of their scope. Writing `'a` cannot keep a `String` alive; it can only describe a relationship the compiler then checks. If the relationship is false, the code is rejected.

## 3. Connecting inputs to outputs

Here is the Book's example, in `longest.rs`. It returns whichever of two string slices is longer:

```
fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if x.len() > y.len() { x } else { y }
}
```

Read the signature as a contract: "for some span `'a` during which both `x` and `y` are valid, the result is valid for `'a` too." In practice `'a` becomes the overlap of the two inputs, so the result may be used only while the shorter-lived input is still alive.

The compiler checks the two sides of the contract separately:

- The body is checked against the signature: returning `x` or `y` is allowed, both are `'a`.

- Each caller is checked against the signature only. The caller never looks inside the body.

That second point explains `longest_scope.rs`. We can see that the result is `string1`, which is still alive. But the signature says "as long as the shorter of the two", and `string2` dies first:

```
error[E0597]: `string2` does not live long enough
  --> longest_scope.rs:19:44
   |
18 |         let string2 = String::from("xyz");
   |             ------- binding `string2` declared here
19 |         result = longest(string1.as_str(), string2.as_str());
   |                                            ^^^^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
20 |     } // string2 is dropped here
   |     - `string2` dropped here while still borrowed
...
23 |     println!("The longest string is {result}");
   |                                      ------ borrow later used here
```

How long each value in longest_scope.rs lives. `'a` covers only the overlap of the two inputs, so using `result` after the inner block breaks the contract.

Why can't the compiler just read the body? Because the signature is the function's public promise. If callers depended on the body, changing the body (say, sometimes returning `y`) could break code in other files and crates. Checking against the signature keeps every function checkable on its own.

## 4. Tie only the inputs the output can come from

A lifetime parameter on an input is a demand on callers: "keep this alive as long as you use the result". So give the output's lifetime only to the inputs the result can actually point into. An input that is only read (a search pattern, a length limit, a flag) should keep its own, unnamed lifetime.

```
// The result is always `line` or a slice of it. `tag` is only compared.
fn strip_tag<'a>(line: &'a str, tag: &str) -> &'a str {
    line.strip_prefix(tag).unwrap_or(line)
}
```

If `tag` were also `&'a str`, the function would still compile, but every caller would have to keep `tag` alive as long as the result, for no reason. A caller that builds the tag in a short block would then get E0597 naming the tag, even though the result never points into it.

A string literal such as `""` has type `&'static str`, which can stand in for any shorter lifetime. So a function declared to return `&'a str` may also return `""`.

## 5. The three elision rules

Early Rust needed annotations on every signature with references. The patterns were so regular that the compiler now fills them in. These are the lifetime elision rules. A lifetime on a parameter is an input lifetime; on the return type, an output lifetime.

RuleSaysExample, written and inferred

1Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime.`fn f(a: &str, b: &str)` becomes `fn f<'a, 'b>(a: &'a str, b: &'b str)`

2If there is exactly one input lifetime, every output gets it.`fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str` becomes `fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str`

3If one input is `&self` or `&mut self`, every output gets self's lifetime.`fn name(&self, p: &str) -> &str` becomes `fn name<'s, 'p>(&'s self, p: &'p str) -> &'s str`

Non-reference parameters (`usize`, `bool`, an owned `String`) have no lifetime and do not count. A function whose output holds no reference needs no output lifetime at all, whatever its inputs.

The rules as a flowchart. If no rule decides the output lifetime, you get E0106 and must write it.

When no rule decides, the compiler refuses to guess. `elision_fail.rs` has two reference inputs and no `self`:

```
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> elision_fail.rs:9:30
  |
9 | fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
  |            ----     ----     ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `a` or `b`
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
9 | fn pick<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
  |        ++++     ++          ++          ++
```

There is a second, different failure. Sometimes a rule does decide, but the body returns something the decided signature does not allow. Then the error is not E0106 but "lifetime may not live long enough": elision wrote a contract and the body broke it. The fix is to write the signature you meant.

The compiler's `help:` suggestion is a guess that makes the signature well formed. It is not always what the body needs, and it may tie more inputs than necessary (section 4). Read it, then decide which inputs the result can really come from.

## 6. Structs that hold references

A struct may hold a reference if it declares a lifetime parameter for it. `excerpt.rs`, adapted from the Book:

```
struct Excerpt<'a> {
    part: &'a str,
}
```

This says: an `Excerpt<'a>` cannot outlive the text its `part` borrows. The lifetime parameter is declared again on the `impl`, `impl<'a> Excerpt<'a>`, and is then available to every method.

Methods can return two different kinds of borrow, and the difference matters:

SignatureResult is tied toCan the result outlive the struct?

`fn announce(&self, note: &str) -> &str`the borrow of `self` (rule 3)no

`fn part(&self) -> &'a str`the text the struct borrows (`'a`)yes, as long as the text lives

In `excerpt.rs`, `kept = short_lived.part()` outlives `short_lived` because `part` returns `&'a str`. Change the return type to `&str` and rule 3 ties the result to `&self` instead:

```
error[E0597]: `short_lived` does not live long enough
  --> excerpt.rs:40:16
   |
39 |         let short_lived = Excerpt { part: &text[0..9] };
   |             ----------- binding `short_lived` declared here
40 |         kept = short_lived.part(); // fine: tied to text, not to short_lived
   |                ^^^^^^^^^^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
41 |     }
   |     - `short_lived` dropped here while still borrowed
42 |     println!("kept: {kept}");
   |                      ---- borrow later used here
```

The same applies to `&mut self` methods: an elided output keeps the struct mutably borrowed for as long as the result is used, so you cannot call the method again meanwhile. Returning `&'a str` instead says the result points into the underlying data, not into the struct.

### Two fields, two lifetimes

If one lifetime `'a` covers two reference fields, both borrows must be valid for the same `'a`, so `'a` shrinks to the shorter of the two. Anything a method returns as `&'a str` is then tied to the shorter-lived field too, even if it points into the longer one. When the fields come from places with different lifetimes, give each its own parameter (`more_lifetimes.rs`):

```
struct Tagged<'v, 'n> {
    value: &'v str,
    note: &'n str,
}
impl<'v, 'n> Tagged<'v, 'n> {
    fn value(&self) -> &'v str { self.value } // not tied to `note`
}
```

## 7. `'static`, owned returns and `T: 'static`

`'static` is the lifetime of the whole program. String literals are `&'static str`: their bytes are stored in the program binary and never freed.

A function can never return a reference to something it created itself: the value is dropped when the function returns, and no annotation changes that.

```
fn make_greeting(name: &str) -> &str {
    let s = format!("hello, {name}");
    &s
}
```

```
error[E0515]: cannot return reference to local variable `s`
 --> d.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     &s
  |     ^^ returns a reference to data owned by the current function
```

The fix is to return an owned value. When some results are fixed text and others are built at run time, `Cow<'static, str>` (08) carries either: `Cow::Borrowed("fixed")` costs nothing, `Cow::Owned(format!(..))` allocates only when needed. The type also tells the caller "sometimes owned".

`'static` also appears as a bound: `T: 'static` means "`T` holds no borrow shorter than the whole program". Every owned type satisfies it (`String`, `Vec<i32>`), and so does `&'static str`. It does not mean the value lives forever: a `String` passed to such a function is still dropped normally.

```
fn store<T: Debug + 'static>(item: T) -> Box<dyn Debug> { Box::new(item) }
fn store_borrowed<'a, T: Debug + 'a>(item: T) -> Box<dyn Debug + 'a> { Box::new(item) }
```

You met the second use in 12: `Box<dyn Trait>` in a signature means `Box<dyn Trait + 'static>`. Write `+ 'a` to box something that borrows. Passing `&local` to `store` fails, and the note points at the bound:

```
error[E0597]: `local` does not live long enough
   |               argument requires that `local` is borrowed for `'static`
note: requirement that the value outlives `'static` introduced here
   |
26 | fn store<T: Debug + 'static>(item: T) -> Box<dyn Debug> {
   |                     ^^^^^^^
```

[entity 942 · elision-flow.png · diagram]
Diagram: a flowchart of the lifetime elision rules.

1. Start: "Rule 1: each reference input gets its own lifetime."
2. Decision: "exactly one input lifetime?" Yes leads to "Rule 2: outputs get that lifetime". No leads to the next decision.
3. Decision: "an input is &self or &mut self?" Yes leads to "Rule 3: outputs get self's lifetime". No leads to a red box "error[E0106] missing lifetime specifier: write it yourself".

Footnotes: if the output has no reference, only rule 1 applies and there is nothing to infer. A rule that decides can still disagree with the body, which gives "lifetime may not live long enough".

// Exercise 1: say which input the result borrows from (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_tie.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

fn after<'a>(text: &'a str, marker: &str) -> &'a str {
    match text.find(marker) {
        Some(i) => &text[i + marker.len()..],
        None => "",
    }
}

fn first_with<'a>(items: &'a [String], needle: &str) -> Option<&'a str> {
    for s in items {
        if s.contains(needle) {
            return Some(s.as_str());
        }
    }
    None
}

fn shorter<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if b.len() < a.len() { b } else { a }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn after_finds_the_rest() {
        assert_eq!(after("key=value", "="), "value");
        assert_eq!(after("a::b::c", "::"), "b::c");
        assert_eq!(after("no marker", "#"), "");
        assert_eq!(after("ends=", "="), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn result_outlives_the_marker() {
        let text = String::from("name: Ada");
        let rest;
        {
            let marker = String::from(": ");
            rest = after(&text, &marker);
        } // marker is dropped here; rest borrows only from text
        assert_eq!(rest, "Ada");
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_with_outlives_the_needle() {
        let items = vec![String::from("red apple"), String::from("green pear")];
        let found;
        {
            let needle = String::from("pear");
            found = first_with(&items, &needle);
        }
        assert_eq!(found, Some("green pear"));
        assert_eq!(first_with(&items, "plum"), None);
        assert_eq!(first_with(&[], "x"), None);
    }

    #[test]
    fn shorter_picks_either_input() {
        assert_eq!(shorter("abc", "de"), "de");
        assert_eq!(shorter("ab", "cde"), "ab");
        assert_eq!(shorter("ab", "cd"), "ab");
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a record that borrows its line (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_record.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

struct Record<'a> {
    line: &'a str,
}

impl<'a> Record<'a> {
    fn field(&self, i: usize) -> Option<&'a str> {
        // self.line is a &'a str (Copy), so the slices borrow the line, not self.
        self.line.split(',').nth(i).map(|f| f.trim())
    }

    fn fields(&self) -> Vec<&'a str> {
        self.line.split(',').map(|f| f.trim()).collect()
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &'a str {
        self.field(0).unwrap_or("")
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn fields_are_trimmed() {
        let r = Record { line: "ada, 36 ,london" };
        assert_eq!(r.field(0), Some("ada"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(1), Some("36"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(2), Some("london"));
        assert_eq!(r.field(3), None);
        assert_eq!(r.fields(), ["ada", "36", "london"]);
    }

    #[test]
    fn name_of_empty_line() {
        assert_eq!(Record { line: "" }.name(), "");
        assert_eq!(Record { line: "solo" }.name(), "solo");
    }

    #[test]
    fn fields_outlive_the_record() {
        let line = String::from("grace, 45, nyc");
        let (name, all);
        {
            let r = Record { line: &line };
            name = r.name();
            all = r.fields();
        } // r is dropped here; name and all borrow from `line`
        assert_eq!(name, "grace");
        assert_eq!(all.len(), 3);
    }
}

// Exercise 3: boxes that own, and boxes that borrow (reference solution)
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_boxes.rs && ./main --test-threads=4

fn greeter(name: &str) -> Box<dyn Fn() -> String> {
    let name = name.to_string(); // owned copy: the box is 'static
    Box::new(move || format!("hello, {name}"))
}

fn checker<'a>(allowed: &'a [&'a str]) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> bool + 'a> {
    Box::new(move |w| allowed.contains(&w)) // moves the reference in; borrows the slice
}

fn counter(words: Vec<String>) -> Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> usize> {
    Box::new(move |w| words.iter().filter(|x| x.as_str() == w).count()) // the Vec is moved in
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn greeter_owns_its_name() {
        let g = {
            let temp = String::from("Ada");
            greeter(&temp)
        }; // temp is gone; the greeter must still work
        assert_eq!(g(), "hello, Ada");
        assert_eq!(g(), "hello, Ada");
    }

    #[test]
    fn checker_borrows_the_list() {
        let words = ["red", "green"];
        let ok = checker(&words);
        assert!(ok("red"));
        assert!(!ok("blue"));
        assert!(!checker(&[])("red"));
    }

    #[test]
    fn counter_owns_its_words() {
        let count = {
            let words = vec![String::from("a"), String::from("b"), String::from("a")];
            counter(words)
        }; // the Vec was moved into the box
        assert_eq!(count("a"), 2);
        assert_eq!(count("b"), 1);
        assert_eq!(count("z"), 0);
    }
}

## 1. Defining and creating structs

A struct groups related values under one name, and gives each value a field name. Where a tuple says "an `(String, String, bool, u64)`", a struct says what each part means.

```
struct Profile {
    name: String,
    email: String,
    active: bool,
    visits: u64,
}
```

The definition is a template. To make a value, write the struct name and a value for every field, in any order. Read a field with a dot.

```
let mut first = Profile {
    email: String::from("a@example.com"),
    name: String::from("a"),
    active: true,
    visits: 0,
};
first.visits += 1;
println!("{} has {} visits", first.name, first.visits);
```

Mutability belongs to the binding, not to fields. To change any field, the whole value must be `let mut`. There is no way to mark one field `mut`.

A struct owns its fields. When the struct goes out of scope, every field is dropped with it. Fields of type `String` or `Vec` follow the move rules you saw in 02.

This lesson adapts The Rust Programming Language, chapter 5 and Rust by Example (MIT/Apache-2.0). Open `define.rs` and `methods.rs` alongside it.

## 2. Shorthand and update syntax

Field init shorthand. When a variable has the same name as the field, write the name once:

```
fn build_profile(name: String, email: String) -> Profile {
    Profile { name, email, active: true, visits: 0 } // name: name, email: email
}
```

Struct update syntax. `..other` at the end of a struct literal means "every field I did not write out comes from `other`".

```
let second = Profile {
    email: String::from("b@example.com"),
    ..first
};
```

Update syntax is not a special copy. It is a set of ordinary field assignments, so each field follows its own rule:

FieldWhere it comes fromWhat happens to `first`'s field

`email`written outuntouched, still usable

`name` (`String`)`..first`moved into `second`; `first.name` is unusable

`active` (`bool`)`..first`copied; still usable

`visits` (`u64`)`..first`copied; still usable

After this, `first.visits` and `first.email` still work, but `first.name` and `first` as a whole do not:

```
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `first.name`
```

Ask per field: did I write it out? If not, is its type Copy? Copy fields are copied, everything else moves. To keep a non-Copy field, write it out (for example `tags: base.tags.clone()`).

## 3. Tuple structs and unit structs

A tuple struct has a name but no field names. Fields are read by position: `.0`, `.1`.

```
struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8);
struct Meters(f64);

let red = Rgb(255, 0, 0);
let run = Meters(5.5);
println!("{} {}", red.0, run.0);
```

Two tuple structs with the same field types are still different types. A function that takes `Meters` will not accept a plain `f64` or some other one-field struct. A one-field tuple struct used this way is called a newtype: it gives a plain number its own meaning, so the compiler stops you mixing metres with seconds.

A unit struct has no fields at all: `struct Marker;`. It is useful later, when a type matters but carries no data (for example, to implement a trait on it in 09).

## 4. Methods

A method is a function defined inside an `impl` block whose first parameter is `self` in some form. It is called with dot syntax on a value.

```
struct Rectangle { width: u32, height: u32 }

impl Rectangle {
    fn area(&self) -> u32 {
        self.width * self.height
    }
    fn scale(&mut self, factor: u32) {
        self.width *= factor;
        self.height *= factor;
    }
}
```

`&self` is short for `self: &Self`, and `Self` is the type the `impl` is for. A method call is plain function call syntax in disguise:

You writeThe compiler calls

`big.area()``Rectangle::area(&big)`

`big.scale(2)``Rectangle::scale(&mut big, 2)`

`big.into_pair()``Rectangle::into_pair(big)`

The compiler adds the `&` or `&mut` for you (automatic referencing). Because `big.scale(2)` really takes `&mut big`, `big` must be declared `let mut`, exactly as if you had written the borrow yourself.

## 5. Associated functions

A function in an `impl` block without `self` is an associated function. It belongs to the type, not to a value, so it is called with `::`.

```
impl Rectangle {
    fn square(size: u32) -> Self {
        Self { width: size, height: size }
    }
}

let small = Rectangle::square(3);
```

- Constructors are usually associated functions. `new` is a convention, not a keyword: name them for what they build (`square`, `empty`, `with_limit`).

- Inside an `impl`, `Self` names the type, so `Self { .. }` and `Rectangle { .. }` mean the same.

- A type can have many `impl` blocks; they all add to the same type.

You will often build text inside methods. `format!` takes the same arguments as `println!` but returns the text as a `String` instead of printing it:

```
fn label(&self) -> String {
    format!("{}x{}", self.width, self.height)
}
```

## 6. Receivers and borrows

The first parameter of a method is its receiver. It is the same choice you make for any function parameter in 02 and 03: borrow, borrow mutably, or take ownership.

ReceiverThe method getsThe caller needsValue usable afterwards?Typical use

`&self`a read-only viewany bindingyes`area`, `len`, `is_empty`

`&mut self`exclusive write accessa `let mut` binding and no other live borrowyes`scale`, `push`, `record`

`self`ownershipany bindingno, it moved (unless the type is Copy)`into_pair`, `build`, `close`

Pick the weakest receiver that works. Reading needs `&self`. Changing needs `&mut self`. Only take `self` when the method uses the value up or turns it into something else.

A method that takes `self` may also change it before handing it back. Write `mut self`: the method owns the value, so it may mutate it.

```
fn doubled(mut self) -> Self {
    self.width *= 2;
    self   // ownership goes back to the caller
}

let r = Rectangle::square(2).doubled(); // calls chain, each one takes and returns
```

### Fields versus methods

Inside one function, the borrow checker tracks fields separately. Holding `&mut s.items` while reading `s.limit` is fine: they are different places in memory.

A method call is different. The checker looks only at the method's signature, never its body. A method `fn items_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Vec<i32>` borrows all of `self` mutably, for as long as the returned reference is in use. While that reference lives, calling even a `&self` method on the same value is a conflict, because the signature does not say which field it touches.

Checking only signatures is deliberate: a library can change a method body without breaking any caller. The price is that the checker cannot see that two methods use different fields.

## 7. Derive: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default

A new struct can do almost nothing: you cannot print it with `{:?}`, compare it with `==` or `clone()` it. The `#[derive(...)]` attribute asks the compiler to write the code for common traits (shared behaviour) for you.

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Default)]
struct Point {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
```

DeriveGives youDerived behaviour

`Debug``{:?}`, `{:#?}` (pretty), `dbg!`prints the type name and each field

`Clone``.clone()`clones each field

`Copy`implicit copies instead of movesbitwise copy; needs `Clone` too, and every field must be Copy

`PartialEq``==`, `!=`equal when every field is equal

`PartialOrd``<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`compares fields in declaration order: the first field decides unless equal, then the next; needs `PartialEq`

`Default``T::default()`each field's own default: 0, `false`, empty `String`/`Vec`

So for `Point`, `Point { x: 1, y: 9 } < Point { x: 2, y: 0 }` is `true`: `x` is compared first and decides. Field order is part of the meaning of a derived ordering.

`dbg!(expr)` prints the file, line, expression and value to stderr, then returns the value, so you can wrap it around any expression.

A derive works only if every field's type has that trait. Deriving `Default` on a struct with a field of a type that has no `Default` fails with `error[E0277]: the trait bound ... is not satisfied`. Same for `Copy` with a `String` field.

### Why nothing is derived automatically

- The derived meaning can be wrong. Field-by-field `==` is wrong if a field is a cache or a counter that should not affect equality. Declaration-order `<` is wrong if "smaller" means smaller area.

- It can leak. `Debug` prints every field, including a password or token.

- It changes cost and rules. `Clone` makes deep copies easy to write; `Copy` changes moves into copies everywhere.

- It is a promise. Once callers rely on `==` or `Copy`, removing it breaks them.

## 8. Writing Default by hand

When zero values are wrong defaults (a retry count of 0, a timeout of 0 seconds), write `Default` yourself instead of deriving it:

```
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct Settings {
    name: String,
    retries: u32,
    verbose: bool,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Settings { name: String::from("main"), retries: 3, verbose: false }
    }
}

let s = Settings { verbose: true, ..Settings::default() };
```

Traits in general are covered in 09. This one shape, `impl Default for T { fn default() -> Self { ... } }`, is all you need now. It combines well with update syntax: `..Settings::default()` fills every field you did not write.

If a type has both `new()` and `Default`, make them agree. A `default()` that quietly gives different values from `new()` surprises every caller.

## 9. Check yourself

Answer these out loud or ask the Tutor about them. Then try the exercises.

- Why must I write `let mut` to call a `&mut self` method?

- When should a method take `self` by value?

- After `let b = Config { name: x, ..a };`, which fields of `a` can I still use?

- Why doesn't Rust derive `Debug` and `PartialEq` for every struct?

- Two fields of a struct, `width` then `height`, with derived `PartialOrd`: which field decides `a < b`?

Exercises: `ex1_steps.rs` (methods and receivers), `ex2_wallet.rs` (a type that guards its own rules), `ex3_version.rs` (derive order and a hand-written `Default`).

// Exercise 1: methods, associated functions and receivers.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex1_steps.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A StepLog keeps a daily step goal and the steps recorded so far.
// Reference solution.
// The receivers below are placeholders: if a method has to change the log,
// change its receiver too.

struct StepLog {
    goal: u32,
    days: u32,
    total: u32,
}

impl StepLog {
    /// A new log with a daily goal and nothing recorded.
    fn new(goal: u32) -> Self {
        StepLog { goal, days: 0, total: 0 }
    }

    /// Record one day's steps.
    fn record(&mut self, steps: u32) {
        self.days += 1;
        self.total += steps;
    }

    /// Average steps per recorded day. 0 when nothing is recorded yet.
    fn average(&self) -> u32 {
        if self.days == 0 {
            return 0;
        }
        self.total / self.days
    }

    /// True when the average reaches the goal.
    fn on_track(&self) -> bool {
        self.average() >= self.goal
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn new_log_is_empty() {
        let log = StepLog::new(8000);
        assert_eq!((log.goal, log.days, log.total), (8000, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn average_of_an_empty_log_is_zero() {
        assert_eq!(StepLog::new(10).average(), 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn records_and_averages() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(5000);
        log.record(4000);
        log.record(7000);
        assert_eq!(log.days, 2);
        assert_eq!(log.average(), 5500);
        assert!(log.on_track());
    }

    #[test]
    fn below_goal_is_not_on_track() {
        let mut log = StepLog::new(9000);
        log.record(3000);
        assert!(!log.on_track());
    }
}

// Exercise 2: a type that keeps its own rules.
// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex2_wallet.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Wallet holds money in cents (whole numbers, so no rounding errors).
// Reference solution.
// Tip: format!("{:02}", 5) gives "05".

struct Wallet {
    owner: String,
    cents: u64,
}

impl Wallet {
    /// A new, empty wallet.
    fn open(owner: &str) -> Wallet {
        Wallet { owner: owner.to_string(), cents: 0 }
    }

    /// Add money.
    fn deposit(&mut self, cents: u64) {
        self.cents += cents;
    }

    /// Take money out. If there is not enough, return false and change nothing.
    fn spend(&mut self, cents: u64) -> bool {
        if cents > self.cents {
            return false;
        }
        self.cents -= cents;
        true
    }

    /// The balance as text, for example "ada: $12.05".
    fn balance_text(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}: ${}.{:02}", self.owner, self.cents / 100, self.cents % 100)
    }

    /// Close the wallet: give back the owner's name and the remaining cents.
    fn close(self) -> (String, u64) {
        (self.owner, self.cents)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn opens_empty() {
        let w = Wallet::open("ada");
        assert_eq!(w.owner, "ada");
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn deposit_and_spend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1500);
        assert!(w.spend(295));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 1205);
    }

    #[test]
    fn refuses_to_overspend() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(100);
        assert!(!w.spend(101));
        assert_eq!(w.cents, 100);
    }

    #[test]
    fn formats_dollars_and_cents() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("ada");
        w.deposit(1205);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $12.05");
        w.spend(1200);
        assert_eq!(w.balance_text(), "ada: $0.05");
    }

    #[test]
    fn close_gives_everything_back() {
        let mut w = Wallet::open("bo");
        w.deposit(42);
        let (owner, left) = w.close();
        assert_eq!(owner, "bo");
        assert_eq!(left, 42);
    }
}

// Run: rustc --edition 2024 --test -o main ex3_version.rs && ./main --test-threads=4
//
// A Version like 1.4.2 must compare the usual way: major first, then minor,

//

// TODO 3: write bump_minor: 1.4.2 becomes 1.5.0.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]
struct Version {
    major: u32, // derived PartialOrd compares fields in declaration order
    minor: u32,
    patch: u32,
}

impl Version {
    fn new(major: u32, minor: u32, patch: u32) -> Version {
        Version { major, minor, patch }
    }

    fn bump_minor(self) -> Version {
        Version { minor: self.minor + 1, patch: 0, ..self }
    }
}

impl Default for Version {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Version::new(0, 1, 0)
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn major_decides_first() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 2) < Version::new(2, 0, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn minor_decides_before_patch() {
        assert!(Version::new(1, 4, 9) < Version::new(1, 10, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn default_is_0_1_0() {
        assert_eq!(Version::default(), Version::new(0, 1, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn bump_minor_resets_patch() {
        assert_eq!(Version::new(1, 4, 2).bump_minor(), Version::new(1, 5, 0));
    }

    #[test]
    fn versions_are_copy() {
        let v = Version::new(1, 0, 0);
        let w = v;
        assert_eq!(v, w);
        assert_eq!(format!("{w:?}").contains("major: 1"), true);
    }
}

What I’d build instead is a layered control plane:
1. Separate instructions from workspace content in the harness itself. Anything under `vendor/` should be classified as data unless it comes from a trusted instruction channel, and the agent should not be able to elevate that text into policy.
2. Move `push_branch`, `open_pr`, and especially any main-branch write behind a server-side policy gate. The token in the environment should not be enough by itself to push to `main`; the server or bot should enforce branch rules and require an approval state that lives outside the repo.

## 1. Vec: a growable array on the heap

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 8.1-8.3, and Rust by Example (Vectors, Strings, HashMap), MIT/Apache-2.0.

A `Vec<T>` stores any number of values of one type `T`, one after another in memory. You use it whenever the count is only known at run time: lines read from a file, scores entered by a user, results of a search.

```
let mut items: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();   // empty, type written out
items.push(10);
items.push(20);
let primes = vec![2, 3, 5, 7];            // vec! macro: type inferred as Vec<i32>
```

Because the number of elements can change while the program runs, the elements cannot live inside the `Vec` value itself (every value on the stack must have a size known at compile time). Instead the `Vec` is a small fixed-size handle of three parts:

PartMeaning

pointerwhere the elements start, in a block on the heap

length (`len()`)how many elements exist right now

capacity (`capacity()`)how many fit in the current block before a bigger one is needed

vec-layout.png: the stack handle, the heap block, what happens on push past capacity, and how remove shifts elements.

A `Vec` holds one element type. When you need different kinds of values in one list, wrap them in an enum (sub-module 05): `vec![Cell::Int(3), Cell::Text(String::from("ok"))]` is one type, `Vec<Cell>`. `vectors.rs` shows this.

## 2. Reading: `[]` or `get`

There are two ways to read element `i`, and they differ only in what happens when `i` is out of range.

```
let items = vec![10, 20, 30];
let a: i32 = items[1];                 // 20
let b: Option<&i32> = items.get(1);    // Some(&20)
let c = items.get(9);                  // None
let d = items[9];                      // panics at run time
```

```
thread 'main' panicked at main.rs:5:14:
index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 9
```

UseWhen

`v[i]`A bad index would be a bug in your program. Crashing loudly is better than carrying on with wrong data.

`v.get(i)`A missing element is a normal case (user input, an optional position). You handle `None` with `match` or `if let`.

`v[i]` on a `Vec<i32>` copies the `i32` out, because `i32` is `Copy`. On a `Vec<String>`, `let s = v[0];` is a compile error (you cannot move out of an index). Write `&v[0]` to borrow it or `v[0].clone()` to copy it.

## 3. Growing and shrinking

CallWhat it doesCost and catch

`push(x)`adds at the endfast; may move the whole buffer (section 4)

`extend([a, b])`adds many at the endsame as several pushes

`insert(i, x)`puts `x` at index `i`shifts every later element one slot right

`pop()`removes the last, returns `Option<T>`fast

`remove(i)`removes index `i`, returns itshifts every later element one slot left; panics if `i >= len`

`swap_remove(i)`removes index `i`, moves the last element into the holefast, but changes the order

`drain(a..b)`removes a range and hands the removed items outshifts the tail left once

`retain(...)`keeps only the items that pass a testtakes a closure; closures are taught in 10

The shifting matters for two reasons. On a long list, `insert(0, x)` and `remove(0)` touch every element. And after a `remove(i)`, every element that was after `i` now has an index one smaller. Code that keeps an index and moves on must take that into account.

```
let mut v = vec![5, 11, 21, 31, 40, 50];
let gone = v.remove(1);         // gone = 11; v = [5, 21, 31, 40, 50]
let swapped = v.swap_remove(0); // swapped = 5; 50 fills slot 0: [50, 21, 31, 40]
```

Before you run `vectors.rs`, write down the line starting `removed` and the line starting `drained`. Predicting, then checking, is the fastest way to make these rules stick.

## 4. Why you cannot hold `&v[0]` across a `push`

When `push` finds the block full (length equals capacity), it allocates a bigger block, copies the elements across, and frees the old block. Capacity grows in jumps (often doubling), so most pushes are cheap; the exact numbers are a library detail and can change between Rust versions.

Now picture a reference to an element taken before that push. It still holds the address in the old block, which has just been freed. Using it would read freed memory. Rust stops this at compile time with the borrowing rules from 03: `push` takes `&mut self`, and you cannot have a `&mut` borrow of `items` while a shared borrow into it is still going to be used.

```
let mut items = vec![1, 2, 3];
let last = &items[items.len() - 1]; // shared borrow of an element
items.push(4);                      // needs &mut items
println!("last was {last}");        // the shared borrow is still used here
```

```
error[E0502]: cannot borrow `items` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
```

The compiler does not know whether this particular push will reallocate. It does not need to: the rule is "no reading through an old borrow after a change", and that rule is always safe. Fix it by finishing with the reference first (move the `println!` up), or by copying the value out (`let last = items[items.len() - 1];` copies an `i32`). Try both in `borrow_push.rs`.

## 5. Looping over a Vec

LoopEach `x` isAfterwards

`for x in &v``&T` (read)`v` unchanged and usable

`for x in &mut v``&mut T`: write with `*x += 1``v` changed in place

`for x in v``T` (owned)`v` is moved: using it is E0382

`for i in 0..v.len()`an indexread with `v[i]`

```
let mut scores = vec![1, 2, 3];
for x in &mut scores {
    *x *= 10;              // * reaches through the &mut to the element
}
let words = vec![String::from("a"), String::from("b")];
for w in words {           // each String moves out of the Vec into w
    println!("{w}");
}
// println!("{words:?}");  // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `words`
```

In `for i in 0..v.len()`, the range `0..v.len()` is built once, before the first pass. If the loop body adds or removes elements, the range does not notice. The borrow checker cannot help here either: each `v[i]` borrow ends at once, so it is legal code, but the logic can still be wrong.

## 6. String is UTF-8 bytes

`String` is an owned, growable buffer, much like a `Vec<u8>`, with one promise on top: the bytes are always valid UTF-8. `&str` borrows UTF-8 text, from a `String` or from a literal in your program.

UTF-8 uses 1 byte for ASCII letters and 2 to 4 bytes for other characters. So the number of bytes and the number of characters can differ:

Text`len()` (bytes)`chars().count()`

`"cafe"`44

`"café"`54

`"日本"`62

utf8-bytes.png: "café" as chars, as bytes, and the byte offsets between them.

Three things count in bytes, and you have to keep that in mind:

- `len()` is the byte length.

- `find(pattern)` returns `Option<usize>`, the byte offset where the match starts.

- Slices `&s[a..b]` take byte ranges.

To walk characters, use `s.chars()` (each `char`), `s.bytes()` (each byte) or `s.char_indices()` (each `char` with the byte offset where it starts).

```
for (i, c) in "aé!".char_indices() {
    print!("{c}@{i} ");    // a@0 é@1 !@3
}
```

## 7. No `s[0]`, careful slices, case changes

`s[0]` does not compile:

```
error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}`
```

What would "the first character" even mean? The first byte may be only half of a character. Rust refuses to guess, and it refuses to hide a slow scan behind something that looks like a fast index. Say what you mean: `s.chars().next()` for the first char, `s.as_bytes()[0]` for the first byte.

A byte range is allowed, because the compiler cannot know the text in advance. It is checked when the code runs: if either end falls inside a character, the program panics.

```
let s = String::from("café");
let a = &s[0..3];        // "caf"
let b = s.get(0..4);     // None: 4 is inside 'é'
let c = &s[0..4];        // panics
```

```
end byte index 4 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 3..5 of string)
```

`s.get(range)` returns `Option<&str>` instead of panicking. To slice "the first n characters", find the byte offset of character n with `char_indices`, or build a new `String` by pushing chars.

Case changes can change the length. `"straße".to_uppercase()` is `"STRASSE"`: one `ß` became two letters. A few characters also change their byte length when lowercased. `char::to_uppercase()` therefore yields one or more chars. The ASCII-only versions (`to_ascii_lowercase`, `to_ascii_uppercase`) change only A-Z and a-z and never change the length.

A byte offset is only meaningful in the string it came from. If you compute an offset in one string (say, a lowercased copy) and use it to slice another, any length difference between them shifts every later offset.

## 8. Building strings

```
let mut s = String::from("caf");
s.push('é');               // one char
s.push_str(" au lait");    // a &str
let a = String::from("tic");
let b = String::from("tac");
let joined = format!("{a}-{b}-toe"); // borrows everything, a and b still usable
let moved = a + "-" + &b;           // takes `a` by value and reuses its buffer
```

`+` calls `fn add(self, s: &str) -> String`: the left side is moved in (and its buffer reused), the right side is only borrowed. After `a + &b`, `a` is gone and `b` is fine. `format!` is easier to read when you join more than two pieces.

Splitting text into words: `for w in text.split_whitespace()` gives each run of non-space characters as a `&str` borrowed from `text`, skipping any number of spaces.

You will meet `Cow<str>` ("clone on write") in library signatures. It holds either a borrowed `&str` or an owned `String`, so a function can return the input unchanged without copying, and allocate only when it must change something. You do not need to write it yet.

## 9. HashMap and the entry API

`HashMap<K, V>` (in `std::collections`) maps keys to values. Looking up a key is fast on average, whatever the size of the map.

```
use std::collections::HashMap;
let mut scores: HashMap<String, u32> = HashMap::new();
scores.insert(String::from("red"), 10);
let old = scores.insert(String::from("red"), 12); // replaces: old == Some(10)
let r: Option<&u32> = scores.get("red");          // Some(&12)
if let Some(v) = scores.get_mut("red") {          // Option<&mut u32>
    *v += 1;
}
```

CallReturnsNotes

`insert(k, v)``Option<V>`, the old valuereplaces an existing value; never merges or appends

`get(&k)` / `get_mut(&k)``Option<&V>` / `Option<&mut V>``map[&k]` panics when the key is missing

`entry(k)`an `Entry`: occupied or vacantone lookup for "find or create"

`.or_insert(v)``&mut V`inserts `v` only if the key was missing

`.or_default()``&mut V`inserts `V::default()` (0, empty Vec, empty String) if missing

`remove(&k)``Option<V>`

The entry API is how you update a value that may not exist yet. Because `or_insert`/`or_default` return a `&mut V` pointing at the value stored in the map, you change it in place:

```
let mut counts: HashMap<&str, u32> = HashMap::new();
for w in ["a", "b", "a"] {
    *counts.entry(w).or_insert(0) += 1;   // counts: a -> 2, b -> 1
}
let mut groups: HashMap<char, Vec<&str>> = HashMap::new();
for word in ["ant", "bee", "asp"] {
    let first = word.chars().next().unwrap();
    groups.entry(first).or_default().push(word); // or_default inserts Vec::new()
}
```

### Ownership

Owned keys and values are moved into the map: after `scores.insert(key, 1)`, a `String` `key` is gone. Lookups take a borrowed form: `scores.get("red")` works on a `HashMap<String, _>`.

### References into a map

A map stores its entries in a table on the heap. When an insert needs more room, the map moves every entry to a bigger table, exactly like a `Vec` growing. So any `&V` or `&mut V` you got from `get`, `get_mut` or `entry` borrows the whole map, not just one key, and must be finished before the next insert or entry call.

### Order

Iterating a `HashMap` (`for (k, v) in &map`, `map.keys()`) visits entries in an order that is not defined and changes from run to run. When output order matters, collect the keys into a `Vec` and `sort()` it, or use `BTreeMap`, which has the same API and keeps keys sorted.

## 10. Practice

Three exercises are open as tabs. Each has `todo!()` stubs and visible tests; Run builds the tests and runs them. Make all tests pass.

- `ex1_vec_moves.rs`: `get`, `remove`, `push` and index loops.

- `ex2_text.rs`: chars vs bytes, upper-casing that can grow.

- `ex3_word_counts.rs`: the entry API and order-independent answers.

## 11. Check yourself

- Why does the compiler stop me holding `&v[0]` while I `push`?

- Why is `"é".len()` equal to 2, and what does `find` count in?

- What does `or_default()` give back, and why is that useful?

- After `v.remove(1)`, where is the element that was at index 2?

pub fn last_two(items: &[i32]) -> Option<(i32, i32)> {
    let n = items.len();
    if n < 2 {
        return None;
    }
    Some((items[n - 2], items[n - 1]))
}

pub fn move_first_to_end(items: &mut Vec<String>) {
    if items.is_empty() {
        return;
    }
    let first = items.remove(0); // shifts every later element left by one
    items.push(first);
}

pub fn with_separator(items: &[i32], sep: i32) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    for i in 0..items.len() {
        if i > 0 {
            out.push(sep);
        }
        out.push(items[i]);
    }
    out
}

pub fn initials(name: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    for word in name.split_whitespace() {
        if let Some(c) = word.chars().next() {
            for u in c.to_uppercase() {
                out.push(u);
            }
        }
    }
    out
}

pub fn capitalize(word: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    let mut first = true;
    for c in word.chars() {
        if first {
            for u in c.to_uppercase() {
                out.push(u);
            }
            first = false;
        } else {
            out.push(c);
        }
    }
    out
}

pub fn count_non_ascii(s: &str) -> usize {
    let mut n = 0;
    for c in s.chars() {
        if !c.is_ascii() {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    n
}

use std::collections::HashMap;

pub fn word_counts(text: &str) -> HashMap<String, usize> {
    let mut counts = HashMap::new();
    for w in text.split_whitespace() {
        *counts.entry(w.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
    counts
}

pub fn most_common(counts: &HashMap<String, usize>) -> Option<(String, usize)> {
    let mut best: Option<(String, usize)> = None;
    for (word, &n) in counts {
        let better = match &best {
            None => true,
            Some((bw, bn)) => n > *bn || (n == *bn && word < bw),
        };
        if better {
            best = Some((word.clone(), n));
        }
    }
    best
}

## 8. Building strings
```
let mut s = String::from("caf");
s.push('é');               // one char
s.push_str(" au lait");    // a &str
let a = String::from("tic");
let b = String::from("tac");
let joined = format!("{a}-{b}-toe"); // borrows everything, a and b still usable
let moved = a + "-" + &b;           // takes `a` by value and reuses its buffer
```

`+` calls `fn add(self, s: &str) -> String`: the left side is moved in (and its buffer reused), the right side is only borrowed. After `a + &b`, `a` is gone and `b` is fine. `format!` is easier to read when you join more than two pieces.

## 4. Why you cannot hold `&v[0]` across a `push`
When `push` finds the block full (length equals capacity), it allocates a bigger block, copies the elements across, and frees the old block. Capacity grows in jumps (often doubling), so most pushes are cheap; the exact numbers are a library detail and can change between Rust versions.

Now picture a reference to an element taken before that push. It still holds the address in the old block, which has just been freed. Using it would read freed memory. Rust stops this at compile time with the borrowing rules from 03: `push` takes `&mut self`, and you cannot have a `&mut` borrow of `items` while a shared borrow into it is still going to be used.

## 6. String is UTF-8 bytes
`String` is an owned, growable buffer, much like a `Vec<u8>`, with one promise on top: the bytes are always valid UTF-8. `&str` borrows UTF-8 text, from a `String` or from a literal in your program.

## 1. Why generics

Adapted from The Rust Programming Language, ch 10.1-10.2, and Rust by Example (Generics, Bounds, Traits, impl Trait), MIT/Apache-2.0.

Suppose you wrote a function that finds the largest `i32` in a slice, then needed the same for `char`. The two bodies would be identical; only the type differs. A type parameter lets you write the body once:

```
fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> &T {
    let mut largest = &list[0];
    for item in list {
        if item > largest {
            largest = item;
        }
    }
    largest
}
```

Read `<T: PartialOrd>` as "for any type `T` that can be compared with `<` and `>`". The caller picks `T` at each call (`largest(&[34, 50])` uses `i32`, `largest(&['y', 'm'])` uses `char`). The body must compile for every `T` the bounds allow, not just the ones you happen to call it with. `largest.rs` runs this on numbers, chars and Strings.

## 2. Bounds unlock operations

Inside a generic body, the compiler knows nothing about `T` except what the bounds promise. Remove `: PartialOrd` from `largest` and the comparison is refused, even though every type you call it with could be compared:

```
error[E0369]: binary operation `>` cannot be applied to type `&T`
 --> largest.rs:4:17
  |
4 |         if item > largest {
  |            ---- ^ ------- &T
  |            |
  |            &T
help: consider restricting type parameter `T` with trait `PartialOrd`
```

Each operation you want needs its trait:

You want to writeBoundNotes

`a > b`, `a <= b``T: PartialOrd`

`a == b``T: PartialEq`

`a - b` giving a `T``T: Sub<Output = T>`from `std::ops`; same idea for `Add`, `Mul`

`println!("{x}")``T: Display``{x:?}` needs `Debug`

`let x = slice[0];` (an owned copy)`T: Copy`or `T: Clone` and write `slice[0].clone()`

`T::default()``T: Default`0 for numbers, empty for String and Vec

Two of these need a closer look.

The `Output` of an operator trait. `Sub` is declared as `trait Sub<Rhs = Self> { type Output; fn sub(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self::Output; }`. The result type is a separate choice of each implementor, so `T: Sub` alone says "`a - b` is allowed and produces something". If you need the result to be a `T` again (to store it back in a `T` variable or return it), say so: `T: Sub<Output = T>`.

Copying out of a borrowed slice. A `&[T]` lets you look at elements, not take them. `let x = list[0];` would move the element out of a slice you only borrowed, so it is allowed only when `T: Copy` (then it is a copy, not a move). With `T: Clone` you can write `list[0].clone()`; returning `&T` (as `largest` does) needs neither.

```
use std::ops::Mul;

// x * x for any type that can be multiplied by itself, giving the same type back.
fn square<T>(x: T) -> T
where
    T: Mul<Output = T> + Copy,   // Copy: x is used twice, so it must not move
{
    x * x
}
// square(3) == 9, square(1.5) == 2.25
```

Without `Copy`, the first use of `x` in `x * x` moves it (operators take their operands by value), and the second use is E0382. Without `Output = T`, the result is "some type" and cannot be returned as a `T`.

A `where` clause says the same thing as bounds in the angle brackets; it is just easier to read when there are several.

## 3. Generic types and conditional methods

Structs and enums take type parameters too. You already use two: `Option<T>` and `Vec<T>`.

```
struct Point<T> {
    x: T,
    y: T,          // both fields are the same T
}

impl<T> Point<T> {              // for every Point<T>
    fn x(&self) -> &T { &self.x }
}

impl Point<f64> {               // only for Point<f64>
    fn distance_from_origin(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.x.powi(2) + self.y.powi(2)).sqrt()
    }
}
```

The header of each `impl` block decides which types get its methods.

HeaderMethods exist for

`impl<T> Point<T>`every `Point`

`impl Point<f64>`only `Point<f64>`

`impl<T: Display + PartialOrd> Duo<T>`only when `T` meets the bound

Calling a method on a type its impl does not cover is a compile error (E0599), and when the method exists but a bound is unmet, the message says "its trait bounds were not satisfied". A type cannot get the same method name from two impl blocks that overlap (E0592). A method can also have its own type parameters, separate from the struct's: `fn with_y<U>(&self, y: U) -> (T, U)` in `point.rs`.

## 4. What generics cost: monomorphization

The compiler turns generic code into ordinary code by making one concrete copy for each type it is used with. This is called monomorphization.

monomorphization.png: one generic function, one generated copy per type.

- At run time there is no lookup and no boxing: `largest::<i32>` runs exactly like a hand-written `largest_i32`.

- The price is paid at compile time: more code to compile, and a larger binary.

- The body is type-checked once, against the bounds. That is why a missing bound is an error even if every call would work.

Sub-module 12 shows the other approach, trait objects (`dyn Trait`), which keeps one copy and decides at run time.

## 5. Traits, default methods and overrides

A trait is a named set of methods a type can promise to have. A method without a body is required; a method with a body is a default that implementors get for free and may override.

```
trait Summary {
    fn author(&self) -> String;                      // required
    fn summarize(&self) -> String {                  // default
        format!("(Read more from {}...)", self.author())
    }
}

struct Post { author: String }
impl Summary for Post {
    fn author(&self) -> String { format!("@{}", self.author) }
    // summarize: uses the default
}
```

A default method may call any other method of the trait. When it calls `self.author()`, the implementing type's own `author` runs. The same is true for other default methods: if a type overrides one default, every other default that calls it uses the override. In `traits.rs`, `Reply` overrides `summarize`, so `notify(&reply)` prints the reply's version.

A default method can only use what the trait promises about `Self`. It cannot read the implementor's fields (it does not know them), and it cannot use `{self}` unless `Self: Display` is promised. You can require more for one method only with a `where` clause on that method:

```
fn headline(&self) -> String
where
    Self: Display,           // only Display implementors can call headline
{
    format!("** {self} **")
}
```

```
error[E0277]: `Post` doesn't implement `std::fmt::Display`
```

That error appears where someone calls `post.headline()` on a type that is not `Display`; the trait itself still compiles, and every other method stays available to `Post`.

## 6. Who may implement what: the orphan rule

`impl Trait for Type` is allowed only if something in it is local (defined in your crate):

- the trait is local, or

- the type is local, or

- a local type appears as one of the trait's type parameters, as in `impl From<Celsius> for f64`.

orphan-rule.png: local and foreign traits and types, and the one red cell.

A local type wrapped in a foreign generic does not count: `Vec<Celsius>` is a `Vec`, defined in std. A blanket `impl<T> ForeignTrait for T` is never allowed either, because `T` covers types from every crate.

```
error[E0117]: only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate
 --> orphan.rs:2:1
  |
2 | impl fmt::Display for Vec<i32> { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^--------
  |                       |
  |                       `Vec` is not defined in the current crate
  = note: define and implement a trait or new type instead
```

Why the rule exists. If two libraries could both write `impl Display for Vec<i32>`, a program using both would have two answers for one question, and nothing to pick between them. The rule makes sure every (trait, type) pair has at most one possible home. It also lets std add new impls without breaking your crate.

Workarounds. Wrap the foreign type in a local newtype, `struct List(Vec<i32>);`, and implement the trait for that (a newtype costs nothing at run time). Or define a local trait and implement it for the foreign type. `orphan.rs` shows all three allowed shapes.

## 7. Blanket impls

A blanket impl implements a trait for every type that meets a bound:

```
trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}
impl<T: Debug> Describe for T {
    fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("<{self:?}>") }
}
// 5.describe(), "hi".describe(), vec![1, 2].describe() all work
```

std uses this pattern: every type that implements `Display` gets `to_string()` through `impl<T: Display> ToString for T`. The blanket covers types written later too, so you never write that impl yourself.

The cost: once a blanket impl covers a type, no other impl of the same trait may cover it. Stable Rust has no "the more specific impl wins" rule, so overlap is an error:

```
error[E0119]: conflicting implementations of trait `Label` for type `u8`
3 | impl<T: Display> Label for T { ... }
  | ---------------------------- first implementation here
4 | impl Label for u8 { ... }
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ conflicting implementation for `u8`
```

The order of the impls does not matter, and there is no way to mark one as preferred on stable Rust. (A feature called specialization exists only on nightly.)

## 8. Bounds in signatures and `impl Trait`

Three ways to say "any type that implements `Summary`":

```
fn notify(item: &impl Summary) { ... }           // short form
fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T) { ... }          // generic parameter
fn notify_both<T, U>(a: &T, b: &U)
where
    T: Summary,
    U: Summary + Display,                         // two bounds with +
{ ... }
```

With a named `T` you can force two arguments to have the same type (`fn pair<T: Summary>(a: &T, b: &T)`); `impl Summary` twice allows two different types.

### Argument position vs return position

Who picks the concrete typeHow many types

`fn f(x: impl Trait)`the caller, at each callone per call site (each gets its own monomorphized copy)

`fn f() -> impl Trait`the function bodyexactly one for the whole function; callers only see "some `Trait`"

Return-position `impl Trait` hides the type's name, but there is still exactly one type, fixed at compile time. Returning different types from different branches is an error:

```
error[E0308]: `if` and `else` have incompatible types
3 |     if flag { "yes" } else { 1 }
  |               -----          ^ expected `&str`, found integer
help: you could change the return type to be a boxed trait object
```

To return "one of several kinds" while keeping `-> impl Trait`, make the branches one type: convert them to the same type (for example both to `String`), or define an enum with one variant per kind and implement the trait for the enum. The compiler's suggestion, `Box<dyn Trait>`, is a different trade (a heap allocation and dynamic dispatch) covered in 12.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
pub struct Pair<T> {
    pub a: T,
    pub b: T,
}

impl<T> Pair<T> {
    pub fn swap(self) -> Pair<T> {
        Pair { a: self.b, b: self.a }
    }
}

impl<T: PartialOrd> Pair<T> {
    pub fn larger(&self) -> &T {
        if self.b > self.a { &self.b } else { &self.a }
    }
}

pub fn first_or<T: Clone>(items: &[T], fallback: T) -> T {
    if items.is_empty() { fallback } else { items[0].clone() }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn swap_any_type() {
        let p = Pair { a: String::from("x"), b: String::from("y") };
        assert_eq!(p.swap(), Pair { a: String::from("y"), b: String::from("x") });
        assert_eq!(Pair { a: 1, b: 2 }.swap(), Pair { a: 2, b: 1 });
    }

    #[test]
    fn larger_numbers_and_strings() {
        assert_eq!(*Pair { a: 3, b: 9 }.larger(), 9);
        assert_eq!(Pair { a: String::from("pear"), b: String::from("apple") }.larger(), "pear");
        assert_eq!(*Pair { a: 4.5, b: 4.5 }.larger(), 4.5);
    }

    #[test]
    fn first_or_fallback() {
        assert_eq!(first_or(&[7, 8], 0), 7);
        assert_eq!(first_or(&[], 0), 0);
        let words = vec![String::from("hi")];
        assert_eq!(first_or(&words, String::from("none")), "hi");
        assert_eq!(words.len(), 1); // still ours
    }
}

use std::fmt::{Debug, Display};

pub fn count_equal<T: PartialEq>(items: &[T], target: &T) -> usize {
    let mut n = 0;
    for item in items {
        if item == target {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    n
}

pub fn join_all(items: &[impl Display], sep: &str) -> String {
    let mut out = String::new();
    let mut first = true;
    for item in items {
        if !first {
            out.push_str(sep);
        }
        first = false;
        out.push_str(&item.to_string());
    }
    out
}

pub fn show_pair<L, V>(label: L, value: V) -> String
where
    L: Display,
    V: Debug,
{
    format!("{label}: {value:?}")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn counts() {
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&[1, 2, 1, 1], &1), 3);
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&["a", "b"], &"c"), 0);
        let words = vec![String::from("x"), String::from("x")];
        assert_eq!(count_equal(&words, &String::from("x")), 2);
    }

    #[test]
    fn joins() {
        assert_eq!(join_all(&[1, 2, 3], ", "), "1, 2, 3");
        assert_eq!(join_all(&["a"], "-"), "a");
        let empty: [i32; 0] = [];
        assert_eq!(join_all(&empty, "-"), "");
    }

    #[test]
    fn pairs() {
        assert_eq!(show_pair("ids", vec![1, 2]), "ids: [1, 2]");
        assert_eq!(show_pair(5, "five"), "5: \"five\"");
    }
}

WHAT A COMPLETE ANSWER TO THE STAGE ABOVE LOOKS LIKE:
The log: mm_alloc_many returns rc=0 but frames is still 0x0, and the first frames[i] read in capture_burst is a read of address zero (SEGV, zero page). Line 83, out_array = &arr;, assigns to the parameter, its own copy of the caller's address: it now points at the local arr, so frames is never written, and at the return both the copy and arr are gone. It compiles with no warning because both sides are void ***. Pointers: frames (void **) lives in capture_burst and is NULL; out_array (void ***) holds &frames; arr (void **) points at the array block, which holds 4 payload pointers, each pointing at a block. What was needed is *out_array = arr;, which stores arr into frames, so frames[i] is arr[i]; line 83 only moves mm_alloc_many's own arrow, so frames is never written. Cost of the bug: the array block and all 4 payloads stay live with handles bound and nobody can free them, 5 blocks and 5 of 64 handles per burst, and mm.h promises the pointer is written on MM_OK. Fix: *out_array = arr;, and *out_array = NULL at entry so a failure is visible. Line 66 passes (void **)&arr: mm_alloc then stores a void * into arr, an object of type void **. C11 6.5p7 lets an object be accessed only through a compatible type (or a qualified or signed/unsigned variant, none of which relates void * to void **) or a character type, and c-faq 4.9 says there is no generic pointer-to-pointer type in C: it works here because every object pointer has the same representation on this target, but the portable form is void *tmp; mm_alloc(m, n, &tmp); arr = tmp;. The roll-back already uses the right level, &arr[j]. Next bug, not highlighted: release_burst calls mm_free(&g_mm, frames[i]); a void * converts to void ** silently, so mm_free reads the frame's first bytes (0x10, 0x11, ...) as the address to free and crashes; it needs &frames[i].

# Email drafter benchmark: how we evaluate

Care AI team | 25 September 2026 | method behind the design note, Table 1

## Eval set

150 customer emails from the Care queue, received 1 to 14 September 2026, each with a snapshot
of the account data as it was when the email arrived.

- 100 drawn at random from the queue.
- 50 added by hand: emails that care agents flagged in #care-ai-feedback as poor v1 drafts, so
  the set covers the emails that matter most.

| Category | Random | Flagged | Eval set |
|---|---|---|---|
| document_request | 24 | 0 | 24 |
| billing_payment | 21 | 4 | 25 |
| policy_change | 17 | 0 | 17 |
| claim_status | 14 | 0 | 14 |
| cancellation_renewal | 6 | 0 | 6 |
| refund_dispute | 7 | 21 | 28 |
| coverage_question | 11 | 25 | 36 |
| All | 100 | 50 | 150 |

The same 150 emails were our development set for v2: we ran each prompt version from v2.0
(26 Aug) to v2.7 (18 Sep) on them and kept the best, v2.7.

## Systems

- v1: the production agent and prompt as of 18 Sep.
- v2: v2.7, four agents.
- v2 without the reviewer (ablation): v2.7 with the first draft taken as final.

One draft per email per system, at the production temperature (0.7). Runs 22 to 24 Sep.

## Judge

- Model: llm-pro, temperature 0, one call per draft.
- Input: the customer's email thread and the draft. The judge does not see the account data,
  the ledger or the policy wording (keeps the judge fast and cheap).
- Rubric R-3, the same checklist the reviewer agent uses, so the judge and the reviewer agree:

| Criterion | 0 to 20 points for |
|---|---|
| Accuracy | facts and amounts are consistent with the information given |
| Completeness | every question in the email is answered |
| Resolution | the customer gets a clear resolution or next step |
| Tone | warm, empathetic, on brand |
| Policy | nothing is promised outside company policy |

The five scores are summed to a score from 0 to 100. Each draft is scored on its own; v1's
drafts were scored on 23 Sep and v2's on 24 Sep.

## What we report

- The mean judge score per system. v2 is better if its mean is higher.
- No confidence intervals: 150 emails is a good-sized set.
- Mean draft length: v1 159 words, v2 221 words.

## Human check

The Care QA lead read 20 v2 drafts picked at random on 24 Sep. 18 were fine. 2 stated
a wrong amount: E-20122 (a refund amount) and E-20116 (a deductible). The judge scored those
two 88 and 85.

## Cost and latency

Measured in the same runs and reported in the design note, Table 1. Not part of the pass or fail.

The all-up 84.0 vs 77.9 is useful as a headline, but the per-category table is what I’d use to decide rollout: v2 is clearly better on refund_dispute and coverage_question, roughly neutral on billing_payment / policy_change / cancellation_renewal, and a bit worse on document_request.

For the eval method, I’d trust that it’s using a held-out set with per-category counts and latency/cost measurements, but I’d be cautious about the sample sizes in the smaller categories. --- README.md ---
# invoice-extractor

Turns the OCR text of a supplier invoice into the 14-field record that is
posted to the customer's ERP. Owned by the Extraction team (#extraction).

September 2026: 1,180,400 documents, **95.9% straight-through**. The rest go to the
AP exceptions queue, where a reviewer keys the invoice by hand.

## How it works

1. `extractor/prompt.py` builds the prompt from the OCR text.
2. `extractor/llm_client.py` calls llm-medium through llmgw, the internal gateway.
3. `extractor/pipeline.py` strips code fences, salvages output that was cut off,
   and parses the JSON.
4. `extractor/validate.py` checks it against `extractor/schema.py` and the allowed
   payment terms and currencies.
5. A failed attempt is retried (`max_retries` in `config/extractor.yaml`). After
   the last attempt the document goes to the AP exceptions queue with reason
   `schema`.
6. Every document's attempts are written to the trace store (`extractor/trace.py`,
   45 days).

## Develop

    pip install -e '.[dev]'
    pytest -q     # offline: the tests replay recorded completions in tests/fixtures/

## Numbers

    python scripts/weekly_report.py traces/2026-09-*.jsonl

Straight-through = documents posted to the ERP without a person, over all documents.

"""Client for llmgw, the internal model gateway."""
from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Completion:
    text: str
    output_tokens: int
    finish_reason: str             # "stop", or "length" when max_tokens was reached
    refusal: str | None = None     # schema mode only: set when the model declines


class LlmClient:
    def __init__(self, gateway_url: str, model: str, timeout_s: int = 30):
        self.gateway_url = gateway_url
        self.model = model
        self.timeout_s = timeout_s

    def complete(self, prompt: str, max_tokens: int, temperature: float = 0.0,
                 json_mode: bool = False, schema: dict | None = None) -> Completion:
        """One call to llmgw, POST /v1/complete.

        json_mode: the gateway guarantees the text parses as JSON (any JSON, no schema).
        schema:    strict schema mode (constrained decoding): the text matches `schema`,
                   or `refusal` is set and the text is empty.
        With neither, the text is whatever the model writes.
        """
        # TODO(2026-03): llmgw rejected Invoice.model_json_schema() in schema mode
        # (400 schema_unsupported: "object nesting depth 4 exceeds 3"). Revisit.
        import httpx

        body = {"model": self.model, "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": max_tokens,
                "temperature": temperature}
        if json_mode:
            body["response_format"] = {"type": "json"}
        if schema is not None:
            body["response_format"] = {"type": "schema", "schema": schema}

        r = httpx.post(f"{self.gateway_url}/complete", json=body, timeout=self.timeout_s)
        r.raise_for_status()
        out = r.json()
        return Completion(text=out.get("text") or "",
                          output_tokens=out["usage"]["output_tokens"],
                          finish_reason=out["finish_reason"],
                          refusal=out.get("refusal"))

"""Turns the OCR text of one supplier invoice into an Invoice, or hands it to a person."""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import logging
import re
from dataclasses import dataclass

from pydantic import ValidationError

from . import trace
from .exceptions_queue import route_to_exceptions
from .llm_client import LlmClient
from .prompt import build_prompt
from .schema import Invoice
from .settings import Settings
from .validate import InvoiceRejected, validate

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

FENCE = re.compile(r"^```json\s*|\s*```$")


@dataclass
class Doc:
    doc_id: str
    customer_id: str
    lang: str
    pages: int
    line_rows: int          # table rows found by the OCR layout step
    ocr_text: str
    pdf_url: str = ""


@dataclass
class Result:
    doc_id: str
    status: str             # "posted" (sent to the customer's ERP) or "exceptions"
    invoice: Invoice | None
    attempts: list[trace.Attempt]


def _repair_truncated(text: str) -> str:
    """Long invoices sometimes stop in the middle of line_items. Keep everything up
    to the last closing brace and close the array and the object, so the record
    isn't lost; the validator decides whether it is usable (TRK-1902)."""
    cut = text.rfind("}")
    if cut == -1:
        return text
    return text[: cut + 1] + "]}"


def _describe(exc: Exception) -> str:
    if isinstance(exc, ValidationError):
        parts = []
        for e in exc.errors():
            part = ".".join(str(p) for p in e["loc"]) + ": " + e["msg"]
            if not isinstance(e["input"], (dict, list)):
                part += f" (got {e['input']!r})"
            parts.append(part)
        more = f" (+{len(parts) - 4} more)" if len(parts) > 4 else ""
        return "ValidationError: " + "; ".join(parts[:4]) + more
    return f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"


def extract(doc: Doc, client: LlmClient, settings: Settings) -> Result:
    prompt = build_prompt(doc.ocr_text)
    attempts: list[trace.Attempt] = []

    for n in range(1, settings.max_retries + 2):
        temperature = settings.temperature if n == 1 else settings.retry_temperature
        completion = client.complete(prompt, max_tokens=settings.max_tokens,
                                     temperature=temperature)
        text = FENCE.sub("", completion.text.strip())

        repaired = False
        if not text.endswith("}"):
            # the output was cut off: salvage what we have
            fixed = _repair_truncated(text)
            repaired, text = fixed != text, fixed

        try:
            invoice = validate(json.loads(text))
        except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValidationError, InvoiceRejected) as exc:
            error = _describe(exc)
            attempts.append(trace.attempt(n, temperature, completion, repaired, error, settings))
            log.warning("%s attempt %d failed: %s", doc.doc_id, n, error)
            continue  # ask again

        attempts.append(trace.attempt(n, temperature, completion, repaired, None, settings))
        trace.emit(trace.to_line(doc, "posted", attempts))
        return Result(doc.doc_id, "posted", invoice, attempts)

    route_to_exceptions(doc, reason="schema", queue=settings.exceptions_queue)
    trace.emit(trace.to_line(doc, "exceptions", attempts))
    return Result(doc.doc_id, "exceptions", None, attempts)

"""The record we post to the customer's ERP (14 fields)."""
from __future__ import annotations

from datetime import date

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field


class Jurisdiction(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")

    country: str
    region: str | None = None


class TaxDetail(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")

    rate: float
    amount: float
    jurisdiction: Jurisdiction


class LineItem(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")

    description: str
    quantity: float
    unit_price: float
    tax: TaxDetail
    amount: float


class Invoice(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")

--- extractor/settings.py ---
"""Runtime settings, read once from config/extractor.yaml."""
from __future__ import annotations

import pathlib
from dataclasses import dataclass

import yaml

CONFIG = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "config" / "extractor.yaml"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Settings:
    gateway_url: str
    model: str
    max_tokens: int
    temperature: float
    retry_temperature: float
    json_mode: bool
    timeout_s: int
    max_retries: int
    exceptions_queue: str
    raw_head_chars: int
    raw_tail_chars: int


def load(path: pathlib.Path = CONFIG) -> Settings:
    cfg = yaml.safe_load(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    llm, pipe, trace = cfg["llm"], cfg["pipeline"], cfg["trace"]
    return Settings(
        gateway_url=llm["gateway_url"],
        model=llm["model"],
        max_tokens=llm["max_tokens"],
        temperature=llm["temperature"],
        retry_temperature=llm["retry_temperature"],
        json_mode=llm["json_mode"],
        timeout_s=llm["timeout_s"],
        max_retries=pipe["max_retries"],
        exceptions_queue=pipe["exceptions_queue"],
        raw_head_chars=trace["raw_head_chars"],
        raw_tail_chars=trace["raw_tail_chars"],
    )

--- extractor/trace.py ---
"""Attempt traces: one JSON line per document, kept 45 days.

The full model output is not kept (it holds bank details): only its first and last
characters and a hash. The worker flushes SINK to the trace bucket every minute.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass

SINK: list[str] = []


@dataclass
class Attempt:
    n: int
    temperature: float
    output_tokens: int
    repaired: bool
    raw_sha1: str
    error: str | None
    raw_head: str
    raw_tail: str


def attempt(n, temperature, completion, repaired, error, settings) -> Attempt:
    raw = completion.text
    return Attempt(n=n, temperature=temperature, output_tokens=completion.output_tokens,
                   repaired=repaired, raw_sha1=hashlib.sha1(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:10],
                   error=error, raw_head=raw[: settings.raw_head_chars],
                   raw_tail=raw[-settings.raw_tail_chars:])


def to_line(doc, status: str, attempts: list[Attempt]) -> str:
    return json.dumps({"doc_id": doc.doc_id, "customer_id": doc.customer_id, "lang": doc.lang,
                       "pages": doc.pages, "line_rows_ocr": doc.line_rows, "status": status,
                       "attempts": [asdict(a) for a in attempts]}, ensure_ascii=False)


def emit(line: str) -> None:
    SINK.append(line)

--- extractor/validate.py ---
"""Checks a parsed model output before it is posted to the customer's ERP."""
from __future__ import annotations

from .schema import Invoice

PAYMENT_TERMS = {"NET_15", "NET_30", "NET_45", "NET_60", "DUE_ON_RECEIPT"}

# ISO 4217 codes our customers' ERPs accept
CURRENCIES = {"EUR", "GBP", "USD", "CHF", "SEK", "NOK", "DKK", "PLN", "CZK"}


class InvoiceRejected(ValueError):
    """The output parsed and matched the schema, but can't be posted."""


def validate(data: dict) -> Invoice:
    invoice = Invoice.model_validate(data)  # raises pydantic.ValidationError

    problems = []
    if invoice.payment_terms not in PAYMENT_TERMS:
        problems.append(f"payment_terms: {invoice.payment_terms!r} is not an allowed value")
    if invoice.currency not in CURRENCIES:
        problems.append(f"currency: {invoice.currency!r} is not an allowed value")
    # TODO: totals check (line items vs subtotal, subtotal + tax_total vs total_amount)

    if problems:
        raise InvoiceRejected("; ".join(problems))
    return invoice
